Corey Dopp

IT Client Support Services Associate

IQSS Staff Member.

item.title: Courtney Hayes
item.description:
Courtney Hayes

Feature Writer

Courtney Hayes is an award-winning writer and documentary filmmaker who started her career at PBS’ Frontline. She has written and produced documentaries for The History Channel, Discovery, and Curiosity Stream, and created digital stories for leading brands. She currently writes interview-based feature articles for IQSS.

item.title: Craig Marris
item.description:
Craig Marris

Executive Affiliate, Startup Foundry; SeeDigital.ai

Craig Marris is an Executive Affiliate at IQSS, where he mentors startups developing applied AI and data science solutions with societal impact. He is the co-founder and Co-CEO of SeeDigital.ai, a company using AI-powered CCTV analytics and agentic automation to elevate workplace safety and operational compliance. Craig is also the co-founder of Coretex, a global telematics and compliance platform that he helped scale from inception to its successful $188 million acquisition by EROAD. With senior executive experience spanning technology, sustainability, transportation, and AI-enabled operations, he brings strategic insight and hands-on leadership to innovators navigating the intersection of data science and real-world problem-solving.

item.title: Crhistian Gonzalez-Cuatianquis
item.description:
Crhistian Gonzalez-Cuatianquis

GIS Research Fellow, CGA

Crhistian Joel Gonzalez-Cuatianquis is a PhD candidate in Regional Science and Economic Geography at GSSI, with an economics background. He previously worked at Mexico’s CONEVAL, coordinating research on social rights, evaluations, and subnational social development policies.

His research focuses on the determinants of regional inequalities and their relationship with subjective well-being, educational aspirations, and perceptions of territorial and personal left-behindness. He uses microdata with econometric and spatial analysis to study how socioeconomic and territorial contexts shape individual perceptions and social outcomes, with applications in Europe and Latin America.

item.title: Crime and Police Reform In America—Does Politics Matter?
item.description:
by Courtney Hayes

On May 25, 2020, a Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd by kneeling on his neck for almost 10 minutes. Floyd’s death sparked the largest mass protest movement in U.S. history and a national reckoning on race and police reform.

In the fall of 2020, pressure to act was intensifying. Protestors called for radical reform while crime rates spiked. Between 2019 and 2020, the U.S. murder rate rose 30%—the largest single-year increase in more than a century. As election season approached, former President Donald Trump began blaming Democratic mayors.

item.title: Crunching Data on American Elections: The CCES
item.description:
Since 2006, Stephen Ansolabehere has been compiling data about who votes in America and why as principal investigator for the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES, now the Cooperative Election Study). Supported by IQSS, the study has become one of the most important resources for understanding American electoral behavior.

The CCES surveys tens of thousands of Americans before and after each election, gathering detailed information about their political attitudes, demographic characteristics, and voting behavior. This massive sample size enables researchers to analyze political dynamics at the state and congressional district level—something impossible with smaller surveys.

item.title: Cynthia Dwork
item.description:
Cynthia Dwork

Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science

Cynthia Dwork “uses theoretical computer science to place societal problems on a firm mathematical foundation.” She received the Edsger W. Dijkstra Prize in 2007 for her earliest work establishing the foundations on which fault tolerant systems have been built for a generation (Dwork, Lynch, and Stockmeyer, 1984).

Her cryptography contributions include launching non-malleable cryptography, which studies and remedies failures of cryptographic protocols to compose securely (Dolev, Dwork, and Naor, 1991). She co-invented “the first public-key cryptosystem based on lattices,” considered the best current candidate for cryptographic constructions resistant to quantum computers (Ajtai and Dwork, 1997). More recently, she led efforts to establish a mathematical foundation for privacy-preserving data analysis. Central to this work is the invention of Differential Privacy (Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, and Smith, 2006, Dwork 2006), which has generated intense cross-disciplinary activity and received the Theory of Cryptography Conference 2016 Test-of-Time award. With its adoption in Apple’s iOS 10 (2016) and Google’s Chrome browser (2014), differential privacy began global-scale deployment.

item.title: Cynthia Dwork wins Knuth Prize
item.description:
IQSS faculty affiliate Cynthia Dwork, Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science, received the 2020 Donald E. Knuth Prize from SIGACT for her impactful work in the foundations of computer science. The prize recognizes sustained excellence in theoretical computer science research over an entire career.

Dwork is best known as the inventor of differential privacy, a mathematical framework that enables statistical analysis of databases while provably protecting individual privacy. This work has had enormous practical impact, with differential privacy now deployed by the U.S. Census Bureau, Apple, Google, and other major organizations.

item.title: Dan Carpenter
item.description:
Dan Carpenter

Allie S. Freed Professor of Government & Chair of the Department of Government, Harvard University

Daniel Carpenter’s research spans political institutions, North American political history, political economy of government regulation, bureaucratic politics and organization, stochastic models of behavioral and bounded rationality, and media behavior and agenda setting.

His major ongoing project is the FDA Project — a large-scale theoretical, historical and statistical analysis of pharmaceutical regulation in the United States.

item.title: Dan Levy
item.description:
Dan Levy

Senior Lecturer in Public Policy

Senior Lecturer in Public Policy and Faculty Chair of the Kennedy School’s SLATE (Strengthening Learning and Teaching Excellence) Initiative, teaches courses in quantitative methods and program evaluation. He recently directed impact evaluations of girl-friendly school construction programs in Burkina Faso and Niger. He was involved in the evaluation of a conditional cash transfer program in Jamaica, a technical assistance project to Mexico’s Social Development Ministry (Sedesol), the evaluation of an after-school program in the U.S., and a methodological review of studies comparing the use of various methods to estimate program impacts. He has served as a senior researcher at Mathematica Policy Research, a faculty affiliate at the Poverty Action Lab (MIT), and as consultant to several organizations including the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, and the Global Development Network (GDN). He received his Ph.D. in Economics from Northwestern University, grew up in Venezuela, and is fluent in Spanish and French.

item.title: Dani Rodrik
item.description:
Dani Rodrik

Ford Foundation Professor of International Political Economy

Dani Rodrik is Ford Foundation Professor of International Political Economy at the Harvard Kennedy School. He has published widely in the areas of economic development, international economics, and political economy. His current research focuses on inclusive economic growth, in both developing and advanced economies. He is the recipient of numerous awards, including the inaugural Albert O. Hirschman Prize of the Social Science Research Council and the Princess of Asturias Award for Social Sciences. Professor Rodrik is co-director of the Reimagining the Economy Program at the Kennedy School and of the Economics for Inclusive Prosperity network. He was President of the International Economic Association during 2021-23 and helped found the IEA’s Women in Leadership in Economics (IEA-WE) initiative. His most recent book is Shared Prosperity in a Fractured World: A New Economics for the Middle Class, the Global Poor, and Our Climate (2025, forthcoming). His previous books include Straight Talk on Trade: Ideas for a Sane World Economy (2017), Economics Rules: The Rights and Wrongs of the Dismal Science (2015), The Globalization Paradox: Democracy and the Future of the World Economy (2011), and One Economics, Many Recipes: Globalization, Institutions, and Economic Growth (2007).

item.title: Daniel Gilbert
item.description:
Daniel Gilbert

Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology

Daniel Gilbert is the Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at Harvard University. He has won numerous awards for his research and teaching, including the American Psychological Association’s Distinguished Scientific Award for an Early Career Contribution to Psychology. In 2008 he was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

His 2007 book “Stumbling on Happiness” spent six months on the New York Times bestseller list, has been translated into 30 languages, has sold a million copies worldwide, and received the Royal Society’s General Book Prize for best science book of the year.

item.title: Daniel Koretz
item.description:
Daniel Koretz

Research Professor on Education

Daniel Koretz is an expert on educational assessment and testing policy. His work has primarily focused on the impact of high-stakes testing. His research has included studies of score inflation, effects of testing programs on educational practice, assessment of students with disabilities, international differences in the variability of student achievement, application of value-added models to educational achievement, and development of methods for validating scores under high-stakes conditions. His current work focuses on “the equity implications of high-stakes testing, the effects of high-stakes testing on postsecondary outcomes,” characteristics of traditional tests that encourage inappropriate test preparation, and the design and evaluation of new testing designs tailored for accountability. He is a member of the National Academy of Education and a Fellow of the American Educational Research Association. His doctorate is in developmental psychology from Cornell University. Before obtaining his degree, he “taught emotionally disturbed students in public elementary and junior high schools.”

item.title: Daniel M Smith
item.description:
Daniel M Smith

Associate Professor of Government

Daniel M. Smith is Associate Professor of Government at Harvard University. His research focuses on “electoral and legislative institutions, party organization, and voter behavior in Japan and Western Europe.”

item.title: Daniel Ziblatt
item.description:
Daniel Ziblatt

Eaton Professor of the Science of Government

Daniel Ziblatt is Eaton Professor of the Science of Government at Harvard University and resident faculty at the Minda de Gunzburg Center for European Studies (CES). His research and teaching interests include democratization, state-building, comparative politics, and historical political economy, with a particular interest in European political development.

His latest book How Democracies Die (co-authored with Steven Levitsky) was on the New York Times bestseller list and has been translated into 22 languages. His second book Conservative Parties and the Birth of Democracy (2017) offers a new interpretation of the historical democratization of Europe, drawing lessons for new and old democracies under siege today. His book Structuring the State: The Formation of Italy and Germany and the Puzzle of Federalism (2006) draws lessons from nineteenth century experiences of state-building in Italy and Germany.

item.title: Dara Kay Cohen
item.description:
Dara Kay Cohen

Professor of Public Policy, HKS

Dara Kay Cohen is Professor of Public Policy at the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University. Her research and teaching interests “span the field of international relations, including international security, civil war and the dynamics of violence, and gender and conflict.” Her first book, Rape During Civil War (Cornell University Press, 2016), examines variation in the use of rape during recent civil conflicts, drawing on “extensive fieldwork in Sierra Leone, Timor-Leste and El Salvador.” Her second book, Lynching and Local Justice: Legitimacy and Accountability in Weak States, was published in 2020 with Cambridge University Press, coauthored with Danielle F. Jung, and draws on “original survey and focus group data collected during fieldwork in Port-au-Prince, Haiti.”

item.title: Data Highway: A Trailblazing Journey into Trucking
item.description:
by Courtney Hayes

As highways become a new digital landscape where every truck serves as a node and every delivery a connection, a Harvard PhD-turned-entrepreneur is helping build tomorrow’s transportation infrastructure. IQSS affiliate Jinyan Zang, founder and COO of Axle, has created a data platform that seeks to transform trucking logistics.

The trucking industry today is massive. With almost four million tractor-trailers on US highways, trucking accounts for over 70% of the nation’s freight. The internet now connects every truck in the United States with the potential to track fuel levels, speed, location, and more. But the industry is highly fragmented, with thousands of brokers and dispatchers working around the clock to manage siloed data streams. As a result, up to 30% of all vehicles are driving empty. Zang notes: “That’s burning a ton of diesel without actually doing any work. That’s money out of the driver’s and shipper’s pocket.”

item.title: Data Science Services
item.description:
Advisory Services

Consulting

We provide short-term support (up to 3 hours per publication) in the form of advice.

Collaboration

We provide extended support over the lifecycle of a research project by embedding a data science specialist in your research team.

Analytical Tool Building

We can develop R code to implement your new statistical method or to automate part of your analysis pipeline.

Training Services

  • Workshop Materials — Self-contained workshops in Python, R, Stata, and more
  • Tutorials — Step-by-step guides for LaTeX, Git, causal inference, web scraping, and more
  • Related Resources — Additional data science resources across IQSS and Harvard University

Impact

  • Research Output — Publications and dissertations supported by Data Science Services

Our Team

Steven Worthington

Director of Data Science Services. At IQSS since 2011. PhD in Biological Anthropology from NYU.

item.title: Data Science Services at IQSS: Harnessing Data Interpretation for Academic Advancement
item.description:
IQSS Data Science Services (DSS) provides research support to the Harvard community through consulting, collaboration, and analytical tool building. The team of PhD data science specialists assists researchers at every stage of the research process, from study design through publication.

The article profiles how academic research cycles follow systematic stages—from formulating research questions through data collection, analysis, and dissemination—and how DSS provides tailored support at each phase. Whether researchers need short-term advice on statistical methods or long-term collaborative partnerships, DSS adapts its services accordingly.

item.title: Data Science Students Visit FTC with Latanya Sweeney
item.description:
Professor Latanya Sweeney traveled with IQSS staff to share her students’ work with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission. As director of the Data Privacy Lab at IQSS, Sweeney has long focused on the intersection of technology, privacy, and public policy.

The visit gave students a rare opportunity to present their research findings directly to federal regulators responsible for protecting consumers from unfair or deceptive practices in the digital marketplace. Projects presented addressed real-world privacy vulnerabilities in commercial technologies and proposed evidence-based policy solutions.

item.title: DataFest 2020 Gathers Researchers
item.description:
DataFest 2020 brought together researchers from across Harvard and beyond for an intensive two-day series of workshops and presentations focused on analyzing, visualizing, and managing data in the modern research environment. This annual event, organized by IQSS, provides graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and faculty with concentrated exposure to cutting-edge data science methods, tools, and best practices that enhance their research capabilities.

The 2020 program featured sessions covering the full lifecycle of data-intensive research, from data collection and cleaning through exploratory analysis, statistical modeling, visualization, and reproducible research workflows. Expert instructors demonstrated contemporary tools and techniques including programming in R and Python, version control with Git, effective data visualization principles, and approaches to managing complex datasets. The intensive format allowed participants to gain hands-on experience with new methods while connecting with peers facing similar methodological challenges across diverse research domains.

item.title: Dataverse 6.0 has arrived!
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is excited to announce the arrival of version 6.0, a major milestone release that brings comprehensive platform upgrades to ensure the software runs on modern, well-supported infrastructure components. This significant update includes upgrades to Payara application server, Solr search engine, and Java runtime environment, positioning Dataverse repositories on a solid foundation for continued growth and development.

The infrastructure upgrades in version 6.0 provide critical improvements to security, performance, and long-term maintainability. Moving to current versions of Payara, Solr, and Java ensures that Dataverse installations benefit from the latest bug fixes, security patches, and performance optimizations available in these core technologies. These platform updates also enable future feature development by providing access to modern capabilities and APIs that weren’t available in older versions. While platform upgrades require careful planning and testing, they are essential for maintaining a healthy, sustainable software ecosystem.

item.title: Dataverse 6.1 is Here
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is pleased to announce the release of version 6.1, the first feature release following the major 6.0 platform upgrade. This release showcases the strength of community-driven development, with significant contributions from institutions and developers across the global Dataverse network who are collectively shaping the future of open-source research data infrastructure.

Version 6.1 builds on the solid foundation established in 6.0, introducing new features and enhancements that improve functionality for researchers and repository administrators. Community contributions in this release span a wide range of improvements, from user interface refinements and workflow optimizations to new API capabilities and administrative tools. These collaborative efforts demonstrate how the open-source model enables institutions to pool expertise and resources, creating solutions that benefit the entire ecosystem rather than individual repositories in isolation.

item.title: Dataverse 6.2 is now available
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is excited to announce that version 6.2 is now available, bringing a valuable collection of updates and new features that enhance the platform’s capabilities for managing and sharing research data. This release continues the steady evolution of the 6.x series, delivering improvements that respond to community feedback and emerging needs in the research data management landscape.

Version 6.2 introduces features that improve both the researcher experience and administrative functionality. Enhanced data management tools make it easier to organize collections and apply appropriate access controls, while improvements to metadata handling support more comprehensive documentation of research outputs. New capabilities for data visualization and preview help users understand dataset contents more effectively, promoting data reuse and discovery. Administrative enhancements provide repository managers with better tools for monitoring system health, managing user permissions, and configuring repository behavior to meet institutional requirements.

item.title: Dataverse 6.5 is here!
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is pleased to announce the release of version 6.5, bringing a robust set of new features, enhancements, and bug fixes to the world’s most widely adopted open-source research data repository platform. This release reflects months of collaborative development by contributors from institutions around the globe, continuing Dataverse’s evolution as an essential infrastructure for research data management and sharing.

Version 6.5 introduces several user-requested features that improve both the researcher and administrator experience. New capabilities enhance metadata management, search functionality, and data visualization tools, making it easier for researchers to discover, access, and understand datasets. Performance optimizations ensure that repositories can handle growing collections efficiently, while security enhancements protect sensitive research data. The release also includes improvements to external tool integrations, expanding the ways researchers can analyze and work with their data directly from the Dataverse interface.

item.title: Dataverse Joins NIH in Increasing Access to Biomedical Data
item.description: The Dataverse Project has joined a major National Institutes of Health data curation initiative aimed at increasing access to biomedical data and supporting the NIH’s commitment to open science and data sharing. This partnership positions Dataverse as a key infrastructure component in the NIH’s strategy to ensure that federally funded biomedical research data is preserved, accessible, and reusable by the scientific community, accelerating the pace of discovery and maximizing the return on research investment.

item.title: Dataverse Office Hours
item.description:
Dataverse Office Hours

Date: Recurring weekly on Wednesdays

Time: 11:00 AM – 1:00 PM EDT

Location: 1737 Cambridge Street, CGIS Knafel Building, Room K350

Open to Harvard researchers and staff for Dataverse platform support. Demo of the current version of Dataverse will begin promptly at 11am. RSVP required to support@dataverse.org.

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Dataverse Publishes Houghton Library SAEF Data Collection
item.description: The Harvard Dataverse has published a significant new collection from Houghton Library: the Slavery, Abolition, Emancipation, and Freedom (SAEF) Data Collection, making valuable historical research data freely available to scholars worldwide. This collection brings together data related to one of the most consequential periods in American history, documenting the experiences of enslaved people, the abolition movement, emancipation processes, and the struggle for freedom and civil rights in the nineteenth century.

item.title: Dataverse Software 5.11.1 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project has announced the release of version 5.11.1, a maintenance update focused on addressing critical bugs and improving system stability. This patch release is part of the Dataverse team’s commitment to providing reliable, production-ready software for research data repositories around the world.

Version 5.11.1 includes important fixes that enhance the overall performance and user experience of the platform. These improvements address issues reported by the global Dataverse community, ensuring that repositories can continue to operate smoothly and researchers can access and share their data without interruption. The release demonstrates the responsive nature of the open-source development process, where community feedback directly shapes software improvements.

item.title: Dataverse Software 5.12 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is pleased to announce the release of version 5.12, delivering a comprehensive set of new features, enhancements, and bug fixes that improve the research data repository experience for both users and administrators. This release continues the project’s commitment to regular, high-quality updates that respond to the needs of the global Dataverse community.

Version 5.12 introduces several highly requested features that enhance data discovery, access management, and metadata handling. Improvements to the user interface make common workflows more intuitive, while new administrative tools give repository managers better control over their collections and improved insight into repository usage. Enhanced API capabilities expand integration possibilities with other research tools and institutional systems, supporting more seamless data management workflows across the research lifecycle.

item.title: Dataverse Software 5.14 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project announces the release of version 5.14, bringing an extensive collection of new features, enhancements, and bug fixes that strengthen the platform’s capabilities as a comprehensive research data repository solution. This release reflects ongoing collaboration among developers, repository administrators, and researchers worldwide who contribute to making Dataverse more powerful and user-friendly.

Version 5.14 introduces meaningful improvements across multiple areas of the platform. Enhanced metadata management features provide researchers with more flexible ways to describe their datasets, improving discoverability and promoting best practices in data documentation. New visualization and preview capabilities make it easier for users to understand dataset contents before downloading, while improved access controls give data owners more granular options for managing who can view and use their research outputs. API enhancements expand programmatic access to repository functions, supporting automation and integration with institutional research infrastructure.

item.title: Dataverse Software 6.10 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project has announced the release of version 6.10 of the Dataverse software, bringing significant improvements to the world’s most widely adopted open-source research data repository platform. This latest release includes enhanced export capabilities, new application programming interfaces (APIs), infrastructure and performance updates, and numerous bug fixes that improve stability and user experience for repositories worldwide.

The export improvements in version 6.10 make it easier for researchers to extract their data and metadata in various formats, supporting interoperability with other research tools and platforms. New APIs expand the programmatic capabilities available to developers and repository administrators, enabling more sophisticated integrations and automation workflows. Infrastructure and performance enhancements ensure that Dataverse continues to scale effectively as datasets grow larger and repository usage increases.

item.title: Dataverse Software 6.4 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is pleased to announce the release of version 6.4, continuing the momentum of the 6.x series with important bug fixes and new features that enhance the platform’s functionality and reliability. This release demonstrates the project’s ongoing commitment to responsive development that addresses community needs while maintaining the stability required for production research data repositories.

Version 6.4 introduces several valuable features that improve the user experience and expand administrative capabilities. Enhancements to data upload and download workflows make it easier for researchers to deposit and retrieve their datasets, while improvements to metadata handling support more comprehensive data documentation. New administrative tools provide repository managers with better oversight and control, and enhanced monitoring capabilities help identify and resolve issues proactively. The release also includes updates to external tool integrations, enabling researchers to connect their data with analysis platforms and visualization tools.

item.title: Dataverse Software 6.6 Release
item.description:
The Dataverse Project announces the release of version 6.6, delivering important bug fixes and new features that continue to advance the platform’s capabilities as the world’s most widely adopted open-source research data repository software. This release reflects the collaborative efforts of the global Dataverse community, combining contributions from developers at institutions worldwide to improve functionality, stability, and user experience.

Version 6.6 introduces features that enhance both researcher and administrator workflows. Improvements to data management capabilities make it easier to organize, describe, and share research datasets according to community standards and funder requirements. Enhanced search and discovery features help users find relevant data more efficiently, while new APIs and integration points support more sophisticated connections with institutional systems and research tools. Administrative enhancements provide repository managers with improved monitoring, reporting, and configuration options to tailor their Dataverse installations to local needs.

item.title: Dataverse Training
item.description:
Dataverse Training Events

Better Research VI: Data Sharing with Harvard Dataverse

Learn about Harvard Dataverse for data sharing and preservation; explore how the repository supports research projects and data sharing needs.

Hands-On Curation Training with Harvard Dataverse Repository

Explore the latest Dataverse features. Hands-on training guiding users in using the Dataverse platform to create their personalized collection.

Introduction to Metadata in Dataverse Repositories

Learn how Dataverse helps installation administrators customize metadata for their repositories.

item.title: Dave Wang
item.description:
Dave Wang

AI Research Fellow; Co-Founder, 99 Capital

Dave is the co-founder of 99 Capital, a venture fund investing in frontier technology and markets. Before that, he led technical investments across blockchain & fintech for SoftBank’s $5B Latin America Fund. He has deep research interests in AI / ML applications particularly in binary outcome events like survey markets, where he is working with Prof. Chase Harrison on research at the IQSS in this area. Dave earned his BA in Statistics from Harvard, Cum Laude with a thesis on AI / ML applications on predictive survey methodology.

item.title: David C. Parkes
item.description:
David C. Parkes

George F. Colony Professor of Computer Science

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: David Cutler
item.description:
David Cutler

Otto Eckstein Professor of Applied Economics

David Cutler has built a notable career spanning academia and public service. He “served as Assistant Professor of Economics from 1991 to 1995” and “was named John L. Loeb Associate Professor of Social Sciences in 1995,” receiving tenure in 1997. He currently holds the position of Otto Eckstein Professor of Applied Economics in the Department of Economics and Kennedy School of Government, and he completed a five-year term as associate dean of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences for Social Sciences.

item.title: David Laibson
item.description:
David Laibson

Robert I. Goldman Professor of Economics

David Laibson is the Robert I. Goldman Professor of Economics and Chairman of the Department of Economics at Harvard University. He leads Harvard University’s Foundations of Human Behavior Initiative. His research focuses on behavioral economics, with emphasis on household finance, macroeconomics, aging, and intertemporal choice. He is a member of the National Bureau of Economic Research, where he co-directs the National Institute of Aging Roybal Center for Behavior Change in Health and Savings, and is a Research Associate in the Aging, Asset Pricing, and Economic Fluctuations Working Groups. He serves on the Board of the Russell Sage Foundation and on Harvard’s Pension Investment Committee. He serves on the advisory board of the Social Science Genetics Association Consortium and has served on the Academic Research Council of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Laibson is a recipient of a Marshall Scholarship. He is a Fellow of the Econometric Society and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He received the TIAA-CREF Paul A. Samuelson Award for Outstanding Scholarly Writing on Lifelong Financial Security. He holds degrees from Harvard University (AB in Economics, Summa), the London School of Economics (MSc in Econometrics and Mathematical Economics), and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (PhD in Economics). He received his PhD in 1994 and has taught at Harvard since then. In recognition of his teaching, he has been awarded Harvard’s ΦΒΚ Prize and a Harvard College Professorship.

item.title: David Lazer
item.description:
David Lazer

IQSS Associate; University Distinguished Professor, Northeastern University

Most of Lazer’s work is based on the idea that how people and organizations are connected together is critical to understanding the functioning, success and failure of actors and systems. Lazer’s teaching and institution building have all centered on that theme. He has taken that essential idea and, with a variety of collaborators, examined a wide array of domains. His research covers everything from very micro social influence processes within groups, to the very macro the development of global-wide regulatory regimes. Thus, for example, he has looked at how a network of trade treaties abruptly emerged in the Europe of the 1860s, how attitudes and social structures co-evolve, and, in more recent work how the pattern of relationships affects how hard people work on teams, and how small world networks can result in system-wide ‘group think.’

item.title: David Pedulla
item.description:
David Pedulla

Professor, Department of Sociology

David Pedulla is Professor of Sociology at Harvard University. His research examines “the consequences of nonstandard, contingent, and precarious employment for workers’ social and economic outcomes” and processes leading to race and gender labor market stratification. His work has appeared in American Sociological Review, American Journal of Sociology, Social Forces, and other journals, with support from the National Science Foundation, the Russell Sage Foundation, and the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. He previously served on the faculty of Stanford University and the University of Texas at Austin, and “received his Ph.D. in Sociology and Social Policy from Princeton University.”

item.title: David Y Yang
item.description:
David Y Yang

Assistant Professor of Economics

David Yang’s research focuses on “political economy, behavioral and experimental economics, economic history, and cultural economics.” He studies “the forces of stability and forces of changes in authoritarian regimes,” drawing from historical and contemporary China. He earned a B.A. in Statistics and B.S. in Business Administration from UC Berkeley, and a PhD in Economics from Stanford.

item.title: Debi Kleiman
item.description:
Debi Kleiman

Director, IQSS Startup Foundry

Email: dkleiman@iq.harvard.edu

Debi Kleiman leads the IQSS Startup Foundry at Harvard, where she catalyzes faculty-led innovation and commercialization across the University.

Her distinguished career includes leadership roles at Harvard Business School’s D^3 Startup Foundry and The Players Impact, where she directed an accelerator for elite athlete entrepreneurs, and as Managing Partner and founder of The Upside Angels. Prior to Harvard, Debi served as Executive Director of Babson College’s Blank Center for Entrepreneurship while also teaching entrepreneurship as an adjunct professor.

item.title: Deborah Hurley
item.description:
Deborah Hurley

Fellow, IQSS

Deborah Hurley is the Principal of the consulting firm she founded in 1996, which advises governments, international organizations, companies, Non-governmental organizations, and foundations on advanced science and technology policy. She is a Fellow of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science at Harvard University and directed the Harvard University Information Infrastructure Project. At the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), in Paris, France, she identified emerging legal, economic, social and technological issues related to information and communications technologies, biotechnology, environmental and energy technologies, nanotechnology, technology policy, and other advanced technology fields. Hurley was responsible for drafting, negotiation and adoption of the OECD Guidelines for the Security of Information Systems. She also initiated the OECD activities on cryptography technologies and policy in the early 1990s. Prior to joining the OECD, she practiced computer and intellectual property law in the United States.

item.title: Dev Patel
item.description:
Dev Patel

Prize Fellow in Economics, History, and Politics

Dev Patel is a development economist focusing on the environment, education, and gender.

item.title: Devika Jain
item.description:
Devika Jain

GIS Data Science Manager

At CGA, Devika Jain leads initiatives in GeoAI, Spatial Data Science and Big Data using High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Cloud Computing. She has led the development of impactful solutions, including TSGI (a UN-recognized spatial well-being metric), RINX- a transformative tool for the handling of raster big data, and a novel K-NN method enabling the first individual-level analysis of partisan segregation in USA. She has also led the development of university-wide Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) at Harvard.

item.title: Digitized Canon: Intisar Rabb on SHARIAsource
item.description:
Professor Intisar Rabb’s career as a legal scholar began during a joint program at Yale Law School and Princeton, focusing on comparative issues in Islamic law. At Harvard, she has developed SHARIAsource—a digital platform that makes primary sources of Islamic legal tradition accessible to researchers worldwide.

SHARIAsource represents an ambitious effort to digitize and organize centuries of Islamic legal texts, judicial opinions, and scholarly commentary, creating a searchable database that can support comparative legal research. The project leverages IQSS’s data infrastructure and computational resources.

item.title: Dissertation Awards
item.description:
The Henry A. Murray Research Archive offers the Jeanne Humphrey Block Dissertation Award to a qualified Ph.D. candidate in the social sciences each spring.

Key Details
Eligibility Harvard PhD candidate (3rd year or above) in the social sciences, not graduating this year
Amount $2,500
Deadline Currently on hold

How to Apply

Submit via CARAT. Applicants must submit:

  1. An abstract/description of the project (maximum 2 pages), identifying which study will be used and significance to the social sciences
  2. Letter of recommendation from dissertation advisor
  3. CV/Resume
  4. Project budget

Requirements for Recipients

  • Recipient must archive final data and dissertation on the Harvard Dataverse Repository
  • Awardee will submit monthly updates on grant progress and confirm when resulting research project has been deposited

Decision Criteria

Award decisions are based on:

item.title: Dominic Skinnion
item.description:
Dominic Skinnion

Affiliate; PhD student, MIT

Dom is interested in political science methodology, survey research, and American politics. Prior to his work at IQSS as a Quantitative Social Science Researcher, Dom worked as a research assistant during undergrad under Professor Gary King and Professor Chase Harrison. He also served as a course assistant for GOV50: Data, under Professor Suzanna Linn and Professor Matthew Blackwell.

item.title: Donald Rubin
item.description:
Donald Rubin

John L. Loeb Professor of Statistics, Emeritus

Professor Rubin’s research interests include “causal inference in experiments and observational studies, inference in sample surveys with nonresponse and in missing data problems,” application of Bayesian and empirical Bayesian techniques, and developing and applying statistical models to data across various scientific disciplines.

He holds the title of John L. Loeb Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, in the Department of Statistics at Harvard University. He is affiliated with the Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS) as Affiliated Faculty.

item.title: Dorota Weziak-Bialowolska
item.description:
Dorota Weziak-Bialowolska

Associate of IQSS; Assoc Professor, Jagiellonian University

Dorota Weziak-Bialowolska is a faculty affiliate at Human Flourishing Program at the Institute for Quantitative Social Science and an associate professor at the Centre for Evaluation and Analysis of Public Policies at the Jagiellonian University. She received her master’s degree in quantitative methods (2003), her doctoral degree in economics (2008) and post-doctoral degree (habilitation) in sociology (2016). Her research interests are in methodology including impact assessment and evaluation as well as psychometrics, composite scales, and indicators. Her recent focus is on determinants of positive health and human flourishing.

item.title: Douglas Richardson Awarded Lifetime Achievement Honors
item.description:
Douglas Richardson, Distinguished Researcher at Harvard’s Center for Geographic Analysis (CGA), received Lifetime Achievement Honors from the American Association of Geographers. The award recognizes his decades of contributions to geographic information science and its applications.

Richardson has been instrumental in advancing the use of GIS technology in academic research, working to make geospatial tools accessible to scholars across disciplines. His work at CGA has helped establish Harvard as a leader in geographic analysis and spatial data infrastructure.

item.title: Drew Johnston
item.description:
Drew Johnston

Research Associate, Opportunity Insights

Drew Johnston is a Research Associate at Opportunity Insights. His research interests span “urban economics, labor economics, and political economy.” He is particularly focused on how social networks interact with these fields and on leveraging new data sources to address questions in these areas.

item.title: Dritan Nesho
item.description:
Dritan Nesho

Fellow, IQSS; Director, Microsoft Corporation

Dritan Nesho is a business executive and entrepreneur with experience in corporate strategy, market research, product development, technology, media, and public policy.

He currently serves as Director of Civic Technology and Engagement at Microsoft Corporation, where he co-founded and oversees Microsoft Pulse, a real-time audience and consumer research platform. He is also a co-director of the Harvard-Harris Poll, conducted by the Harvard Center for American Political Studies (CAPS) and The Harris Poll.

item.title: DSM recognizes moral injury, thanks to Human Flourishing Program research
item.description:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, frontline physicians, nurses, and first responders faced impossible choices—who would receive a ventilator, whether to keep working without adequate protection, and how to protect their families while serving the public. In those moments, moral injury, a phenomenon once linked primarily to the military, became an everyday reality in healthcare.

Recognizing this urgent need, the Human Flourishing Program at IQSS, directed by Dr. Tyler VanderWeele, launched a global initiative to advance research and equip leaders across healthcare, military, and first responder sectors with tools for identifying moral injury and promoting healing. Moral injury occurs when individuals in high-stakes roles must navigate wrenching ethical dilemmas where no option feels right, leaving lasting scars on conscience and well-being. The consequences include persistent anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, substance use, and an erosion of trust and meaning.

item.title: Dustin Tingley
item.description:
Dustin Tingley

Professor of Government

Dustin Tingley is Professor of Government in the Government Department at Harvard University. Dustin is Deputy Vice Provost for Advances in Learning. His research has spanned international relations, international political economy, climate change, causal inference, data science/machine learning, and digital education, with most focus now on the politics of climate change and energy transitions.

His book on American foreign policy with Helen Milner, Sailing the Water’s Edge, was published in fall 2015, and was awarded the Gladys M. Kammerer Award for the best book published in the field of U.S. national policy.

item.title: Dylan Carlson Sirvent Leon
item.description:
Dylan Carlson Sirvent Leon

Pre-Doctoral Fellow, IQSS

Dylan is a member of the Strengthening Communities cluster, “an interdisciplinary group researching energy transition politics at the local level.” He graduated from Yale with a BA in Political Science, writing his senior thesis on the congressional politics of climate change.

item.title: Edward Glaeser
item.description:
Edward Glaeser

Fred and Eleanor Glimp Professor of Economics

Edward Glaeser is the Fred and Eleanor Glimp Professor of Economics in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences at Harvard University, where he has been teaching since 1992. He “regularly teaches microeconomic theory, and occasionally urban and public economics.” He has published extensively on “cities, economic growth, and law and economics,” with his work particularly focusing on “the determinants of city growth and the role of cities as centers of idea transmission.” He earned his PhD from the University of Chicago in 1992.

item.title: Eileen McNeely
item.description:
Eileen McNeely

Executive Director, SHINE, Human Flourishing Program

Dr. McNeely founded SHINE (Sustainability and Health Initiative for Netpositive Enterprise) to explore how “work can be a platform for societal flourishing and business can be a force for good.” SHINE’s research spans organizational and behavioral psychology, public health, epidemiology, sociology, business economics and ethics, data science, and social policy. The program partners with academics, businesses, unions, and non-profits to foster mutual learning about real-world challenges and solutions.

item.title: Elhanan Helpman
item.description:
Elhanan Helpman

Galen L. Stone Professor of International Trade

Elhanan Helpman holds the Galen L. Stone Professorship of International Trade at Harvard University and is a Fellow of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research. He earned his B.A. in Economics and Statistics and M.A. in Economics from Tel Aviv University, and his Ph.D. in Economics from Harvard.

His contributions span balance of payments, exchange rate regimes, stabilization programs, and foreign debt. His most significant work covers international trade, economic growth, and political economy. He is “a cofounder of the ’new trade theory’ and the ’new growth theory,’” which highlight economies of scale and imperfect competition. His work is summarized in seven books, co-authored with Paul Krugman and Gene Grossman, as well as solo volumes including The Mystery of Economic Growth and Understanding Global Trade.

item.title: Eli Ben-Michael
item.description:
Eli Ben-Michael

Post-Doctoral Fellow; Asst Prof, Carnegie Mellon

Eli is an assistant professor in the Department of Statistics & Data Science and the Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on “developing statistical and computational methods to solve practical issues in public policy and social science research.” He is particularly interested in “bringing together ideas from statistics, optimization, and machine learning” to create methods for credible and robust causal inference and data-driven decision making.

item.title: Elizabeth Jackson
item.description:
Elizabeth Jackson

Executive Director of IQSS

Email: ejackson@iq.harvard.edu

Elizabeth Jackson is the Executive Director of IQSS. Elizabeth joined IQSS in July 2022 from both Greater Portland Health in Maine, and the Department of Global Health and Population at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health. Elizabeth has dedicated her career to work in alignment with the mission of IQSS. She served most recently as the Chief Administrative Officer of Greater Portland Health, has provided health system and community strengthening efforts with partners in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and has led trauma-informed resilience trainings. Elizabeth has developed, implemented, and overseen health and education programs in several academic, community, public sector, and health settings. She has also previously worked at the World Health Organization, the Yale Global Health Leadership Institute, and the Harvard Global Health Institute. Elizabeth received her Masters in Public Health from Yale University and her Bachelors from Bates College.

item.title: Elizabeth Linos
item.description:
Elizabeth Linos

Associate Professor of Public Policy, HKS

Dr. Elizabeth Linos is the Emma Bloomberg Associate Professor for Public Policy and Management. Her research primarily centers on improving government through its workforce and service delivery. She applies behavioral science insights and public management evidence to address three key areas: recruiting, retaining, and supporting government workers; reducing administrative burdens faced by low-income households in government interactions; and integrating evidence-based policymaking into government operations.

item.title: Elizabeth Richard
item.description:
Elizabeth Richard

Executive-In-Residence, LISH

Elizabeth E. Richard is founder and principal of EER Strategies, LLC and a visiting fellow of the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard at the Institute for Quantitative Social Science. She was previously a senior strategist for NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate where she handled strategic planning and partnership development, and played a key role in establishing the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation. She specializes in innovation strategy, collaborative engagement, organizational change management, open innovation, and strategic planning across public, private, and nonprofit sectors. She frequently speaks and writes on strategy innovation and collaborative engagement, and has designed and led many client workshops. She earned her bachelor’s degree from Pennsylvania State University and her MBA from the University of Houston.

item.title: Ellen J Langer
item.description:
Ellen J Langer

Professor of Psychology

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Emmanuel Akyeampong
item.description:
Emmanuel Akyeampong

Oppenheimer Faculty Director; Ellen Gurney Professor of History and of African and African American Studies

Email: akyeamp@fas.harvard.edu

Professor Akyeampong joined Harvard’s History faculty after earning his PhD in African History from the University of Virginia in 1993. He received his master’s degree at Wake Forest University in 1989, focusing on English labor history, and his bachelor’s degree in History and Religions from the University of Ghana at Legon in 1984.

item.title: Eric Mazur
item.description:
Eric Mazur

Balkanski Professor of Physics and Applied Physics

Eric Mazur is the Balkanski Professor of Physics and Applied Physics and Area Chair of Applied Physics at Harvard University, Member of the Faculty of Education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, and Past President of the Optical Society.

He is described as “a prominent physicist known for his contributions in nanophotonics, an internationally recognized educational innovator,” and a widely sought speaker. In education, he is best known for Peer Instruction, an interactive teaching method designed to engage students both in and outside the classroom. In 2014, he became the first recipient of the Minerva Prize for Advancements in Higher Education. He has received numerous awards in both physics and education and has founded several successful companies.

item.title: Eric Wood
item.description:
Eric Wood

IT Client Support Services

Eric works at Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Sciences. He provides desktop support to clients at IQSS as well as support to users of IQSS’s Resource Computing Environment. He has been instrumental in the shift to work from home for faculty and staff since the beginning of the pandemic. He shall continue to play a vital role in the “return to the new normal” on campus.

item.title: Erik Buunk
item.description:
Erik Buunk

IQSS Affiliate

Erik has a master’s in Environmental Science and experience in IT implementations, software development, SCRUM and Lean/Six Sigma and graphic design.

When he was an Institute Fellow from 2019-2020, Erik Buunk worked on IQSS-affiliated Scientific Programs. He was also involved in internal IQSS projects such as the improvement of metrics, the cross-check of user stories for the migration of the computer cluster environments (RCE to Sid) and the development of a data visualization for the Harvard Dataverse homepage.

item.title: Eva Guinan
item.description:
Eva Guinan

Faculty Co-director, Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard

Eva Guinan, MD, is a pediatric hematologist/oncologist and an international expert in bone marrow failure and stem cell transplantation. She graduated from Harvard College and Harvard Medical School. She has been the senior investigator for clinical trials in human stem cell transplantation, as well as innovative proof of concept studies arising from her laboratory work where she developed the use of novel biological approaches to the problem of mismatched transplantation. She and her collaborators have discovered a novel radiation mitigation strategy also for use after unintended radiation exposures such as Fukishima, or to moderate therapeutic radiation toxicity. This agent appears to have unexpected roles in hematopoiesis that can be used to address other diseases states. To pursue that research and put her background in clinical/translational research to full use, she joined the Department of Radiation Oncology at the DFCI as its first director of Translational Research. She is also the director of the Harvard Catalyst Translational Innovation program which works to initiate novel approaches to important clinical questions and, in her LISH role, implement empiric experiments designed to explore whether distributed innovation techniques, alternative evaluation approaches, and novel concepts in team formation can be effective within the academic biomedical community.

item.title: Evan DeFilippis
item.description:
Evan DeFilippis

Associate of Dept of Psychology, FAS

My research lies at the intersection of behavioral economics and psychology, applying formal modeling techniques to understand complex social systems. My research focuses on three main topics:

  1. How to optimize organizational and project design principles to enhance creative ideation, crowdsourcing, and collaborative outcomes.
  2. Behavioral interventions to increase the likelihood of conflict resolution
  3. The psychology of persuasion and negotiation

Through my affiliation with IQSS, I am implementing a theoretically-grounded intervention designed to reduce affective polarization between political partisans and quantifiably increase receptivity to cross-ideological persuasion.

item.title: Explore the CGAs 2026 Training Schedule
item.description:
The Center for Geographic Analysis has unveiled a completely revamped training workshop schedule for 2026, offering Harvard community members an extensive array of geospatial technology and data science courses. All workshops are free for Harvard ID holders and cover essential tools and platforms including ArcGIS, QGIS, Python, R, KNIME, and many other technologies used in geographic analysis and spatial data science.

The 2026 training program reflects CGA’s commitment to keeping pace with rapidly evolving geospatial technologies and methodologies. The schedule includes both introductory courses for those new to GIS and advanced workshops for experienced users looking to expand their skills. Topics range from fundamental mapping and spatial analysis techniques to sophisticated applications of machine learning, remote sensing, and big data analytics in geographic contexts. The workshops are designed to serve researchers across all disciplines who work with spatial data in their research.

item.title: Extraordinary Claims, Extraordinary Evidence
item.description:
Program Overview

IQSS invites Harvard social science tenure-track faculty to collaborate on research that challenges dominant scientific, political, or cultural assumptions. The program provides tailored support including high-level data expertise, infrastructure, and funding to help investigators collect the extraordinary evidence required to move the scientific community’s dominant position the farthest distance.

What is an “Extraordinary Claim”?

An extraordinary claim is an empirical claim that is unusually distant from the current dominant view of the scientific community.

item.title: Fall Workshops from Data Science Services
item.description:
IQSS Data Science Services is excited to announce a comprehensive schedule of 12 free data science workshops for the fall semester, offering Harvard researchers valuable opportunities to develop new skills and enhance their computational research capabilities. These workshops cover a diverse range of topics essential to modern quantitative research, from programming fundamentals to advanced statistical methods and specialized tools for data analysis.

The fall workshop series is designed to serve researchers at various skill levels, from those just beginning to incorporate computational methods into their work to experienced practitioners looking to expand their toolkit. Topics span popular programming languages like R and Python, version control with Git, data visualization techniques, machine learning methods, text analysis, and more. Each workshop provides hands-on, practical instruction that participants can immediately apply to their own research projects. The workshops are taught by experienced data science consultants who understand the specific needs and challenges facing academic researchers.

item.title: Feyaad Allie
item.description:
Feyaad Allie

Postdoctoral Fellow, Dept of Government

Feyaad Allie is a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Government. In July 2024, he will begin his appointment as an Assistant Professor of Government. His research “broadly focuses on identity, democracy, and representation.” His book project examines the causes and consequences of political inclusion of marginalized groups, focusing on India. In additional work, he studies the intersection of technology and politics and religion’s role in intergroup relations. His methods include “large-scale administrative data, original surveys, archival documents, and in-depth interviews during fieldwork.” He earned his Ph.D. in Political Science from Stanford University and a BA in Government from Dartmouth College.

item.title: Fiery Cushman
item.description:
Fiery Cushman

John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Social Sciences

Cushman holds the title of John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Social Sciences, FAS.

His research focuses on how people learn and make decisions in social settings, with a particular emphasis on moral judgment and decision-making. His current research projects explore questions such as: “Why, and how, did punishment evolve?” and “What are the emotional systems that prevent us from doing harm to each other?” He also investigates how humans interpret each other’s behavior and how people decide which actions are worth considering among all possibilities. He combines “empirical methods with computational modeling in order to make progress on these questions.”

item.title: Florian Hillen
item.description:
Florian Hillen

Visiting Fellow, LISH

Florian Hillen is a Visiting Fellow at Harvard University, IQSS, at the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard. He studies Management & Technology at TUM, Technology Management at CDTM, and Medicine at LMU. His research focuses on “management practices and organizational structures in medical research laboratories.”

item.title: Following in Ancient Footsteps: Jeff Blossom Maps an Explorer Walk
item.description:
Jeff Blossom of the Center for Geographic Analysis collaborated for six years on a National Geographic Society project—Paul Salopek’s Out of Eden Walk, an intercontinental journey retracing the path of human migration out of Africa. Blossom provided GIS expertise to map and document the walk.

The project required creating detailed cartographic representations of diverse terrains across multiple continents, integrating satellite imagery, ground-truth data, and historical geographic information. Blossom’s work transformed Salopek’s physical journey into a rich digital archive accessible to researchers and the public.

item.title: Forgotten Graves: A New Lens on Colonial Slavery
item.description:
by Courtney Hayes

Jason Ur, Stephen Phillips Professor of Archaeology and Ethnology and IQSS affiliate, is working to unearth histories long hidden in Cambridge. Known for pioneering archaeological work in the Middle East, Ur has turned his attention to Cambridge’s Old Burying Ground, where questions about segregation and slavery have remained buried for centuries. Using drones, ground-penetrating radar, and a geospatial database, he is re-mapping the past and challenging how we understand it.

item.title: Francesca Dominici
item.description:
Francesca Dominici

Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics

Dr. Dominici earned her “B.S. in Statistics from University La Sapienza in Rome, Italy” and her “Ph.D. in Statistics from the University of Padua in Italy.” She completed postdoctoral training with Scott L. Zeger and Jonathan M. Samet at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health. In 1999, she became Assistant Professor at the Bloomberg School and received promotion to Full Professor with tenure in 2007. She was recruited to Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health as a tenured Professor of Biostatistics in 2009, became Associate Dean of Information Technology in 2011, and “Senior Associate Dean for Research in 2013.”

item.title: From Harvard Research to National Security Innovation: The Story of Thresher
item.description:
In 2015, Weatherhead University Professor Gary King co-founded Thresher, a company born from his academic research at Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS).

Thresher’s origins trace back to two groundbreaking research programs. The first focused on censorship and fabrication of Chinese social media posts, conducted with then graduate students Patrick Lam (now at Airbnb), Jennifer Pan (now professor at Stanford), and Molly Roberts (now professor at UCSD). While analyzing data from an earlier startup, Crimson Hexagon (now Brandwatch), King and his collaborators discovered a method to download Chinese social media content before it could be censored by the government. This serendipitous finding gave them access to the entire corpus of posts Chinese citizens were not allowed to read, becoming the foundation for deeper analysis of online information manipulation.

item.title: From NASA to the Enterprise: LISH Expands Programs
item.description:
The Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard (LISH), one of IQSS’s scientific programs, has experienced unprecedented growth over the past two years. Originally evolving from the NASA Tournament Lab, LISH now works with partner organizations across government, industry, and non-profit sectors on crowd-sourced problem solving.

Under its new expanded mandate, LISH conducts research on how organizations can leverage distributed intelligence, open innovation, and AI to solve complex problems. The lab’s work combines rigorous experimental methods with practical applications in areas ranging from space exploration to drug discovery.

item.title: From the Directors: A Fall Update
item.description:
This last year has brought a lot of exciting and transformative advancements at IQSS and across the social sciences. Here are a few highlights.

Dataverse Project

The Dataverse Project continued its community growth worldwide, reaching 100 installations, thousands of dataverses, and millions of dataset downloads. IQSS is undertaking a major restructuring of the Dataverse UI as a “single-page application,” which will enable custom UIs, integration with other applications, and make novel statistical innovations instantly available to users. The Dataverse Project is also part of an effort by the Office of Data Science Strategy (ODSS) at the NIH to launch a new data curation, sharing, and interoperability initiative across repositories. The team is also testing experimental code leveraging large language model (LLM) applications within Dataverse, allowing users to interact with and ask questions about Dataverse conversationally.

item.title: From the Directors: An Update on Dataverse
item.description:
IQSS leadership shared an update on the Dataverse Project, reflecting on deep dives into the many areas and layers of their work. The institute has been looking for ways to maximize its impact and position itself for even greater success in research data management.

The directors discussed strategic priorities for the Dataverse platform, including expanding its global reach, improving user experience, and strengthening the community of contributors who maintain and extend the open-source software. These efforts come as research data sharing requirements from funders and journals continue to grow.

item.title: Fumiya Uchikoshi
item.description:
Fumiya Uchikoshi

Harvard Academy Scholar

Fumiya Uchikoshi is an Academy Scholar (stipendiary postdoctoral fellow) at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies, housed at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University.

He is a social demographer who studies family inequality and educational stratification in Japan and East Asia. Broadly speaking, his research interests include 1) causes and consequences of demographic change and 2) the relationship between the “diversified” college expansion and social stratification.

item.title: Funding
item.description:
IQSS supports affiliated faculty, graduate students, and undergraduates through various funding opportunities designed to advance social science knowledge.

For Faculty

rapidPeer (Magaro Peer Pre-Review)

A peer pre-review similar to journal peer review, but faster, more complete, and constructive. Reviewers read the full paper and offer constructive suggestions throughout.

Undergraduate Research Scholars Program

An opportunity for Harvard College students to gain firsthand research experience working with faculty members across the University. Faculty receive up to $1,250/year in funding.

item.title: Future of Media Project: Who Owns Canadian News Media?
item.description:
IQSS Future of Media Project fellow Heidi Legg published a Canadian Media Ownership Index detailing ownership and digital consumption patterns of Canada’s top 125 news outlets. The research comes at a critical time for media industry analysis, as ownership concentration raises questions about editorial independence and information diversity.

The index provides transparency about who controls the information channels that Canadians rely on for news, revealing patterns of consolidation and the growing influence of digital platforms on traditional media business models. This data-driven approach to media analysis reflects the Future of Media Project’s mission at IQSS.

item.title: Gal Bitton
item.description:
Gal Bitton

Postdoctoral Fellow, Weatherhead Center

Gal Bitton is a postdoctoral researcher at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University and an Azrieli Fellow. She earned her Ph.D. in Political Science from Tel Aviv University in January 2025. Her research lies at the intersection of international political economy and political psychology, with a focus on financial decision-making and policymaking. She explores issues such as financial liberalization, cultural influences on financial behavior, and voter attitudes toward redistribution policies. More broadly, her interests span political economy, political behavior, and voting preferences. Methodologically, she specializes in experimental and observational research, with expertise in survey design and in-depth data analysis.

item.title: Gary King
item.description:
Gary King

Director of IQSS; Albert J. Weatherhead III University Professor

Email: king@harvard.edu

Gary King is the Albert J. Weatherhead III University Professor at Harvard University – one of 22 with the title of University Professor, Harvard’s most distinguished faculty position. He is based in the Department of Government (in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences) and serves as Director of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science. King develops and applies empirical methods in many areas of social science research, focusing on innovations that span the range from statistical theory to practical application.

item.title: Gary King instrumental in new academic-industry collaboration model
item.description:
IQSS Director Gary King and Nate Persily of Stanford Law School developed a new model for academic collaboration with industry, addressing the growing tension between researchers’ need for data and companies’ obligations to protect user privacy. Their working paper proposes frameworks for structured data access.

The model acknowledges that most data about people is now held by private companies rather than governments or academic institutions, creating a fundamental challenge for social science research. King and Persily argue that incentive-compatible arrangements can benefit both parties—companies gain research insights while academics access data that would otherwise be unavailable.

item.title: Gary King Receives 2019 Excellence in Mentoring Award
item.description:
The Society for Political Methodology named Gary King, Albert J. Weatherhead III University Professor and IQSS Director, as the 2019 recipient of the Excellence in Mentoring Award. The award recognizes sustained contributions to training the next generation of political methodologists.

King has mentored dozens of PhD students who have gone on to faculty positions at leading universities, building a network of scholars who advance quantitative methods in political science. His mentoring approach emphasizes both technical rigor and the practical skills needed to build successful academic careers.

item.title: Gary King: A Welcome Back Update
item.description:
Dear: IQSS Staff and Affiliates
From: Gary King, Director IQSS
Subj: A welcome back update
Date: 8/19/2021

King opens by noting the IQSS community has been away from CGIS for nearly two years, with exceptions for the Client Support Services team and others. He announces the official return the week of August 23rd.

He describes the pre-pandemic intellectual community at IQSS as unique “not only among Harvard groups, but throughout academia” and outlines goals to preserve the virtual community, reconstitute the physical one, and build on lessons learned about workplace flexibility.

item.title: Gautam Nair
item.description:
Gautam Nair

Assistant Professor of Public Policy, HKS

Gautam Nair is an Assistant Professor of Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. He “conducts research in comparative politics and international political economy, and focus primarily on the politics of inequality, redistribution, and special interests in South Asia.”

item.title: Geocoding with ArcGIS
item.description:
Geocoding with ArcGIS

Date: February 6, 2026

Time: 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM EST

Location: CGIS Knafel room SB-12

A two-hour workshop covering geocoding concepts and practical applications. Participants will geocode single addresses and cities using Bing Maps, Google Maps, and ArcGIS Online, then batch-geocode multiple addresses in ArcGIS Pro and map results. Emphasis on evaluating accuracy of geocoded outputs. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Georgia Kernell
item.description:
Georgia Kernell

Postdoctoral Fellow, Univ of Pennsylvania

Georgia Kernell successfully defended her PhD dissertation in political science at Columbia University in September 2008. Her research interests include political parties, methodology, behavior and comparative institutions. Her dissertation, “Political Party Organizations and Representation: Party Responsiveness, Candidate Heterogeneity and Voter Behavior in Mature Parliamentary Systems,” examines how a party’s organization–especially its decentralization with respect to candidate selection, resource allocation, and recruitment of delegates to the national party convention–shapes its electoral appeal and constituent support. The thesis uses an original data set of party institutions, party statutes, and interviews for 66 parties in 20 mature parliamentary democracies. Georgia also studies quantitative methods, and has two publications in Political Analysis. Currently, Georgia is working on several projects that examine the institutions that regulate party diversity, the normative implications of party organizations for representation, and the information strategies that affect consumers’ economic forecasts. During the spring she will teach a freshman seminar on “Comparative Political Parties and Party Systems” at Penn, where she is a postdoctoral fellow in Penn’s Program on Democracy, Citizenship, and Constitutionalism.

item.title: Get Help
item.description:
Become an Affiliate

Learn about IQSS affiliation opportunities for faculty, students, visiting scholars, and fellows.

Find People

item.title: Getting Started Making Maps with QGIS and ArcGIS
item.description:
Getting Started Making Maps with QGIS and ArcGIS

Date: February 20, 2026

Time: 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM EST

Location: CGIS Knafel Building, Room SB-12

A three-hour workshop covering map-making with QGIS and ArcGIS Pro. Participants will create general reference and thematic maps, learn fundamental principles of cartography, and pick up map design basics. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Getting Started with AI for Spatial Data
item.description:
Getting Started with AI for Spatial Data

Date: April 10, 2026

Time: 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM EDT

Location: CGIS Knafel Building, Room SB-12

A 2-hour hands-on workshop on using Large Language Models for text classification with geotagged Twitter data. Participants use Python and LM Studio to work with models like Gemini, learning to call OpenAI APIs, design prompts, and integrate LLMs into data workflows. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

item.title: Getting Started with Spatial Analysis in R
item.description:
Getting Started with Spatial Analysis in R

Date: March 6, 2026

Time: 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM EST

Location: CGIS Knafel Building, Room SB-12

A two-hour workshop introducing spatial analysis concepts and applications. Participants will use R to perform proximity, overlay, and geostatistical operations on a variety of data and learn to interpret, export, and visualize results. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Gianluca Busilacchi
item.description:
Gianluca Busilacchi

Visiting Scholar; Assoc Prof, Univ of Macerata

Gianluca Busilacchi is an Associate Professor of Economic Sociology at the University of Macerata (Italy). He has also been a Visiting Fellow at the University of Barcelona, the London School of Economics, the European University Institute, and the Center for European Studies at Harvard University, and was a Marie Curie Fellow at the Centre for Social Policy of the University of Antwerp.

item.title: GIS for Humanities and Social Sciences
item.description:
GIS for Humanities and Social Sciences

Date: December 5, 2025

Time: 9:30 AM – 4:30 PM EST

Location: CGIS South, room S020

Full-day hands-on workshop on GIS and mapping techniques for humanities and social sciences research.

Presenter: Jeff Blossom, Center for Geographic Analysis

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: GIS Institute Summer 2026
item.description:
GIS Institute Summer 2026

Date: June 8–18, 2026

Time: 9:30 AM – 5:00 PM EDT

Location: 1737 Cambridge Street, CGIS Knafel Building, Room K350

A two-week training course in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and its application to research. Designed for Harvard graduate students, post-docs, faculty, staff, and external researchers seeking to integrate spatial thinking, incorporate GIS methods, learn spatial analysis tools, and communicate with maps. Registration fee is $100 for Harvard affiliates, $3,150 for others. Application deadline: March 22, 2026.

item.title: GIS Training
item.description:
GIS Training Events

GIS Institute Summer 2026

A two-week training course in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and its application to research. Designed for Harvard graduate students, post-doctoral fellows, faculty, staff, and external researchers.

Getting Started with AI for Spatial Data

A 2-hour interactive workshop on practical use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for text classification using geotagged Twitter data with Python and LM Studio.

Satellite Imagery Analysis with Google Earth Engine

Two-hour workshop on satellite imagery analysis with GEE using KNIME's extension. Covers remote sensing for Social Science, Health, and Humanities research.

item.title: Glen Comiso
item.description:
Glen Comiso

Executive Director, Human Flourishing Program

Email: gcomiso@fas.harvard.edu

Glen Comiso is the Executive Director of the Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS). In this role, Glen oversees all aspects of the program’s strategic vision, donor relations, external partnerships, day-to-day operations, and program leadership. He has extensive experience building organizations, policies and programs at the intersection of academia, government, and industry.

item.title: Glenn Lopez
item.description:
Glenn Lopez

Director of Engineering, VPAL

Glenn is the Director of Engineering for VPAL (Vice Provost for Advances in Learning) at Harvard. Since 2014, he has developed multi-cloud platform software to address the challenge of connecting teaching and learning data from decentralized systems across Harvard. These efforts matured into a cloud data platform infrastructure powering H.U.D.A.T.
