(Harvard University Data Aggregation and Transformation System), which is described as “a comprehensive centralized database that links critical teaching and learning management systems (LMS) at Harvard.” This work has enabled various projects including Harvard Link, Syllabus Explorer, platform data analytics, and research.

item.title: Global Flourishing Study Releases Wave One Open Research Data
item.description:
Wave one of the Global Flourishing Study dataset is now available to researchers, representing a partnership among Baylor University, Harvard’s Human Flourishing Program, Gallup, and the Center for Open Science. The dataset covers approximately 200,000 participants across 22 countries.

The study measures six domains of flourishing: happiness and life satisfaction, mental and physical health, meaning and purpose, character and virtue, close social relationships, and financial and material stability. This comprehensive approach moves beyond pathology-focused measures to capture what it means to truly thrive.

item.title: Global Flourishing Study Wave 2 Extended Datasets Available Now
item.description:
The Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University has released Wave 2 data from the Global Flourishing Study, marking a significant milestone in one of the most comprehensive longitudinal research efforts on human well-being ever undertaken. This new wave of data is now freely available to researchers worldwide through the Center for Open Science, continuing the study’s commitment to open science and collaborative research.

The Wave 2 extended datasets build upon the groundbreaking first wave by tracking the same cohort of approximately 200,000 participants across 22 countries over time. This longitudinal design allows researchers to examine how flourishing changes across different life stages and in response to various life events and circumstances. The data captures information across six key domains of human flourishing: happiness and life satisfaction, physical and mental health, meaning and purpose, character and virtue, close social relationships, and financial and material stability.

item.title: Hands-On Curation Training with Harvard Dataverse Repository
item.description:
Hands-On Curation Training with Harvard Dataverse Repository

Date: April 18, 2025

Time: 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM EDT

Location: Virtual via Zoom

A hands-on training session guiding participants in using the Dataverse platform to create personalized collections, customize spaces with logos and links, configure metadata and facets for discoverability, and learn best practices for sharing data. Covers making data accessible and user-friendly and building research data curation and management skills. Participants can use provided training data files or bring their own. Registration with an institutional email required.

item.title: Hanspeter Pfister
item.description:
Hanspeter Pfister

An Wang Professor of Computer Science

Hanspeter Pfister is An Wang Professor of Computer Science and Director of the Institute for Applied Computational Science at the Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences. His research in visual computing lies at the intersection of visualization, computer graphics, and computer vision. It spans a wide range of topics, including bio-medical visualization, image and video analysis, 3D fabrication, and data science. Dr. Pfister has a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the State University of New York at Stony Brook and an M.S. in Electrical Engineering from ETH Zurich, Switzerland. Before joining Harvard he worked for over a decade at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories where he was Associate Director and Senior Research Scientist. He was the chief architect of VolumePro, Mitsubishi Electric’s award-winning real-time volume rendering hardware for PCs. He is the recipient of the 2010 IEEE Visualization Technical Achievement award in recognition of his seminal technical achievements in real-time volume rendering. He is co-inventor of over 50 US patents and co-author on more than 80 peer-reviewed publications, including over 20 ACM SIGGRAPH papers, the premier forum in Computer Graphics. He was technical papers chair for SIGGRAPH 2012. He is co-editor of the first textbook on Point-Based Computer Graphics, published by Elsevier in 2007, and of the 2006 NIH/NSF Visualization Research Challenges Report. He received the IEEE Golden Core Award, the IEEE Meritorious Service Award, and the Petra T. Shattuck Excellence in Teaching Award. He is currently on the editorial board of the ACM Transaction on Graphics (TOG). You can contact him at pfister@seas.harvard.edu.

item.title: Harvard Climate Justice Design Fellowship Announces Inaugural Fellows
item.description:
The Harvard Climate Justice Design Fellowship selected seven inaugural fellows who are leaders in environmental justice advocacy, organizing, and law from across the United States. The program, launched by IQSS, supports climate justice work through data science and design.

Fellows participate in intensive training on data analysis, visualization, and design thinking, then apply these skills to climate justice challenges in their home communities. The program bridges the gap between technical capability and grassroots organizing, ensuring that data tools serve community needs.

item.title: Harvard IQSS and Microsoft announce major OpenDP collaboration
item.description:
Gary King led IQSS’s announcement of a major collaboration with Microsoft to build a platform ensuring data is kept private while remaining useful for research. The partnership aims to develop open-source differential privacy tools accessible to researchers and organizations handling sensitive information.

The collaboration brings together Harvard’s theoretical expertise in privacy-preserving computation with Microsoft’s engineering resources and practical experience deploying privacy technologies at scale. Together, they aim to create tools that make differential privacy practical for everyday use by researchers and data analysts.

item.title: Harvard Thinking - Preserving learning in the age of AI shortcuts
item.description:
In an episode of Harvard Thinking, IQSS affiliate Michael Brenner explores one of the most pressing questions facing educators today: how has artificial intelligence affected learning and critical thinking, and how can these powerful tools be embraced to enhance rather than diminish educational outcomes? Brenner, the Glover Professor of Applied Mathematics and Applied Physics at Harvard, brings both technical expertise and pedagogical insight to this critical discussion.

Brenner examines the double-edged nature of AI in educational contexts. While AI tools can provide instant answers and automate routine tasks, there is growing concern that students may become overly reliant on these technologies, bypassing the cognitive struggle that leads to deep understanding and skill development. The conversation addresses how educators can design learning experiences that leverage AI’s capabilities while ensuring students still develop fundamental thinking skills, creativity, and problem-solving abilities that remain uniquely human.

item.title: Harvesting Data From the Field to the Cloud: The 2024 Dataverse Community Meeting
item.description:
The 10th anniversary Dataverse Community Meeting was held March 4-8 at CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center) in Texcoco, Mexico. The location reflected Dataverse’s growing importance in agricultural and development research.

The meeting focused on collaboration and the future of data systems, bringing together Dataverse users and developers from institutions around the world. Sessions covered topics from repository administration to data curation best practices, with particular attention to the needs of researchers in the Global South.

item.title: Heidi R Legg
item.description:
Heidi R Legg

IQSS Affiliate; Former Fellow, Future of Media Project

Heidi Legg was the Future of Media fellow at IQSS at Harvard (2020-2022), where she indexed the entire US and Canadian media system with extensive ownership details. She mapped commercial and non-profit media ecosystems to offer solutions on transparency and trust in news. Her work appeared in Axios, USA Today, Nieman Labs, CJR, and Press-Gazette.

item.title: Hila Lifshitz Assaf
item.description:
Hila Lifshitz Assaf

Associate Professor, NYU Stern; Affiliate, LISH

Hila Lifshitz-Assaf is an Associate Professor of Information, Operations and Management Sciences at New York University Stern School of Business. She is also an affiliate of the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard.

Her research centers on understanding the “micro-foundations of scientific and technological innovation and knowledge creation processes in the digital age.” She investigates how innovation capacity is being transformed and what challenges and opportunities this presents for R&D organizations and professionals. She carried out a three-year longitudinal field study of NASA’s experimentation with open innovation platforms and communities, which resulted in a scientific breakthrough. This work received the best dissertation Grigor McClelland Award at EGOS 2015, Best ASQ paper based on dissertation (2018), and Best published paper from the organizational communication and information systems division of the Academy of Management (2018).

item.title: Hillel Bavli
item.description:
Hillel Bavli

Assistant Professor of Law, SMU Dedman School of Law

Hillel Bavli is an Assistant Professor of Law at SMU Dedman School of Law and an affiliate of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science. He is described as “an experienced litigation attorney” with teaching and scholarship interests in “evidence law, tort law, complex litigation, law and economics, and empirical legal studies.” He is noted as being “particularly interested in applications of statistics to law.”

item.title: Hirotaka Miura
item.description:
Hirotaka Miura

Research Associate, Laboratory for Innovation Science

Hirotaka Miura is a Research Associate at Harvard Business School, primarily supporting research by Professor Chiara Farronato, an affiliated researcher at the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard. He holds “a master’s degree in Mathematics of Finance from Columbia University” and a bachelor’s in Mathematics/Economics from UCLA. His prior work experience includes positions at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, NEC Corporation, GE Japan, GE Healthcare Japan, the Center for Infection and Immunity at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

item.title: Hongxiao Fu
item.description:
Hongxiao Fu

Digital Humanities Researcher

Hongxiao Fu “is interested in the fields of Digital Humanities, with a particular focus on geographical distribution and social network analysis of archaeological data.”

item.title: How forgiving can improve well-being
item.description:
Researchers at the Human Flourishing Program have published groundbreaking findings revealing a strong connection between the regular practice of forgiveness and significant improvements in psychological well-being and character development. The study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that forgiveness is not merely a moral or spiritual concept but a powerful contributor to mental health and personal growth that can be cultivated through intentional practice.

The research examined individuals who engaged in regular forgiveness practices over time, tracking changes in various dimensions of psychological well-being including life satisfaction, positive emotions, depression, anxiety, and overall mental health. Beyond these psychological benefits, the study also documented meaningful changes in character traits, suggesting that the practice of forgiveness can fundamentally reshape how individuals relate to themselves and others. These findings indicate that forgiveness functions as more than just a way to resolve specific grievances, instead serving as a transformative practice that enhances overall quality of life.

item.title: How to Apply — For Faculty
item.description:
Faculty Affiliates: Apply for Funding

Faculty seeking URS funding should complete the URS Grant Application survey form. After review, a URS Program administrator will follow up.

Submission Deadlines

URS Funding is currently on hold. We hope to re-open applications in the future.

How It Works

  1. Fill out the grant application form
  2. Wait for administrative review
  3. Receive contact from a URS administrator

After Receiving Funding

After receiving funding, faculty have two options:

item.title: How to Apply — For Students
item.description:
For Students: Get Experience

Interested undergraduates should visit the Current Opportunities section for projects needing researchers. To apply, students should send a resume and cover letter with relevant qualifications to the contact listed under the project description.

Even without listed opportunities, students can reach out directly to faculty whose research interests them to inform them about URS. Once a faculty member receives grant approval, they work with IQSS administrators to hire undergraduates.

item.title: How to regulate AI
item.description: IQSS affiliate David Y. Yang, Professor of Economics at Harvard University, has joined other leading experts in addressing one of the most pressing policy questions of our time: how to effectively regulate artificial intelligence development and deployment. As US legislators pass measures at both state and federal levels, the debate over AI regulation has intensified, with scholars and policymakers grappling with balancing innovation against risks ranging from privacy violations and algorithmic bias to potential existential threats from advanced AI systems.

item.title: Human Flourishing Program Launches Global Flourishing Study
item.description: The Human Flourishing Program at Harvard’s IQSS has launched the ambitious Global Flourishing Study, a groundbreaking international research initiative designed to explore fundamental questions about what it means to live well across diverse cultures and societies. This comprehensive, multi-year study represents one of the most extensive efforts ever undertaken to understand human well-being in all its dimensions, moving beyond narrow measures of happiness or economic prosperity to examine flourishing holistically.

item.title: Human Flourishing Program, Baylor, & Gallup Release Wave 1 Findings
item.description: The Global Flourishing Study (GFS), a multi-year collaborative research effort conducted by the Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University, Baylor’s Institute for Studies of Religion, Gallup, and the Center for Open Science, has released its First Wave findings on human flourishing. This represents one of the most comprehensive studies of human well-being ever undertaken, defining flourishing as “living in a state in which all aspects of a person’s life are good.”

item.title: Hunter Rendleman
item.description:
Hunter Rendleman

Postdoctoral Researcher, UC Berkeley

Hunter’s research agenda seeks to understand how political institutions structure the behavior of racial minorities and members of marginalized communities in American politics. Her work embodies a mixed-method approach, employing techniques for causal inference, interviews, and formal theory. Hunter graduated with her PhD from from the Department of Government at Harvard in 2024, and will join the UC Berkeley faculty in fall 2025.

item.title: Illai Gescheit
item.description:
Illai Gescheit

Executive Affiliate, Startup Foundry

Illai is an Entrepreneur, Senior Advisor, Investor and Lecturer. He is a Founding Partner of Gescheit & Partners, a multi-stage venture advisory firm and a Venture Partner in a few venture funds. He serves as an Affiliate Lecturer teaching Strategy and Entrepreneurship at the London Business School and an Executive Affiliate at the Institute of Quantitative Social Sciences at Harvard University. He previously served as Venture Partner at Siemens Energy Ventures and as Entrepreneur-in-Residence at BP. He is an inventor of over 20 patents, and his early entrepreneurial story was featured in the Harvard-MIT book publication Entrepreneurial Negotiation. He is described as “a Top Voice on Linkedin sharing insights and thought leadership content.” He is a member of the Ashoka Entrepreneur-to-Entrepreneur Network and a member of the Expert Network for the World Economic Forum.

item.title: In touch with our emotions, finally
item.description:
Jennifer Lerner, IQSS affiliate and Bradshaw Professor of Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School, examines how emotion and gender factor into decision making. Her research challenges long-held assumptions about rationality and shows that emotions can both help and hinder good judgment depending on the context.

Lerner’s work has revealed systematic patterns in how specific emotions influence economic decisions, risk assessment, and policy preferences. For example, anger tends to make people more optimistic about risks and more punitive in their judgments, while sadness promotes more careful deliberation but can also lead to impatience in financial decisions.

item.title: Intermediate Curation on the Dataverse Platform
item.description:
Intermediate Curation on the Dataverse Platform

Location: Virtual

Intermediate-level curation training covering advanced features of the Dataverse platform for data management and sharing.

Presenter: Sonia Barbosa, The Dataverse Project, IQSS

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Intisar Rabb
item.description:
Intisar Rabb

Professor of Law; Professor of History

Intisar A. Rabb is a Professor of Law, a Professor of History, and the faculty director of the Program in Islamic Law at Harvard Law School. She has held appointments as a Susan S. and Kenneth L. Wallach Professor at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, as an Associate Professor at NYU Department of Middle Eastern and Islamic Studies and at NYU Law School, and as an Assistant Professor at Boston College Law School. She previously served as a law clerk for Judge Thomas L. Ambro of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, as a Temple Bar Fellow in London with the American Inns of Court, and as a Carnegie Scholar for her work on contemporary Islamic law. At Harvard, she launched SHARIAsource – an online portal combining historical texts and data science tools to facilitate new insights on Islamic studies, with the help of AI and machine learning. She is editor-in-chief of the Islamic Law Blog, Journal of Islamic Law, and book series, the Harvard Series in Islamic Law (published with Harvard University Press). She has published on Islamic law in historical and modern contexts, including the monograph, Doubt in Islamic Law (Cambridge University Press 2015), the edited volumes, Justice and Leadership in Early Islamic Courts (with Abigail Balbale, Harvard University Press, 2017) and Law and Tradition in Classical Islamic Thought (with Michael Cook et al., Palgrave 2013), and numerous articles on Islamic constitutionalism, on Islamic legal canons, and on the early history of the Qur’an text. She received a BA from Georgetown University, a JD from Yale Law School, and an MA and PhD from Princeton University. She has conducted research in Egypt, Iran, Syria, and elsewhere.

item.title: Introducing Extraordinary Claims, Extraordinary Evidence
item.description:
by Elizabeth Salazar

The Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS) launched a program offering Harvard faculty exceptional help in providing extraordinary evidence for their extraordinary claims. Called Extraordinary Claims, Extraordinary Evidence (ECEE), the program aims to catalyze rigorous research that would shift dominant scientific positions significantly.

The program recognizes that many extraordinary claims are “explicitly contrarian positions” that, if validated, reveal flawed assumptions or unsupported conclusions in existing research. Others address subjects not actively studied—topics scholars incorrectly assume are understood or consider unworthy of investigation—yet which hold potential for major shifts in a field’s dominant view.

item.title: Introducing Version 0.4 of the OpenDP Library
item.description:
The OpenDP Project is pleased to announce the release of version 0.4 of the OpenDP Library, introducing important new measurements and significant floating point improvements that enhance both the functionality and reliability of the differential privacy toolkit. This release represents substantial progress toward making differential privacy practical and trustworthy for protecting sensitive data in real-world applications.

Version 0.4 expands the library’s capabilities with additional measurements that enable new types of differentially private analyses. These new statistical tools provide data practitioners with more options for extracting insights from sensitive datasets while maintaining rigorous privacy guarantees. The floating point improvements address critical technical challenges in implementing differential privacy algorithms, ensuring that computations maintain accuracy and reliability even when dealing with numerical precision issues that can arise in complex calculations.

item.title: Introduction to Data Handling on the Dataverse Platform
item.description:
Introduction to Data Handling on the Dataverse Platform

The IQSS Dataverse Repository provides researchers with a robust data management and file handling system for sharing, managing, and preserving research datasets.

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Introduction to Dataverse APIs
item.description:
Introduction to Dataverse APIs

Location: Virtual

While Dataverse supports file uploads through its standard web interface, there are big data use cases where the Dataverse API and related tools are useful. This session introduces participants to the Dataverse API for programmatic access to data.

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Introduction to GIS
item.description:
Introduction to GIS

Date: January 30, 2026

Time: 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM EST

Location: CGIS Knafel Building, Room SB-12

A two-hour workshop covering what GIS are and their uses. It will describe geographic file types and data formats, explain how geographic data supports visualization and analysis, and introduce various GIS use cases. Participants will use QGIS and ArcGIS Online to perform GIS tasks. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

item.title: Introduction to Metadata in Dataverse Repositories: For Installation Administrators
item.description:
Introduction to Metadata in Dataverse Repositories: For Installation Administrators

Location: Virtual

Learn how Dataverse helps installation administrators customize metadata for their repositories.

Register

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Introduction to Metadata on the Dataverse Platform
item.description:
Introduction to Metadata on the Dataverse Platform

Location: Virtual

Learn how Dataverse helps researchers describe and find data. Covers how metadata fields are organized and how Dataverse features help with discovery.

Presenter: Julian Gautier, The Dataverse Project, IQSS

General Inquiries: gen_inquiries@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: IQSS Affiliate-Led HDSI Receives Sloan Grant
item.description:
The Harvard Data Science Initiative (HDSI), led by IQSS affiliate Professor Xiao-Li Meng, has received a prestigious $1 million grant from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation to advance research at the intersection of causal inference and machine learning. This significant funding recognizes the importance of integrating these two powerful approaches to data analysis and supports HDSI’s mission to advance data science methods that address pressing societal challenges.

The grant will support research that bridges causal inference—the rigorous statistical framework for understanding cause-and-effect relationships—with machine learning techniques that excel at finding patterns in complex, high-dimensional data. This integration is crucial for many applications where researchers need not just to predict outcomes but to understand what interventions will actually cause desired changes. The work has important implications across fields including public health, education policy, economics, and social science research.

item.title: IQSS and Collaborators Announce How We Feel Project
item.description:
IQSS, Pinterest, and Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health scientists collaborated to address the gap in recorded cases of the novel coronavirus in the United States through the How We Feel Project. The initiative launched in early April 2020 as COVID-19 testing remained severely limited.

The project developed a mobile application that collected self-reported health data from users, creating a real-time picture of symptom prevalence across the country that complemented official testing data. This crowd-sourced epidemiological approach leveraged smartphone technology to gather information at a scale and speed that traditional surveillance systems could not match.

item.title: IQSS Celebrates 20 years
item.description:
The year 2025 marks the 20th anniversary of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science at Harvard University. The milestone was celebrated at the Center for Geographic and International Studies (CGIS) with faculty, staff, and students from across the IQSS community who work to advance research at Harvard and other institutions.

Over two decades, IQSS has developed into a hub where leading minds in data and social science collaborate on solutions to pressing societal issues. As the institute marks this milestone and reflects on its accomplishments, projects, and innovations, it is also looking ahead—including new programs and partnerships that will launch at IQSS.

item.title: IQSS Co-Hosts Comparative Politics and Formal Theory Conference
item.description: IQSS co-hosted the 8th Comparative Politics and Formal Theory (CPFT) Conference at Harvard, bringing together political scientists who use formal modeling and rigorous empirical methods to study comparative politics. This specialized conference provides a venue for researchers working at the intersection of game theory, formal models, and comparative political analysis to present work, receive feedback, and build connections across institutions. The gathering reflects IQSS’s commitment to supporting methodologically sophisticated political science research.

item.title: IQSS Computer Labs
item.description:
Who Can Access?

The labs serve faculty, visiting scholars, post-docs, students, and staff. They use University active directory accounts that need activation. New patrons can sign up via the access request form.

Current/active MIT affiliates who do not have University active directory accounts may sign up for lab access — IQSS will sponsor a University active directory account; the process may take several days for new users.

The labs are open to all active members of the Harvard and MIT Community.

item.title: IQSS Data Science Hosts First Dataverse Community Meeting
item.description:
IQSS Data Science Services hosted the inaugural Dataverse Community Meeting, bringing together repository administrators, developers, and data professionals from institutions worldwide for the first gathering centered on the Dataverse platform. This historic event marked an important milestone in the evolution of Dataverse from a Harvard project into a global open-source community, creating opportunities for knowledge sharing, collaborative problem-solving, and collective planning for the platform’s future development.

The first Dataverse Community Meeting featured presentations about repository implementations, technical workshops, discussions of data curation challenges, and planning sessions for future software development. Attendees shared experiences managing Dataverse repositories in diverse institutional contexts, from small university libraries to large international collaborations. The gathering enabled face-to-face connections among people who had primarily interacted through online channels, strengthening relationships and building the sense of community essential for successful open-source projects.

item.title: IQSS Dataverse joins NIH-funded collaboration on climate change and health
item.description: IQSS’s Dataverse Project has joined an NIH-funded collaboration focused on climate change and health, bringing research data repository expertise to a major interdisciplinary initiative examining the health impacts of environmental change. This partnership reflects growing recognition that climate change poses profound threats to human health through pathways including extreme heat, air quality degradation, infectious disease patterns, food security, and mental health impacts. Understanding and addressing these challenges requires integration of climate science, epidemiology, and health research—and the data infrastructure to support such work.

item.title: IQSS Director on Science Magazine Podcast
item.description: IQSS Director Gary King appeared on the Science Magazine podcast to discuss his research on media influence on public discourse and how new data sources and computational methods are transforming understanding of how information spreads and shapes public opinion. The conversation explored King’s pioneering work analyzing large-scale social media data to understand patterns of censorship, propaganda, and information manipulation, particularly in authoritarian contexts where traditional research methods face significant barriers.

item.title: IQSS Establishes Digital Lab for Social Science
item.description: IQSS has established the Digital Lab for the Social Sciences (DLABSS), a dedicated space and program designed to support computationally intensive social science research and provide researchers with access to expertise, tools, and collaborative environment for digital scholarship. The lab represents IQSS’s commitment to advancing methodological innovation by creating infrastructure that enables researchers to work with new data sources, apply cutting-edge analytical methods, and collaborate on projects that push the boundaries of traditional social science.

item.title: IQSS Faculty and Student Question Replicability Crisis
item.description:
IQSS faculty members and graduate students have entered a major scientific debate by challenging influential claims about the so-called replicability crisis in psychology. Their work questions the interpretation of a large-scale replication study that appeared to show widespread failure to reproduce findings from published psychology research, arguing that the original analysis may have overstated problems with replicability and potentially mischaracterized the state of psychological science.

The IQSS researchers employ sophisticated statistical methods to reanalyze replication study data, demonstrating that different analytical approaches and assumptions can lead to substantially different conclusions about replication success rates. Their work highlights methodological challenges in assessing replication, including how to define replication success, account for statistical power in both original and replication studies, and interpret differences between original and replication effect sizes. This intervention in a high-profile scientific debate exemplifies IQSS’s role in advancing methodological rigor and statistical understanding across the sciences.

item.title: IQSS Honors Staff Service Milestones
item.description:
The Institute for Quantitative Social Science recently gathered to celebrate staff members who have reached important service milestones. At IQSS they value their community, and their dedicated staff is at the heart of that community. This annual recognition honors colleagues who in 2025 reached a work anniversary of 10 years or more, in 5-year increments. Their long-term commitment, talent, and collaboration make our work possible.

This year’s IQSS Service Award recipients are:

item.title: IQSS launches Climate Justice Design Fellowship program
item.description:
IQSS has launched the Climate Justice Design Fellowship program, an innovative initiative that brings together data science, design thinking, and climate justice principles to address environmental challenges in ways that center equity and community needs. This fellowship program reflects growing recognition that climate change disproportionately affects marginalized communities and that addressing climate challenges requires not just technical solutions but approaches grounded in justice and participatory design.

The Climate Justice Design Fellowship supports interdisciplinary teams combining expertise in data science, environmental science, design, and social science to develop tools, visualizations, and interventions that help communities understand and respond to climate impacts. Fellows work on projects that might include mapping climate vulnerability in environmental justice communities, creating accessible data visualization tools for community organizations, or developing platforms that amplify community voices in climate policy discussions. The program emphasizes participatory approaches that involve affected communities as partners rather than subjects of research.

item.title: IQSS launches Sid cloud research software
item.description:
IQSS has launched Sid, a groundbreaking cloud-agnostic multi-user research computing platform that revolutionizes how researchers access and use high-performance computing resources. Named in honor of Sidney Verba, the pioneering political scientist who championed making research resources accessible to all scholars, Sid provides an intuitive web-based interface that democratizes access to powerful computing capabilities without requiring deep technical expertise in command-line computing or system administration.

Sid represents a fundamental shift in research computing philosophy, moving from the traditional model where researchers must learn complex technical skills to access computing power, to one where sophisticated capabilities are presented through user-friendly interfaces. The platform supports diverse workflows including interactive data analysis, batch computing jobs, visualization, and collaborative work, all accessible through a web browser from anywhere. Its cloud-agnostic architecture means researchers can leverage computing resources from different providers, avoiding vendor lock-in while maintaining consistent workflows.

item.title: IQSS Startup Foundry - Academic Founders
item.description:
Commercialization Help for Academic Founders

The program supports Harvard social scientists from any school in exploring commercialization of their research into new ventures. The focus is on very early-stage concepts derived from validated Harvard research.

The program is designed for busy faculty members and other Harvard academics who want to see their research make a difference but lack time, business expertise, or simply want assistance with commercialization.

item.title: IQSS Startup Foundry - Innovation Community
item.description:
The Innovation Community

The IQSS Startup Foundry helps Harvard social scientists turn research insights into viable startups, supporting early-stage software and AI ventures with commercialization typically taking 6-18 months depending on industry complexity, regulation, and development stage.

The program guides academic founders and business drivers through customer discovery, market research, MVP development, pilot customer programs, go-to-market plans, and fundraising. After spinning out from Harvard, operating founders stay connected as alumni while academic founders typically remain at Harvard as company advisors.

item.title: IQSS Welcomes Dr. Stefano Iacus
item.description:
The Institute for Quantitative Social Science is delighted to welcome Dr. Stefano Iacus as Senior Research Scientist, bringing extensive expertise in computational statistics, time series analysis, and statistical software development to IQSS’s research and methodological innovation initiatives. Dr. Iacus’s arrival strengthens IQSS’s capacity to support cutting-edge quantitative research and advance the development of statistical tools used by scholars worldwide.

Dr. Iacus joins IQSS with an impressive background spanning academic research, open-source software development, and practical applications of statistical methods to real-world problems. His expertise in simulation-based inference, computational methods, and statistical software has contributed to major research computing projects and the development of widely used R packages. His work bridges theoretical statistics and applied data science, making sophisticated methods accessible to researchers across disciplines.

item.title: IQSS Welcomes New Executive Director Elizabeth Jackson
item.description:
IQSS announced the arrival of its new Executive Director, Elizabeth Jackson, who comes from Greater Portland Health in Maine and from Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health’s Department of Global Health and Population.

Jackson has built a career aligned with IQSS’s mission. She most recently served as Chief Administrative Officer of The Greater Portland Health Center and has engaged in health system and community strengthening work with partners across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. She has also led trauma-informed resilience trainings.

item.title: IQSS Welcomes WashU into Magaro Peer Pre-Review Consortium
item.description:
by Liz Salazar

The Institute for Quantitative Social Science at Harvard University is expanding the Alexander and Diviya Magaro Peer Pre-Review Program—a service designed to improve scholarship by speeding up the journal submission process—into a multi-institutional consortium. The Weidenbaum Center on the Economy, Government, and Public Policy at Washington University in St. Louis is the first affiliate to partner with IQSS, adding its own network of associate editors and peer reviewers to Harvard’s existing cohort. Washington University professors Gaetano Antinolfi and Ian Filmore will work with senior preceptor Chase Harrison at IQSS to coordinate the review process for submitted drafts.

item.title: Iris Bohnet
item.description:
Iris Bohnet

Albert Pratt Professor of Business and Government, HKS

Email: iris_bohnet@harvard.edu

Iris Bohnet is Professor of Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School. She directs the Women and Public Policy Program, serves as associate director of the Harvard Decision Science Laboratory, vice-chair of the Program on Negotiation, and faculty co-chair of the executive program “Global Leadership and Public Policy for the 21st Century” for the World Economic Forum’s Young Global Leaders. She is affiliated with the Center for Business and Government, the Center for Public Leadership, the Dubai Initiative, and the Institute for Quantitative Social Science at Harvard. She sits on the Global Agenda Councils on Diversity and Development and the Gender Gap of the World Economic Forum, and serves on boards including the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva and the advisory board of the Vienna University of Economics and Business Administration, along with numerous academic journals in economics, management, negotiation, decision analysis, and law.

item.title: Is AI dulling our minds?
item.description: As artificial intelligence tools become increasingly integrated into educational settings and professional workflows, questions about their impact on critical thinking and cognitive development have moved to the forefront of academic discourse. IQSS faculty affiliate Dan Levy, Senior Lecturer in Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, joined other Harvard faculty members in a thoughtful discussion examining whether AI will ultimately help or harm the human capacity for critical thinking.

item.title: Is the Two-Parent Family the Great Equalizer?
item.description: Research from IQSS scholars examines a provocative question in debates about inequality and family structure: does marriage and the two-parent family serve as a great equalizer, helping to reduce economic and social disparities? This question sits at the intersection of research on family structure, economic mobility, and social stratification, with important implications for how we understand pathways out of poverty and the role of family policy in addressing inequality.

item.title: Isaac Kohane
item.description:
Isaac Kohane

Chair, Dept. of Biomedical Informatics, HMS

Isaac (Zak) Kohane is the inaugural Chair of the Department of Biomedical Informatics and the Marion V. Nelson Professor of Biomedical Informatics at Harvard Medical School. He served as co-author of the Institute of Medicine Report on Precision Medicine that has been the template for national efforts. He “develops and applies computational techniques to address disease at multiple scales” — from healthcare systems functioning as “living laboratories” to functional genomics of neurodevelopment, particularly autism.

item.title: Ismail Erkam Sula
item.description:
Ismail Erkam Sula

Post-Doctoral Researcher, IQSS

Dr. Sula specializes in foreign policy and research methodology in social sciences, currently working on computer-assisted data collection methods. His research combines event data analysis with content analysis to observe the parallelism of words and deeds in foreign policy.

During his PhD at Bilkent University, he collected data on Turkey’s foreign policy, developing the Turkish Foreign Policy Roles and Events Dataset (TFPRED), which contains data from Turkish leaders’ speeches and 36,000 international news reports. He has published on Role Theory, Event Data, Middle East, Turkish foreign policy, and eclectic methodology. He is a faculty member at Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University.

item.title: J'reyesha Brannon
item.description:
J’reyesha Brannon

Harvard Climate Justice Design Fellow

J’reyesha is a born and raised Portlander. She is a University of Portland alumni (‘15), where she graduated with a degree in civil engineering with an environmental focus and minor. J’reyesha currently works as a design engineer and project manager for the City of Portland, Bureau of Environmental Services. She is passionate about accessibility and inclusion for communities of color, particularly in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) fields. Outside of work she is a lifelong volunteer, holding roles in a variety of community organizations - NAACP Portland Branch 1120B Environmental Justice Chair, President of the National Society of Black Engineers (NSBE) Portland Professionals, Good in the Hood Planning Committee, and more.

item.title: Jack Hayes
item.description:
Jack Hayes

Geospatial Data Scientist, Center for Geographic Analysis

Jack Hayes is a senior at William & Mary pursuing a major in Data Science with a focus in Spatial Data Analytics. He is “passionate about using spatial science and machine learning to advance efforts in various environmentalism fields.” Previously serving as an NSF REU Student Research Fellow at the Center for Geographic Analysis and now a Data Scientist, he aims to help “forward research through the use of big data and spatiotemporal analysis.”

item.title: Jacob Gersen
item.description:
Jacob Gersen

Sidley Austin Professor of Law

Professor Jacob E. Gersen is Professor of Law at Harvard Law School, Affiliate Professor in the Department of Government, and the Founder and Director of the Food Law Lab at the Petrie-Flom Center at Harvard Law School. The Food Law Lab supports academic research on the legal treatment of food in society. He is also the co-editor of Food Law & Policy, a new casebook to be published by Wolters Kluwer. Professor Gersen is currently working on a book titled From Court To Table about the relationship between law and food. Before joining the Harvard faculty in 2011, he was Professor of Law at the University of Chicago. He holds a Ph.D. in Political Science and a J.D. from the University of Chicago, and an A.B. in Public Policy from Brown University. His main areas of research and teaching are food law, administrative law, environmental law, torts, and constitutional theory.

item.title: Jacqueline Claudia
item.description:
Jacqueline Claudia

Executive Associate, IQSS Startup Foundry

Jacqueline Claudia is an operator, strategist, and founder whose work spans applied AI, data-driven policy, sustainability, and organizational scaling. She is an Executive Affiliate at the Institute for Quantitative Social Science and a mentor in the Startup Foundry, where she works with teams to sharpen their analytical approach, test assumptions against real-world conditions, and build solutions capable of scaling beyond the lab. Jacqueline is also Executive Director of The White Line Foundation and founder of Signal North Group, advising high-growth companies and mission-driven organizations on translating strategy into execution with clarity, speed, and disciplined customer focus. She is an Unreasonable Fellow, recognized for leadership at the intersection of technology, sustainability, and systems change.

item.title: Jacqueline Ng Lane
item.description:
Jacqueline Ng Lane

Postdoctoral Fellow, Laboratory for Innovation Science

Jacqueline Ng Lane’s research examines how diverse teams in science, medicine, and knowledge-work can make use of their resources and informational advantages to achieve innovation breakthroughs, greater creativity, and performance. She is particularly interested in how new information communication technologies can enhance performance outcomes.

Her research takes an experimental approach to understand how interventions can promote more effective team functioning and outcomes and uses a social network perspective to examine team member relations within and between teams, and their broader environmental context.

item.title: James Alt
item.description:
James Alt

Frank G. Thomson Professor of Government, Emeritus

Email: jalt@iq.harvard.edu

James E. Alt is the Frank G. Thomson Professor of Government, Emeritus. His current interests are in comparative political economy, focusing on the interaction of voters, political parties, budget and other political institutions, financial markets, and fiscal policies in industrial democracies. His recent research analyzes institutional transparency, accountability and corruption, and fiscal policy outcomes in OECD countries and US states.

item.title: James Robins
item.description:
James Robins

Mitchell L. & Robin LaFoley Dong Professor of Epidemiology

The principal focus of Dr. Robins’ research has been the development of analytic methods appropriate for drawing causal inferences from complex observational and randomized studies with time-varying exposures or treatments. The new methods are to a large extent based on the estimation of the parameters of a new class of causal models - the structural nested models - using a new class of estimators - the G estimators. The usual approach to the estimation of the effect of a time-varying treatment or exposure on time to disease is to model the hazard incidence of failure at time t as a function of past treatment history using a time-dependent Cox proportional hazards model. Dr. Robins has shown the usual approach may be biased whether or not further adjusts for past confounder history in the analysis when: (A1) there exists a time-dependent risk factor for or predictor of the event of interest that also predicts subsequent treatment, and (A2) past treatment history predicts subsequent risk factor level. Conditions (A1) and (A2) will be true whenever there are time-dependent covariates that are simultaneously confounders and intermediate variables.

item.title: James Robins Recognized with COPSS Distinguished Achievement Award
item.description:
James Robins—IQSS faculty affiliate and Mitchell L. and Robin LaFoley Dong Professor of Epidemiology at the TH Chan School of Public Health—has been recognized by the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies (COPSS) with the 2025 Distinguished Achievement Award and Lectureship.

The prestigious annual award, previously known as the RA Fisher Award and Lectureship from 1963–2019, recognizes “outstanding contributions to statistical methods that have had significant impact on scientific investigation.”

item.title: James Snyder
item.description:
James Snyder

Leroy B. Williams Professor of History and Political Science

Professor Snyder’s primary research and teaching interests are in American politics. He has written on “elections, campaign finance, legislative behavior and institutions, direct democracy, the media, and corruption.” He is a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

item.title: Jan Kinne
item.description:
Jan Kinne

CGA Visiting Fellow

Jan Kinne is a postdoc in the research area “Economics of Innovation and Business Dynamics” at the Center for European Economic Research (ZEW Mannheim). He studied geoinformatics at the University of Heidelberg and received his PhD from the University of Salzburg on the topic of “web-based innovation indicators for microgeographic analyses”. He continues to conduct methodological research around the use of (text-based) web data for innovation research. He is also the co-founder and CEO of ISTARI.AI. The company specializes in AI-based analysis of enterprise web data.

item.title: Jana Gallus
item.description:
Jana Gallus

Visiting Fellow, LISH

Jana Gallus is Assistant Professor of Strategy and Behavioral Decision Making at UCLA’s Anderson School of Management. Her research interests lie in behavioral economics and strategy, with a focus on nonfinancial incentives and their effects on human decision-making. She investigates how incentive schemes can be designed to enhance employee motivation and organizational performance in the private and non-profit sectors. Jana’s work has been published or is forthcoming in Management Science, Strategic Management Journal, Labour Economics, and Applied Economics, among other journals. Her research is informed by consulting activities for organizations on the design of incentives and recognition schemes. Jana joined UCLA from Harvard, where she was a postdoctoral fellow. She received her PhD in Economics from the University of Zurich, with the distinction summa cum laude, and holds two Master’s degrees, from Sciences Po Paris in France and the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland.

item.title: Jared Ellias
item.description:
Jared Ellias

Professor of Law

Jared Ellias is a Professor of Law and Affiliated Faculty at IQSS. He “studies corporate law, corporate financial distress and bankruptcy law using quantitative methods and text analysis.”

item.title: Jason Nemirow
item.description:
Jason Nemirow

Director, Program on Higher Education Research

Email: nemirow@fas.harvard.edu

Jason Nemirow is the director of the Program on Higher Education Research (PHER) at IQSS. In this role, he leads the program’s strategic development and research agenda, manages donor and partner engagement, and oversees operations and initiatives that advance the study of higher education through rigorous social science methods.

He is also the director of the Council for Academic Freedom at Harvard (CAFH), a 200+ member faculty association housed within PHER—all under the administrative umbrella of IQSS.

item.title: Jason Ur
item.description:
Jason Ur

Professor of Archaeology and Ethnology

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Jeff Frieden Traded to New York! Celebrating 30 Years at Harvard
item.description:
A celebration of Jeffry Frieden—a die-hard Yankees fan—and his 30 years at Harvard. Frieden, an IQSS faculty affiliate and Stanfield Professor of International Peace, has been a leading scholar of international political economy throughout his distinguished career.

Frieden’s research examines how economic interests shape political outcomes, with particular focus on exchange rate politics, financial crises, and the political economy of European integration. His work combines rigorous quantitative analysis with deep historical knowledge, exemplifying the kind of interdisciplinary scholarship IQSS supports.

item.title: Jennifer Hochschild
item.description:
Jennifer Hochschild

Henry LaBarre Jayne Professor of Government

Jennifer Hochschild is the Henry LaBarre Jayne Professor of Government at Harvard University, Professor of African and African American Studies, and Harvard College Professor. In 2011, she held the John R. Kluge Chair in American Law and Governance at the Library of Congress. She holds lectureships in the Harvard Kennedy School and Harvard Graduate School of Education. She studies and teaches about the intersection of American politics and political philosophy, particularly regarding race, ethnicity, immigration, educational and social welfare policies, public opinion, political culture, and American political thought.

item.title: Jennifer Lerner
item.description:
Jennifer Lerner

Thornton Bradshaw Professor of Public Policy

Dr. Jennifer Lerner is Thornton Bradshaw Professor of Public Policy, Decision Science, and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government and Co-founder of the Harvard Decision Science Laboratory. She is the first psychologist in the history of the Harvard Kennedy School to receive tenure. Drawing insights from psychology, economics, and neuroscience, her research examines human judgment and decision making. Together with colleagues, she has developed a theoretical framework that successfully predicts the effects of specific emotions on specific judgment and choice outcomes. Applied widely, the framework has been especially useful in predicting emotion effects on perceptions of risk, economic decisions, and attributions of responsibility. For example, she has shown that fear and anger – although both negative emotions – exert opposing effects on the perception of risk. She also actively pursues two other programs of research, examining (a) mechanisms through which accountability and other authority systems shape judgment and choice outcomes; and (b) causes and consequences of stress. Her work has, for example, revealed pathways through which bio-behavioral factors (e.g., testosterone, cortisol, and anxiety) predict stress and leadership rank among government, military, and corporate professionals. Across all areas, her work aims to expand the evidentiary base for designing public policies that maximize human wellbeing.

item.title: Jeremy Wei
item.description:
Jeremy Wei

Program Instructor, DCE

Jeremy Wei has extensive experience in research methodologies, ethics, and data analysis, having facilitated various research projects at New York University and UTSC. His research “employs advanced statistical techniques and machine learning to examine complex relationships among variables.” His current work explores AI and data privacy connections, resistance to AI adoption, and how reflective practices affect users’ intentions to adopt AI technologies. He “assists organizations in transforming disadvantages into strengths” and founded iDox.ai, described as a leading AI-driven data privacy management organization.

item.title: Jeremy Yang
item.description:
Jeremy Yang

Assistant Professor of Business Administration

Jeremy Yang is an Assistant Professor of Business Administration in the Marketing Unit at Harvard Business School. His research centers on “developing data products to improve advertising, targeting, and pricing decisions.” These algorithmic solutions draw on economic or behavioral insights and are implemented using machine learning and causal inference techniques. He is also “broadly interested in the creator economy and web3.” He earned his PhD in management from MIT.

item.title: Jeremy Yuenger
item.description:
Jeremy Yuenger

IT Client Support Services II, Harvard-MIT Data Center

Jeremy joined IQSS in 2013, and most recently has been serving in an application specialist role supporting the Dataverse Project and the FASRC cluster. In his spare time, he enjoys building mechanical keyboards, learning circuitry and PCB design, photography, and curating a vast collection of bad movies.

item.title: Ji Ma
item.description:
Ji Ma

China Biographical Database

I’m a PhD candidate and Instructor in Philanthropic Studies at Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, with PhD minor in Data Science at IU School of Informatics and Computing. I mainly use data science methodologies in my studies which include: the impact of social relation on social, political, and economic behavior; education and knowledge production in nonprofit and philanthropic studies; open data in policy studies; computational social science research methods. In 2018 spring and summer, because of my focuses on China and data science, I am at IQSS and working on the China Biographical Database (CBDB) project, which is a “freely accessible relational database with biographical information about approximately 370,000 individuals as of April 2017, primarily from the 7th through 19th centuries.” Starting from 2018 August, I’ll join UT Austin LBJ School of Public Affairs as Assistant Professor.

item.title: Ji Su Yoo
item.description:
Ji Su Yoo

Visiting Fellow

Ji Su Yoo conducts research with Professor Latanya Sweeney on data analysis to evaluate the impact of technology on society through various projects. She recently co-wrote a paper on vulnerabilities in voter registration websites called Voter Identity Theft: Submitting Changes to Voter Registrations Online to Disrupt Elections. She also co-wrote the De-anonymization of South Korean Resident Registration Numbers in 2015. She is currently interested in exposing how technology and its use in government and policy-making may exacerbate or reflect existing political and societal inequalities. Her interests also include national identification systems and data privacy in health care research. She graduated from Harvard College in 2015 with a B.A. in Social Studies.

item.title: Ji Su Yoo Awarded P.D. Soros Fellowship
item.description:
Ji Su Yoo, a Harvard alumna and IQSS Fellow, was named a 2020 recipient of the Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans. The prestigious fellowship supports outstanding graduate students who are immigrants or children of immigrants in the United States.

Yoo’s research focuses on technology in decision-making, exploring how algorithmic systems affect fairness, accountability, and transparency in high-stakes contexts. Her work at the intersection of computer science and public policy reflects IQSS’s interdisciplinary approach to studying technology’s social impact.

item.title: Jianping Xu
item.description:
Jianping Xu

Associate Professor, Fudan University

Main research direction is the political geography during historical period of China, Particularly concerned about the border demarcation of the administrative regions in the Republican Period.

item.title: Jim Waldo
item.description:
Jim Waldo

Gordon McKay Professor of the Practice of Computer Science

Jim Waldo is a Gordon McKay Professor of the Practice of Computer Science in the School of Engineering and Applied Sciences at Harvard, where he teaches courses in distributed systems and privacy. He also teaches topics in technology and policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, is the Chief Technology Officer for the School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, and is a Distinguished Engineer with Harvard University Information Technology.

item.title: Jingjia Qiu
item.description:
Jingjia Qiu

Visiting Scholar, Chinese Biographical Database

Jingjia Qiu “works on Digital Humanities and History Research of Liao-Jin dynasties in Ancient China: Centering on the CBDB Project.”

item.title: Jocelyn Kelly
item.description:
Jocelyn Kelly

Assistant Professor, Harvard Medical School

Dr. Jocelyn Kelly is the Director for Harvard Humanitarian Initiative’s (HHI) Gender, Rights and Resilience (GR2) program, where she “implements projects to examine issues relating to gender, peace, and security in conflict-affected and climate-fragile environments.” Her work centers on understanding and preventing gender-based violence and human trafficking in complex crises, with emphasis on strengthening resilience and social cohesion mechanisms. She has briefed the UN Security Council, the U.S. State Department, USAID, the World Bank, OFDA, the Woodrow Wilson Center, and the U.S. Institute of Peace on gender and security issues. She received the Paula Kantor Award for Excellence in Field Research from ICRW in 2019 and was first author on a publication voted among the “most influential articles of 2016” by the journal Conflict and Health. More recently, her work has explored connections between human rights and environmental protection. Her other research interests include promoting and measuring GBV risk mitigation in humanitarian emergencies, understanding the continuum of GBV before, during, and after crisis, and “measuring and promoting social cohesion and community resilience as a pathway to reducing violence.”

item.title: Joeri Smits
item.description:
Joeri Smits

Postdoctoral Research Fellow

Dr. Joeri Smits conducts research in “applied microeconomics, econometrics, and political economy.” He earned his PhD from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich and held a postdoctoral position at Yale before joining Harvard.

item.title: Join Dataverse for the GREI Collaborative Webinar Series
item.description:
The Dataverse Project invites the research data management community to participate in the GREI Collaborative Webinar Series, which focuses on repository resources and best practices specifically tailored for NIH-funded research. This series provides valuable guidance for researchers, repository administrators, and data managers working to meet the National Institutes of Health’s data sharing policies and requirements while leveraging Dataverse as a trusted repository platform.

The GREI (Generalist Repository Ecosystem Initiative) Collaborative brings together major research data repositories to provide coordinated support for biomedical researchers navigating data sharing requirements. The webinar series covers practical topics including metadata best practices, preparing datasets for sharing, understanding access controls and restricted data considerations, and ensuring long-term preservation of research data. These sessions are particularly valuable as NIH continues to strengthen its data sharing policies, requiring researchers to plan for and execute robust data management from the beginning of their projects.

item.title: Jon C Rogowski
item.description:
Jon C Rogowski

Assistant Professor, Government Department

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Jonas Heite
item.description:
Jonas Heite

Visiting Fellow, LISH; Max Planck Institute

Jonas is a Research Fellow and PhD Candidate at the Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition and at the LMU Munich, Germany. He is a Visiting Scholar at the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard, Institute for Quantitative Social Sciences (IQSS). His research focuses on incentives, behavior and performance of individuals in tournaments, particularly investigating the effect of pressure due to heterogeneous abilities of contestants through field and lab experiments.

item.title: Jonathan D Teubner
item.description:
Jonathan D Teubner

Visiting Scholar, Human Flourishing Program

Jonathan D. Teubner is a Visiting Scholar at Harvard’s Human Flourishing Program and a Fellow at the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture at UVA. He has led initiatives in academia, business, and nonprofits, and pioneered the application of machine learning to improving peace building methods.

From 2021-2024, he led Social Connectedness Research at Harvard’s IQSS. Previously, he was Associate Director of the Initiative on Religion, Politics and Conflict at UVA, where he led a team developing NLP tools. He founded FilterLabs.AI, a data analytics company tracking the impact of global propaganda on local communities, and directed Global Covenant Partners (2016-2019), an NGO focused on reducing religion-related violence.

item.title: Joseph Blitzstein
item.description:
Joseph Blitzstein

Professor of the Practice in Statistics

Email: blitz@fas.harvard.edu

Joe Blitzstein is a Professor of the Practice in Statistics at Harvard University. He completed his Ph.D. at Stanford University in 2006, with advisor Persi Diaconis. His research combines “statistics, probability, and combinatorics.” He is particularly interested in “graphical models, complex networks, and Monte Carlo algorithms” including “sequential importance sampling and Markov chains.”

item.title: Joseph Newhouse
item.description:
Joseph Newhouse

John D. MacArthur Professor of Health Policy

Dr. Newhouse holds the John D. MacArthur Professorship in Health Policy and Management at Harvard University, where he directs the Division of Health Policy Research and Education, chairs the Committee on Higher Degrees in Health Policy, and leads the Interfaculty Initiative in Health Policy. He belongs to the faculties of the Kennedy School of Government, Harvard Medical School, Harvard School of Public Health, and the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, while also serving as a Faculty Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research. He earned both his B.A. and Ph.D. in Economics from Harvard and was a Fulbright Scholar in Germany. He spent his first twenty years at RAND, where he “designed and directed the RAND Health Insurance Experiment, which studied the consequences of different ways of financing medical services.” From 1981 to 1985 he headed the RAND Economics Department.

item.title: Josh Lerner
item.description:
Josh Lerner

Jacob H. Schiff Professor of Investment Banking

Josh Lerner is the Head of the Entrepreneurial Management Unit and the Jacob H. Schiff Professor of Investment Banking at Harvard Business School. He graduated from Yale College with a special divisional major combining physics with the history of technology. He worked for several years on technological innovation and public policy issues at the Brookings Institution, for a public-private task force in Chicago, and on Capitol Hill. He then earned a Ph.D. from Harvard’s Economics Department.

item.title: Joshua D. Kertzer
item.description:
Joshua D. Kertzer

Professor of Government, FAS

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Joshua Lieberman
item.description:
Joshua Lieberman

Senior Researcher, Center for Geographic Analysis

Josh is a senior researcher at the Center for Geographic Analysis with a background in “earth and environmental sciences, as well as geographic information / interoperability science and information standards innovation.” His research interests include “geospatial semantics, spatial data science, hydrology, and predictive modeling / decision support for disaster management.”

Josh is a “Retired Director of Innovation Programs at the Open Geospatial Consortium” and sometime instructor of advanced geospatial analysis in Harvard DCE.

item.title: Jukka-Pekka Onnela
item.description:
Jukka-Pekka Onnela

Assistant Professor of Biostatistics

JP Onnela is an Assistant Professor of Biostatistics. Before joining the faculty, he spent two years as a Postdoctoral Fellow at Harvard Medical School, one year as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar at the Kennedy School, and two years as a Junior Research Fellow at Oxford University. He obtained his doctorate at the Helsinki University of Technology (now Aalto University) in 2006. He is interested in a broad range of theoretical and applied problems in network science. His current research focuses on statistical and mathematical analysis and modeling of social networks and their connection to human health; development of metrics and methods for network analysis; and online social systems and social media. His applied work uses large datasets, such as those derived from cell phone metadata, to learn about the structure and dynamics of human social systems.

item.title: Junghwan Kim
item.description:
Junghwan Kim

Postdoctoral Fellow, CGA

Junghwan Kim is a postdoctoral fellow at CGA. He earned his “Ph.D. in Geography (2021) from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).” He also holds a “B.S. in Urban Planning and Engineering (Summa Cum Laude) from Yonsei University (2016)” in South Korea and a Master of Urban Planning from UIUC (2018).

His research has appeared in several peer-reviewed journals, including the Annals of the American Association of Geographers, Journal of Transport Geography, Cartography and Geographic Information Science, Environmental Research, and Transactions in GIS.

item.title: Justin de Benedictis-Kessner
item.description:
Justin de Benedictis-Kessner

Assistant Professor of Public Policy, Kennedy School

Justin de Benedictis-Kessner is a political scientist and Assistant Professor of Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School. He researches American politics, focusing on “political behavior, public policy, local politics, elections, and experimental and quantitative methodology.”

item.title: Kaixuan Zhang
item.description:
Kaixuan Zhang

Data Science Fellow

Kaixuan Zhang is a Data Science Fellow with a research focus on “computer vision and document intelligence.”

item.title: Karim Lakhani
item.description:
Karim Lakhani

Charles Edward Wilson Professor of Business Administration

Karim R. Lakhani is a Professor of Business Administration at the Harvard Business School and one of the Principal Investigators of the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard (LISH). He specializes in the management of technological innovation in firms and communities. His research focuses on distributed innovation systems and how innovative activity moves to the edges of organizations and into communities. He has extensively studied open source software communities and their unique innovation and product development strategies. He has also investigated how critical knowledge from outside organizations can be accessed through innovation contests.

item.title: Katelyn Long
item.description:
Katelyn Long

Post-Doctoral Fellow, Human Flourishing Program

Katelyn Long’s current work focuses on the group dynamics of religion on human flourishing and the development of tradition-specific spiritual well-being measures. She completed her doctoral studies at Boston University School of Public Health where her dissertation focused on the role of faith-based and charitable health providers in the context of the broader health system. Her other public health work has been in the areas of chronic disease prevention, adolescent health, mental health, and positive deviance in vulnerable communities. She earned her Master of Science in Public Health from the University of Utah and her undergraduate degree in religion with a minor in music from Vanguard University.

item.title: Kathryn Davidson
item.description:
Kathryn Davidson

Assistant Professor of Linguistics

I’m an assistant professor in Linguistics at Harvard University where my research investigates the unique capacity that we have to understand an infinite number of sentences that we’ve never heard before (semantics), how we incorporate contextual information into these meanings (pragmatics), and how we ever learn to do this (development). I’m especially interested in what we can learn about linguistic meaning from visual language, both in full natural languages like American Sign Language and in co-speech gestures to spoken languages like English. My background is in math and theoretical linguistics, and in my research I make balanced use of theory for hypothesis creation with psycholinguistic experimental methods for gathering and analyzing data.

item.title: Katie Mika
item.description:
Katie Mika

Data Services Librarian

IQSS Staff Member.

item.title: Kenneth Shepsle
item.description:
Kenneth Shepsle

George D. Markham Professor of Government

Kenneth A. Shepsle is the George D. Markham Professor of Government. He has authored or co-authored numerous books including Politics in Plural Societies: A Theory of Democratic Instability, The Giant Jigsaw Puzzle: Democratic Committee Assignments in the Modern House, Models of Multiparty Electoral Competition, Making and Breaking Governments, American Government: Power and Purpose, and Analyzing Politics. He has edited or co-edited works such as The Congressional Budget Process: Some Views From the Inside, Political Equilibrium, Perspectives on Positive Political Economy, and Cabinet Ministers and Parliamentary Government.

item.title: Kenneth Shepsle Awarded William H. Riker Prize
item.description:
Kenneth A. Shepsle, IQSS affiliate and George D. Markham Professor of Government, received the 2023 William H. Riker prize in Political Science from the University of Rochester. The prize recognizes lifetime contributions to the scientific study of politics through formal theory and its applications.

Shepsle’s career has been defined by groundbreaking work on legislative institutions, congressional committees, and the structure of political choice. His research on institutional design and legislative bargaining has fundamentally shaped how political scientists understand how rules and procedures affect policy outcomes.

item.title: Kevin Croke
item.description:
Kevin Croke

Assistant Professor of Global Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

He is an “assistant professor of global health in the Department of Global Health and Population at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.” Previously he worked as an economist in the World Bank’s Development Impact Evaluation (DIME) group. During 2014-2015, he served as a postdoctoral fellow in political economy and research associate at HSPH. He earned his PhD from Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) in 2011 and his BA from the College of William and Mary in 2001.

item.title: Kevin Ryan
item.description:
Kevin Ryan

Professor of Linguistics

Kevin M. Ryan is Professor of Linguistics at Harvard University, where he chaired the Department from 2019 to 2025. His research centers on phonology and poetics, using “quantitative corpus analysis to model the cognitive organization of speech and verbal arts.” A major thread of this work examines prosodic systems such as stress, weight, meter, and phrasal phonology, showing how “gradient statistical patterns in language data inform phonological theory.” He authored Prosodic weight: categories and continua (Oxford University Press, 2019).

item.title: Kosuke Imai
item.description:
Kosuke Imai

Professor of Government and Statistics, FAS

Kosuke Imai is Professor of Government and of Statistics at Harvard University. His research focuses on political methodology and applied statistics in social sciences. He has “extensively worked on the development and applications of statistical methods for causal inference with experimental and observational data.” His other methodological research areas include survey methodology and computational algorithms for data-intensive social science research. His substantive applications range from “the randomized evaluation of Mexican universal health insurance program to the study of public opinion and insurgent violence in Afghanistan.” Before joining Harvard in 2018, he taught at Princeton University for 15 years. He currently serves as President of the Society for Political Methodology and holds a visiting professorship in the Graduate Schools of Law and Politics at the University of Tokyo.

item.title: Kosuke Imai Returns to Harvard
item.description:
by Jonathan Colburn

Changing Seasons: Kosuke Imai Returns to Harvard to Expand the Reach of Quantitative Social Science at Harvard and Abroad

When he last occupied office space at Harvard, Kosuke Imai, IQSS’s newest resident faculty affiliate, had a decidedly different experience than he does in his current location at CGIS Knafel overlooking Cambridge Street.

“IQSS didn’t exist yet, but its predecessor was housed in a little yellow house where the Ukrainian Research Institute is,” Imai recalls. His graduate student office was upstairs in the attic, and demolition of the old building nearby meant that construction equipment would shake his entire workspace.

item.title: Kwok-Leong Tang
item.description:
Kwok-Leong Tang

Managing Director, Digital China Initiative

Kwok-Leong Tang serves as the Managing Director of the Digital China Initiative and a lecturer in the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at Harvard University. By training, Kwok-Leong is a historian. He received his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a Ph.D. in history and East Asian studies from Pennsylvania State University. In recent years, he has focused on exploring the potential of new technologies in humanities research. Over the last two years, he has organized and instructed workshops on adopting generative AI in Chinese studies and humanities research at Harvard and other institutions.

item.title: Large Data Support in Harvard Dataverse
item.description:
Large Data Support in Harvard Dataverse

Date: March 26, 2025

Time: 12:00 PM – 1:00 PM EDT

Location: Virtual via Zoom

This webinar covers Harvard Dataverse Repository new services for stewardship and archiving of large-scale research data. It highlights scalable, sustainable solutions using advanced storage for researchers, institutions, and groups handling large and complex datasets, offering a comprehensive and cost-effective approach to this service.

Presenter: Sonia Barbosa and Leonid Andreev, The Dataverse Project, IQSS

item.title: Latanya Sweeney
item.description:
Latanya Sweeney

Daniel Paul Professor of Government and Technology

Latanya Sweeney is the Daniel Paul Professor of the Practice of Government and Technology at the Harvard Kennedy School and in the Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences, director and founder of the Public Interest Tech Lab, Editor-in-Chief of Technology Science, director and founder of the Data Privacy Lab, former Chief Technology Officer at the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and Distinguished Career Professor of Computer Science, Technology and Policy at Carnegie Mellon University. She has 3 patents, more than 100 academic publications, pioneered the field known as data privacy, launched the emerging area known as algorithmic fairness, and was first to present technology challenges in U.S. elections. Her work is explicitly cited in two U.S. regulations, including the U.S. federal medical privacy regulation (known as HIPAA). She is a recipient of the prestigious Louis D. Brandeis Privacy Award, the American Psychiatric Association’s Privacy Advocacy Award, an elected fellow of the American College of Medical Informatics, and has testified before government bodies worldwide. She earned her PhD in computer science from MIT in 2001, being the first black woman to do so, and her undergraduate degree in computer science from Harvard University.
