Dr. Sweeney creates and uses technology to assess and solve societal, political and governance problems, and teaches others how to do the same. Her most recent work focuses on “technology tools to strengthen elections, analyses of social media platforms, and new real-world privacy paradigms.” She is also helping to pioneer a new field known as public interest technology.

item.title: Latanya Sweeney Appointed to FTC
item.description:
IQSS affiliate Latanya Sweeney, director of the Data Privacy Lab and Professor of Government, was appointed to join the Federal Trade Commission as Chief Technologist in January 2014. The appointment brought deep technical expertise on data privacy to the nation’s primary consumer protection agency.

Sweeney’s research has demonstrated how supposedly anonymous data can be re-identified, revealing fundamental vulnerabilities in how organizations handle personal information. Her work has influenced privacy regulations and corporate data practices worldwide, making her uniquely qualified for the FTC role.

item.title: Latanya Sweeney Featured in Forbes List
item.description:
IQSS faculty affiliate and Data Privacy Lab director Latanya Sweeney was profiled in a Forbes list of Incredible Women Advancing A.I. Research. The recognition highlighted her pioneering work at the intersection of artificial intelligence, data privacy, and public policy.

Sweeney’s contributions to the field include demonstrating that 87% of the U.S. population could be uniquely identified by just their ZIP code, birth date, and gender—a finding that fundamentally changed how organizations think about data anonymization. Her research continues to expose hidden privacy risks in commercial and government data systems.

item.title: Latanya Sweeney Technology Science Research Collaboration
item.description:
In 2015, Latanya Sweeney received a $250,000 MacArthur Foundation grant to engage scholars and students investigating unforeseen consequences of technology. The funding supported the Technology Science Research Collaboration Network, bringing together researchers across disciplines to study how technology affects society.

The network connects scholars who might otherwise work in isolation, facilitating collaborative research on topics including algorithmic bias, surveillance, data privacy, and digital discrimination. This interdisciplinary approach recognizes that technology’s social impacts cannot be understood through any single disciplinary lens.

item.title: Launching the Differential Privacy Deployments Registry
item.description:
OpenDP at IQSS has launched the Differential Privacy Deployments Registry, a groundbreaking initiative designed to empower organizations and researchers to share detailed information about their differential privacy implementations. This new resource addresses a critical need in the data privacy community by creating a centralized platform where practitioners can document their approaches, methodologies, and lessons learned from real-world deployments of differential privacy technologies.

Differential privacy has emerged as the gold standard for protecting individual privacy while enabling valuable data analysis, but understanding how to implement it effectively in practice remains challenging. The registry provides a venue for organizations to transparently share their deployment strategies, parameter choices, and practical considerations, helping others learn from existing implementations. By documenting both successes and challenges, the registry aims to accelerate the adoption of differential privacy across various sectors including government, healthcare, technology, and research.

item.title: Laura Rosendahl Huber
item.description:
Laura Rosendahl Huber

Visiting Fellow, LISH; Max Planck Institute

Laura Rosendahl Huber holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Amsterdam and is currently working as a Senior Research Fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition in Munich, Germany. Her research integrates entrepreneurship research with experimental methods and focuses on the empirical analysis of entrepreneurship education, entrepreneurial teams, and the evaluation of policies aimed at fostering entrepreneurship and innovation. In particular, she is interested in gaining a better understanding of the gender inequality among both entrepreneurs and inventors (and potential solutions), and how team composition affects team performance in creative processes. A common denominator in her research is the use of field experiments.

item.title: Len Wisniewski
item.description:
Len Wisniewski

Senior Director of Research Computing

Email: lwisniewski@iq.harvard.edu

Len Wisniewski is Senior Director of Research Computing at IQSS. Before IQSS, Len was Engineering Manager for the High Performance Computing group at Sun Microsystems, leading the teams developing the Sun HPC ClusterTools and Sun Studio Performance Analyzer products. In that role, he actively supported the Open MPI open-source community. Before entering a management role, Len held software engineering roles at various companies, including Sun/Oracle, Acopia Networks (acquired by F5 Networks), and Thinking Machines (acquired by Sun). His primary technical interests have been in developing algorithms and file systems for parallel and distributed computers.

item.title: Leopoldo Biffi
item.description:
Leopoldo Biffi

PhD Candidate, Geneva Graduate Institute

Leopoldo Biffi is a PhD candidate in international relations/political science at the Graduate Institute in Geneva. He was previously a visiting fellow in the Department of Government at Harvard University. His research interests include international institutions, international trade and investment, the European Union, and Japan. His work focuses on the institutional design of international trade and investment agreements, and more recently on treaty implementation. He holds a BA in International Relations from King’s College London (Department of War Studies) and an MA in International Relations/Political Science from the Graduate Institute in Geneva.

item.title: Li Cong
item.description:
Li Cong

Visiting Scholar, China Biographical Database

Li Cong’s research interests include “digital humanity and local gazetteer, and national culture park.”

item.title: Libby Jenke
item.description:
Libby Jenke

Visiting Assistant Professor of Public Policy

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Lingbo Liu
item.description:
Lingbo Liu

Visiting Scholar, CGA

Lingbo Liu is a Lecturer at the Department of Urban Planning, School of Urban Design, Wuhan University, vice director of Urban Innovation Lab, and a Visiting Scholar at Harvard University. His research field focuses on healthy cities, using multi-source data and spatial quantitative models to capture the spatiotemporal features of urban system, analyze the coupling mechanism of the space-human system, and provide decision support for public policy, urban planning and design. His research highlights the characteristics of the entropy models in analyzing urban complex systems and explores a potential systematic path of Social Physics 2.0. Since 2019, as one of the core members, he has participated in the workflow-based spatial analysis platform project initiated by CGA of Harvard University.

item.title: Luke Miratrix
item.description:
Luke Miratrix

Assistant Professor of Education

Luke Miratrix is an assistant professor in the Harvard School of Education and affiliate faculty in the Harvard Department of Statistics. His primary research focus is on causal inference methods. Much of his work develops methodology to assess and characterize treatment effect heterogeneity in randomized clinical trials and observational studies, and to characterize variation in treatment impact on post-treatment or latent subgroups such as from non-compliance. He also works on statistical evaluations of cluster-randomized and multi-site trials. Other research interests include data mining using high-dimensional and sparse (regularized) methods, with a focus on text summarization in contexts such as newspaper corpora, legal decisions, and databases of free-text reports. His main concerns relate to the “applicability and legitimacy” of “data-driven arguments,” which leads him to examine the “performance and usability of simple, minimal-assumption methods.” He received his Doctorate in Statistics from University of California, Berkeley in Spring 2012 after switching to that field in 2009 from SESAME, a doctorate program in Mathematics and Science education also at Berkeley. He also has a MS in Computer Science from M.I.T., a BS in Computer Science from the California Institute of Technology, and a BA in Mathematics from Reed College. Between graduate careers, he was a high school teacher and tutor for 7 years.

item.title: Maha R. Farhat
item.description:
Maha R. Farhat

Assistant Professor of Biomedical Informatics, HMS

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Mahnum Shahzad
item.description:
Mahnum Shahzad

Instructor, Harvard Medical School

Mahnum Shahzad is a PhD Candidate in Health Policy and Economics at Harvard University. Her research focuses on decision making in healthcare at consumer and provider levels, with projects based in the US and Pakistan. Prior to graduate school, she worked as a research assistant at NBER with Professor Heidi Williams on “questions relating to pharmaceuticals and innovation.” She earned a bachelor’s of arts in economics and mathematics from Dartmouth College.

item.title: Mahzarin Banaji
item.description:
Mahzarin Banaji

Richard Clarke Cabot Professor of Social Ethics, Department of Psychology

Email: mahzarin_banaji@harvard.edu

Banaji taught at Yale University from 1986-2002 as Reuben Post Halleck Professor of Psychology. She currently holds the Richard Clarke Cabot Professorship of Social Ethics in Harvard’s Department of Psychology and simultaneously held the “George A. and Helen Dunham Cowan Chair in Human Dynamics at the Santa Fe Institute (2011-2014).” She also served as the inaugural Carol K. Pforzheimer Professor at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study (2002-2008).

item.title: Making Historical Figure Search 500X Faster
item.description:
The China Biographical Database (CBDB) team at IQSS redesigned their name indexing method to make text analysis research considerably faster—achieving a 500-fold improvement in search performance. The optimization enables researchers to search across thousands of years of Chinese historical records with unprecedented speed.

The breakthrough came from rethinking how the database indexes Chinese names, which present unique computational challenges due to the nature of Chinese characters and historical naming conventions. The previous approach required sequential scanning of large text corpora, but the new indexing method allows near-instantaneous lookup even across millions of historical records.

item.title: Malika Zeghal
item.description:
Malika Zeghal

Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal Professor in Contemporary Islamic Thought

Malika Zeghal is the Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal Professor in Contemporary Islamic Thought and Life in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilization at Harvard University. She is also an Affiliated Professor of Government and a member of the Committee on the Study of Religion. Her research centers on the interaction between Islam and politics in the modern Middle East, with particular interest in the formation of modern Muslim states and their religious institutions, as well as the intellectual and political genealogies of Islamist movements. She also studies modern Islamic intellectual history in the Middle East, Europe, and North America.

item.title: Mapping Chinese History: The China Biographical Database
item.description:
The China Biographical Database (CBDB) aims at identifying and cataloging individuals across millennia of Chinese society and their shared connections. This ambitious digital humanities project, based at IQSS, represents one of the largest biographical databases ever constructed for historical research.

CBDB contains biographical information from Chinese historical records spanning the 7th through 19th centuries, enabling researchers to conduct statistical analysis, social network analysis, and spatial analysis of historical Chinese society. The database reveals patterns of social mobility, political networks, and cultural transmission that traditional historical methods could not detect.

item.title: Marcello Carammia
item.description:
Marcello Carammia

Assoc Professor, University of Catania

Marcello Carammia is an Associate Professor of Political Science at the Department of Political and Social Sciences, University of Catania (Italy). Between 2015 and 2019, he was a Senior Researcher at the European Union Asylum Agency, where he was responsible for the Agency’s Research Programme on the push and pull factors of asylum migration.

He is a member of the Comparative Agendas Project, where he is a founding co-director of the Italian Agendas Project and of the European Union Agendas Project. His research focuses on the comparative analysis of institutions and policy processes, with special interest in the interaction between migration dynamics, politics, and policy. He is also interested in computational social science, notably in developing approaches to forecasting social processes.

item.title: Marco Tabellini
item.description:
Marco Tabellini

Assistant Professor, Harvard Business School

Marco Tabellini is an Assistant Professor in the Business, Government, and International Economy unit at Harvard Business School and a Research Affiliate at CEPR and IZA. He “earned his PhD in Economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2018” and was a Postdoctoral Fellow at HBS in 2018-2019 before joining the faculty. He also holds a B.S. and M.S. in Economics and Social Sciences from Bocconi University.

item.title: Margo I. Seltzer
item.description:
Margo I. Seltzer

Herchel Smith Professor of Computer Science

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Maria Soledad Hershey
item.description:
Maria Soledad Hershey

Research Associate, Human Flourishing Program

Maria Soledad Hershey’s research focuses on “understanding upstream sociocultural and behavioral determinants of health to advance chronic disease prevention and well-being.” Her work bridges epidemiology, lifestyle medicine, and human flourishing. She has studied the potential synergistic interaction between the Mediterranean diet and physical activity, and protective associations of other modifiable lifestyle factors using an overall Mediterranean lifestyle index, on premature mortality and chronic disease. Her previous postdoctoral work at the Human Flourishing Program at Harvard assessed “a virtue-based leadership intervention on context-sensitive decision-making and flourishing.” She previously completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health as part of the Harvard Educational Resource Center Training Grant, where she conducted the primary analysis of a randomized controlled trial on adherence to the Mediterranean diet in a non-Mediterranean working population. She is passionate about “translating empirical research into holistic, evidence-based interventions and policy advocacy for preventive health and well-being.”

item.title: Marie Thursby
item.description:
Marie Thursby

Visiting Scholar, LISH; Professor Emeritus, Georgia Tech

IQSS Visitor/Affiliate.

item.title: Mark Esposito
item.description:
Mark Esposito

Faculty Associate, Berkman Klein Center

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Mark Ramseyer
item.description:
Mark Ramseyer

Mitsubishi Professor of Japanese Legal Studies

Mark Ramseyer spent most of his childhood in provincial towns and cities in southern Japan, attending Japanese schools for K-6. He returned to the U.S. for college. Before attending law school, he studied Japanese history in graduate school. Ramseyer graduated from HLS in 1982. He clerked for the Hon. Stephen Breyer (then on the First Circuit), worked for two years at Sidley & Austin (in corporate tax), and studied as a Fulbright student at the University of Tokyo. After teaching at UCLA and the University of Chicago, he came to Harvard in 1998. He has also taught or co-taught courses at several Japanese universities (in Japanese). In his research, Ramseyer primarily studies Japanese law, and primarily from a law & economics perspective. In addition to a variety of Japanese law courses, he teaches the basic Corporations course. With Professors Klein and Bainbridge, he co-edits a Foundation Press casebook in the field.

item.title: Mark Schelker
item.description:
Mark Schelker

Professor of Economics, University of Fribourg

Mark is a professor of economics at the University of Fribourg. He mostly works in political economics and public economics. He is interested in how political institutions affect political, economic and social outcomes, and how economic and political networks interact over time and space.

item.title: Matthew Baum
item.description:
Matthew Baum

Marvin Kalb Professor of Global Communications and Professor of Public Policy, HKS

Email: matthew_baum@harvard.edu

Matthew A. Baum is Marvin Kalb Professor of Global Communications and Professor of Public Policy at Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government. His research focuses on “delineating the effects of domestic politics on international conflict and cooperation” generally and American foreign policy specifically, as well as the role of mass media and public opinion in contemporary American politics. His work has appeared in over a dozen leading scholarly journals, including the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, and Journal of Politics. His books include Soft News Goes to War: Public Opinion and American Foreign Policy in the New Media Age and War Stories: The Causes and Consequences of Public Views of War (Forthcoming 2009, Princeton University Press). He has contributed op/ed articles to various newspapers and magazines in the U.S. and abroad. Before coming to Harvard, Baum was associate professor of political science and communication studies at UCLA. He received his PhD in political science at UC San Diego in 2000.

item.title: Matthew Blackwell
item.description:
Matthew Blackwell

Associate Professor of Government, FAS

Email: mblackwell@gov.harvard.edu

Matthew Blackwell is an Associate Professor of Government at Harvard University. He studies political methodology, focusing on “dynamic causal inference, instrumental variables, experimental design, missing data, and panel data.” His substantive interests include “the lasting effects of slavery on political attitudes in the US South.”

item.title: Matthew F. Wilson
item.description:
Matthew F. Wilson

Senior Director, Baylor University

Matthew F. Wilson, Ph.D., serves as Senior Director of Research Translation and AI Strategy at Baylor University’s Institute for Global Human Flourishing. Prior to receiving a Ph.D. in Philosophy from Baylor University, Matthew led a successful corporate career where he held various roles in finance, marketing, and product management. He holds an M.B.A. in Marketing from Indiana University, a B.A. in Economics from Wake Forest University, and an M.A. in the Philosophy of Religion from Trinity Evangelical Divinity School. His book, Ownership Unlocked: 4 Principles to Build Self-Driven Teams That Take Initiative, Innovate, and Win, draws on his corporate leadership experience and doctoral research to present a practical framework for cultivating psychological ownership in teams — the invisible force that motivates people to treat a business like their own. His current research interests lie at the intersection of virtue theory and artificial intelligence, motivated by his belief that philosophy has practical value for human flourishing. Dr. Wilson can be reached at matthewfwilson.com.

item.title: Matthew Stephenson
item.description:
Matthew Stephenson

Eli Goldston Professor of Law

Matthew Stephenson is Eli Goldston Professor of Law at Harvard Law School, where he teaches administrative law, legislation and regulation, and political economy of public law. His research focuses on applying positive political theory to public law, especially administrative procedure, judicial institutions, and separation of powers. Before joining Harvard Law School’s faculty, he clerked for Senior Judge Stephen Williams on the D.C. Circuit and for Justice Anthony Kennedy on the Supreme Court. He received his J.D. and Ph.D. in political science from Harvard in 2003 and his B.A. from Harvard College in 1997.

item.title: Matthew T Lee
item.description:
Matthew T Lee

Research Associate, Human Flourishing Program

Matthew T. Lee is a Research Associate and Director of the Flourishing Network at the Human Flourishing Program. His research explores well-being and flourishing, benevolent service to others, and the integration of social science and the humanities.

item.title: Matthew W. Wilson
item.description:
Matthew W. Wilson

Visiting Scholar, CGA; Assoc Professor, University of Kentucky

Matthew W. Wilson, PhD, is Associate Professor of Geography at the University of Kentucky and Visiting Scholar at the Center for Geographic Analysis at Harvard University. He co-founded and co-directs the New Mappings Collaboratory which studies and facilitates new engagements with geographic representation. He is co-editor of Understanding Spatial Media, published by SAGE, and his most recent book is New Lines, published with the University of Minnesota Press. He has previously taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, and his current research examines mid-20th century, digital mapping practices.

item.title: Max Bazerman
item.description:
Max Bazerman

Jesse Isidor Straus Professor of Business Administration, Harvard Business School

Email: mbazerman@hbs.edu

Max H. Bazerman holds the Jesse Isidor Straus Professorship of Business Administration at Harvard Business School and serves as Co-Director of the Center for Public Leadership at Harvard Kennedy School.

His research centers on decision making, negotiation, and ethics. He has authored, co-authored, or co-edited twenty books, including The Power of Noticing (Simon and Schuster, 2014) and Blind Spots (with Ann Tenbrunsel, Princeton University Press, 2011), along with over 200 research articles and chapters. He serves on editorial boards of multiple journals including American Behavioral Scientist, Journal of Management and Governance, Mind and Society, and others.

item.title: Maya Sen
item.description:
Maya Sen

Professor of Public Policy, Kennedy School

Maya Sen is a political scientist and Professor of Public Policy at Harvard University. Her research interests include law, political economy, race and ethnic politics, and statistical methods. Her research has been published in journals such as the American Political Science Review, the American Journal of Political Science, and the Journal of Politics, and has been covered by the New York Times, the Washington Post, The Economist, National Public Radio, and other outlets.

item.title: Mehrnoush Soroush
item.description:
Mehrnoush Soroush

Visiting Fellow

Mehrnoush Soroush is a landscape archaeologist specializing in ancient water management systems in the Middle East. She holds a Ph.D. in the Study of the Ancient World, from New York University an MA in Architecture from the University of Tehran, Iran. Her research primarily revolves around remote sensing of historic aerial and satellite imagery and use of Geographic Information System to map and study archaeological remains of hydraulic and urban infrastructures that are often lost or threatened by development, war etc. As a CGA fellow, she will work with Professor Jason Ur on the systematic use of multitemporal historic and modern satellite imagery for the purpose of the reconstruction of archaeological landscape of Erbil Plain, in the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

item.title: Melani Cammett
item.description:
Melani Cammett

Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs, Department of Government; Professor in the Department of Global Health and Population, Chan School of Public Health

Email: mcammett@gov.harvard.edu

Melani Cammett is Professor of Government at Harvard University, specializing in the political economy of development and the Middle East and North Africa. She has authored four books:

  • A Political Economy of the Middle East (with Ishac Diwan, Alan Richards, and John Waterbury, 2015)
  • Compassionate Communalism: Welfare and Sectarianism in Lebanon (2014), which won the 2015 APSA Giovanni Sartori Book Award and received Honorable Mention for the 2015 APSA Gregory Luebbert Book Award
  • The Politics of Nonstate Welfare (coedited with Lauren Morris MacLean, 2014)
  • Globalization and Business Politics in North Africa: A Comparative Perspective (2007, 2010)

She has received fellowships from organizations including the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Qualitative and Multi-Methods Research Section of APSA, the Comparative Politics Section of APSA, the Smith Richardson Foundation, the U.S. Institute of Peace, the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies, and the Social Science Research Council. She has “published numerous articles in scholarly and policy journals, and consults for development policy organizations.”

item.title: Melissa Dell
item.description:
Melissa Dell

Professor of Economics, Department of Economics

Melissa Dell is a professor in the Economics Department and a faculty research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. Her research focuses on long-run economic development, primarily in Latin America and Asia. She has examined the impacts of weather on economic growth and is currently conducting research about the long-run effects of agrarian reform and agricultural technology investments in Mexico and East Asia. She received a PhD in Economics from MIT, a masters degree in Economics from Oxford, and a BA from Harvard College.

item.title: Melissa Dell Wins 2020 Clark Medal
item.description:
IQSS faculty affiliate Melissa Dell received the American Economic Association’s 2020 John Bates Clark Medal, granted annually to an economist under 40 judged to have made the most significant contributions to economic thought and knowledge. The medal is often considered a precursor to the Nobel Prize in Economics.

Dell’s research examines how historical institutions—from colonial forced labor systems to authoritarian regimes—shape economic development over centuries. Her innovative use of geographic discontinuities, historical records, and computational methods has produced some of the most compelling evidence for the long-run effects of institutions on economic outcomes.

item.title: Melody Huang
item.description:
Melody Huang

Postdoctoral Fellow, Harvard Data Science Initiative

Melody is a Wojcicki Troper Harvard Data Science Institute Postdoctoral Fellow. Her research focuses on developing methods for credible causal inference under real world complications. Before Harvard, Melody received her PhD in Statistics from UC Berkeley, where she was generously supported by the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program. Her research was awarded the John T. Williams dissertation prize by the Society of Political Methodology.

item.title: Memorious: Building Infinite Memory with AI
item.description:
Forgetting is universal—conversations, names, moments all slip away. But what if it were optional? That’s the ambitious vision behind Memorious, a company founded by Spandan Madan and Gabriel Kreiman at Harvard. Their goal is to reinvent human memory using AI, building tools that allow people to recall experiences, conversations, and information instantly without searching or prompting.

From Research to Reality

The science powering Memorious originates from Gabriel’s lab at Harvard. As a Professor of Neuroscience and AI at Harvard Medical School, Gabriel has spent decades researching how the brain encodes and retrieves memory. His lab’s findings formed the technological foundation for the company. He partnered with Spandan Madan, a Harvard Computer Science PhD with extensive machine learning experience from Microsoft, Adobe, and IIT. Together they recognized the chance to merge neuroscience and AI to create what they term “Ambient Intelligence.”

item.title: Merce Crosas Departs to be Secretary of Open Government in Catalonia
item.description:
After 15 years at Harvard as Chief Data Science and Technology Officer at IQSS, Merce Crosas departed to serve as Secretary of Open Government in Catalonia, Spain. Her departure marked the end of an era in which she helped build IQSS’s data science infrastructure from the ground up.

Crosas led the development of the Dataverse Project, growing it from a Harvard-centric tool to a globally adopted research data platform with over 100 installations worldwide. Under her leadership, the project became a model for how academic institutions can create sustainable open-source infrastructure that serves the broader research community.

item.title: Michael Hiscox
item.description:
Michael Hiscox

Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs

Michael J. Hiscox is the Clarence Dillon Professor of International Affairs at Harvard University. He earned his B. Econ. (First Class Honours) from the University of Sydney in 1989 and his Ph.D in Government from Harvard in 1997. He served as Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC San Diego from 1997 to 2001, then held the John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Social Sciences position at Harvard from 2001 to 2005.

item.title: Michael Kremer
item.description:
Michael Kremer

Gates Professor of Developing Societies

Michael Kremer is the Gates Professor of Developing Societies in the Department of Economics at Harvard University and Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a recipient of a MacArthur Fellowship and a Presidential Faculty Fellowship, and was named a Young Global Leader by the World Economic Forum. His recent research focuses on “education and health in developing countries, immigration, and globalization.” He and Rachel Glennerster co-authored Strong Medicine: Creating Incentives for Pharmaceutical Research on Neglected Diseases.

item.title: Michael P. Brenner
item.description:
Michael P. Brenner

Michael F. Cronin Professor of Applied Mathematics and Applied Physics and Professor of Physics

Email: brenner@seas.harvard.edu

His research group uses applied mathematics methods to address scientific and engineering problems. They are described as “first and foremost problem solvers” who search for problems where mathematics can answer scientific questions.

Over the past decade, the research has focused on theoretical modeling in physical sciences and engineering, much of it arising from close contact with experimentalists. Problems addressed include “the breaking of fluid droplets; sonoluminescence (the production of light from small bubbles)” as well as sedimentation of small particles, device design, and electrospinning.

item.title: Michael Porter
item.description:
Michael Porter

Bishop William Lawrence University Professor

Michael E. Porter

Bishop William Lawrence University Professor

Michael Porter is an economist, researcher, author, advisor, speaker and teacher. Throughout his career at Harvard Business School, he has brought economic theory and strategy concepts to bear on many of the most challenging problems facing corporations, economies and societies, including market competition and company strategy, economic development, the environment, and health care. His extensive research is widely recognized in governments, corporations, NGOs, and academic circles around the globe. His research has received numerous awards, and he is the most cited scholar today in economics and business. While Dr. Porter is, at the core, a scholar, his work has also achieved remarkable acceptance by practitioners across multiple fields.

item.title: Michael Walsh McGarrah
item.description:
Michael Walsh McGarrah

Visiting Scholar, HGSE

Michael Walsh McGarrah is a Visiting Scholar at HGSE whose research focuses on risk factors for early substance use among children and the dimensionality of psychopathology regarding internalizing and externalizing behaviors. He employs advanced psychometric and statistical methods in structural equation modeling, including latent class growth models and auto-regressive latent trajectory models with structured residuals.

His secondary research interest explores the psychology of curiosity, including inter- and intra-individual differences in information-seeking behavior and possible interventions to cultivate intellectual appetite.

item.title: Michael Wilson
item.description:
Michael Wilson

Instructor in Emergency Medicine, HMS

Michael Wilson received his M.D. from the University of Michigan and his Ph.D. in Health Economics from Johns Hopkins University in 2010. He is a board certified Emergency Physician at Brigham and Women’s Hospital with fellowship training in Trauma and Critical Care Medicine and an Instructor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School. His research interests focus on measuring the value of emergency department care. At the broadest level, he seeks to develop a measure of emergency department performance along both quality and cost dimensions. His research projects examine variations in quality and cost and disparities by race, gender, and socioeconomic status for cohorts of patients who present to emergency departments for care. The goal of this research is to provide an evidence base for the construction of ED-specific value-based incentives for physicians and hospitals.

item.title: Michele Lamont
item.description:
Michele Lamont

Robert I. Goldman Professor of European Studies

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Milo Trujillo
item.description:
Milo Trujillo

PhD student, University of Vermont

Milo’s research applies network science and complex systems to understanding intentional community design. His past work includes “propaganda simulations, constraint-based automatic community design, analysis of alt-tech social platforms,” and coordinating volunteer groups through the Pursuance Project. He is working with IQSS to recreate network structure and community behavior patterns from limited organizational data.

item.title: Mina Cikara
item.description:
Mina Cikara

Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology

Professor Cikara studies “how the mind, brain, and behavior change when the social context shifts from ‘me and you’ to ‘us and them.’” Her primary focus is on how group membership, competition, and prejudice disrupt empathy and the ability to see others as human. She employs diverse methodological tools including “standard laboratory experiments, implicit and explicit behavioral measures, fMRI and psychophysiology” to investigate failures of empathy, dehumanization, and intergroup misunderstanding. She is also interested in behavioral outcomes of these processes, particularly “willingness to harm out-group members.”

item.title: Mind2Market Demo Day
item.description:
Harvard researchers gathered for the Mind2Market Demo Day, a showcase event highlighting cutting-edge artificial intelligence projects that have reached the stage where they are ready to transition from academic research to market-ready ventures. The event featured several teams from the IQSS Startup Foundry, Harvard’s initiative designed to help social science researchers transform their innovations into commercial applications with real-world impact.

The Demo Day provided researchers with a platform to pitch their AI-powered projects to potential partners, investors, and collaborators interested in bringing academic innovations to market. Teams presented projects spanning various domains of artificial intelligence and social science, demonstrating how research developed within Harvard’s academic environment can address practical challenges and create value in the commercial sector. The presentations showcased the maturity of these ventures and their readiness for the next stage of development.

item.title: Mindich Encounters with Authors Conference Series
item.description:
The annual Eric M. Mindich Encounters with Authors Conference is an opportunity for one or more authors to present a major work still in progress.

Key Details
Eligibility IQSS faculty affiliates
Amount $10,000 maximum
Deadline Rolling

IQSS covers all conference expenses, arranges invitations, and provides necessary administrative and staff support.

How to Apply

Contact funding@iq.harvard.edu to submit a proposal, including:

  • Potential speakers
  • Idea for conference topic
  • Proposed date range

Contact: funding@iq.harvard.edu

item.title: Misha Teplitskiy
item.description:
Misha Teplitskiy

Postdoctoral Fellow, LISH

Misha Teplitskiy is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard (LISH). Previously, he was in the Sociology PhD program at the University of Chicago, where he worked with James Evans to apply computational social science techniques to studying the evaluation, robustness, and diffusion of scientific knowledge. His research bridges Sociology of Science and Management, focusing on how institutional and organizational factors affect scientific discovery and collaborative knowledge production.

item.title: Moises de Freitas Cunha
item.description:
Moises de Freitas Cunha

Postdoctoral Fellow, Weatherhead Center

Moisés de Freitas Cunha is a PhD specialist in Urban Historical Studies, Fulbright Fellow, Harvard Postdoctoral Fellow, and holds a master’s and doctorate from the PEPG – Postgraduate Studies Program in Social Sciences at the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo.

His postdoctoral studies (PUCSP/Weatherhead Research Cluster on Global History at Harvard), funded by FAPESP and IBRAM Motores e Máquinas, aim to measure historical, urban inequalities and environmental racism in cities throughout the Americas and Europe, among other objectives and expected results.

item.title: Murat Kantarcioglu
item.description:
Murat Kantarcioglu

Visiting Scholar, Data Privacy Lab

Murat Kantarcioglu is an Associate Professor of Computer Science and Director of the UTD Data Security and Privacy Lab at the University of Texas at Dallas. He received the NSF CAREER award and the Purdue University CERIAS Diamond Award for Academic excellence. He has published over 100 papers on data security and privacy in peer-reviewed journals and conferences. His research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Office of Naval Research, National Security Agency, Army Research Office, and National Institutes of Health. His work has been featured by the Boston Globe, ABC News, and other media outlets, and he has received two best paper awards.

item.title: Naijia Liu
item.description:
Naijia Liu

Assistant Professor, Department of Government

Naijia is a political methodologist with “a broad interest on quantitative methods on social sciences.” She works on projects involving missing data imputation, text analysis/NLP, and social media studies.

item.title: NASA Tournament Lab Launches Asteroid Hunter Contest
item.description:
The NASA Tournament Lab at IQSS challenged competitors to develop better asteroid detection methods, leveraging crowd-sourced innovation to address a critical space safety challenge. The lab, a collaboration among NASA, Harvard Business School, and TopCoder, uses competition-based approaches to solve complex technical problems.

The Asteroid Hunter Contest asked participants to develop algorithms that could identify potentially hazardous asteroids from astronomical observation data more accurately and efficiently than existing methods. By opening the problem to a global community of problem-solvers, the contest aimed to tap expertise beyond traditional astronomy and aerospace engineering.

item.title: Nate Silver to Lead Political Analytics 2017
item.description:
The Center for American Political Studies announced the second annual Political Analytics Conference on March 31, 2017, with FiveThirtyEight founder Nate Silver as the keynote speaker. The conference, co-sponsored by IQSS, brings together academics, journalists, and practitioners working at the intersection of data science and politics.

The conference examines how quantitative methods are transforming political campaigns, journalism, and governance. Topics range from election forecasting and survey methodology to social media analytics and political communication strategies.

item.title: Neil Shephard
item.description:
Neil Shephard

Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science

Neil Shephard has been Professor of Economics and of Statistics at Harvard University since 2013. He holds a B.A. in Economics and Statistics (first class awarded with distinction) from the University of York and a M.Sc. in Statistics (awarded with distinction) and Ph.D. from the London School of Economics (LSE). He previously was a faculty member at the LSE and Nuffield College, Oxford University. His research interests are mainly focused on theoretical and applied econometrics and statistics. He has been a leader in the development of the econometrics of stochastic volatility as well as simulation based inference. He is credited with important contributions to the development in sequential learning (e.g. the auxiliary particle filter). He is currently focusing on non-parametric Bayesian methods, simulation, high frequency finance and valuing income contingent student loans. During his time at Oxford University he cofounded the Masters in Financial Economics and founded the interdisciplinary Oxford-Man Institute, which he directed from 2007-2011. He is an emeritus fellow at Nuffield College, Oxford, a Fellow of the Econometric Society, a Fellow of the British Academy and received an honorary doctorate in economics from Aarhus University. He was awarded the Richard Stone Prize in Applied Econometrics in 2012.

item.title: Neil Thompson
item.description:
Neil Thompson

Visiting Fellow, LISH; Asst Professor, MIT Sloan

Neil is an Assistant Professor of Innovation and Strategy at the MIT Sloan School of Management and co-director of the Experimental Innovation Lab (X-Lab). He is also an associate member of the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL) and the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT. He earned his PhD in Business and Public Policy at Berkeley, along with master’s degrees in Computer Science and Statistics. He holds “a masters in ecoNomics from the London School of Economics, and undergraduate degrees in Physics and International Development.” Before entering academia, he worked at organizations including Lawrence Livermore National Laboratories, Bain and Company, The United Nations, the World Bank, and the Canadian Parliament.

item.title: Neru Health - From Sleep Challenges to Scaling Chronic Care with AI
item.description:
When Neru Health first came to the IQSS Startup Foundry, they had a big idea: transform the way people solve sleep problems. Millions struggle with conditions like sleep apnea, and while treatments exist, staying consistent with therapy is notoriously difficult. Neru’s early vision centered on improving patient engagement and adherence to sleep therapy.

But as the team dug deeper during their time in the Foundry, they uncovered a bigger and more urgent opportunity. Durable Medical Equipment (DME) providers, responsible for supplying and supporting patients with CPAP machines and other critical devices, were stuck between trying to grow while maintaining excellent patient care and adherence to treatment. Staffing shortages, rising costs, and manual support processes left DMEs unable to keep up with patient needs.

item.title: New IQSS Web Site Launched!
item.description:
The Institute for Quantitative Social Science is proud to announce the launch of a completely redesigned website, developed through an extensive cross-team collaboration that brought together expertise from across the organization. The new site reflects IQSS’s evolution as a hub for quantitative research methods, data science innovation, and collaborative scholarship, providing improved access to information about programs, services, and research initiatives.

The redesigned website features enhanced navigation, making it easier for visitors to discover the breadth of resources and support available through IQSS. From data science consultation services and training opportunities to information about affiliated faculty research and major projects like Dataverse, the new site provides clearer pathways to the tools and expertise that support quantitative research across Harvard. The modern design better showcases the innovative work happening at IQSS while maintaining accessibility and usability for diverse audiences.

item.title: New R Package {clarify}
item.description:
Data Science Services at IQSS has released a new R package {clarify} to provide functionality previously provided by the {Zelig} package.

The package “uses simulation to make interpretable inferences about any quantity of interest from a wide variety of statistical models.” It restores and extends functionality that was previously available through the {Zelig} package for R and the Clarify package for Stata. The package supports many model classes from a variety of other R packages and offers methods for computing interpretable quantities from models fit to multiply imputed data.

item.title: Newspaper Endorsements and the Importance of Candidate Quality in Politics
item.description:
Kevin DeLuca (Yale, Harvard PhD 2023, IQSS alumnus) describes political endorsement data he collected as part of his dissertation research, exploring how newspaper endorsements relate to candidate quality and electoral outcomes.

DeLuca’s research assembled a comprehensive dataset of newspaper endorsements across multiple election cycles, enabling systematic analysis of patterns that were previously only studied anecdotally. His findings contribute to understanding the role of institutional media in democratic elections.

The project demonstrates the value of IQSS’s training environment, where graduate students develop both the methodological skills and the data collection persistence needed to produce original datasets that advance political science. DeLuca’s subsequent position at Yale reflects the competitive academic placements that IQSS affiliates regularly achieve.

item.title: Nicole Alexander
item.description:
Nicole Alexander

Visiting Researcher, CGA

Nicole is a Visiting Researcher at the CGA and was previously a Principal Member of Technical Staff on the Oracle Spatial development team. Nicole has a Ph.D. in Geography from the University of California, Santa Barbara, a M.S. in Geographic and Geodetic Information Systems from the University of London, and a B.S. in Land Surveying from the University of the West Indies. Prior to working for Oracle Corporation, Nicole’s experience in the field of geomatics included, a data capture engineer/GIS specialist at Trimble, a GIS consultant at Fujitsu-ICL, and a land surveyor on the Channel Tunnel project linking England to France.

item.title: Nima Hejazi
item.description:
Nima Hejazi

Assistant Professor of Biostatistics

Dr. Hejazi’s research combines causal inference and machine learning, aiming to develop “tailored, assumption-lean statistical procedures for efficient and robust inference about scientifically informative” parameters. He is driven by methodological challenges in “robust non- and semi-parametric inference, high-dimensional inference, targeted loss-based estimation, and biased sampling designs.” His statistical work is informed by collaboration in clinical trials and computational biology, particularly regarding “vaccine efficacy and drug treatment trials, infectious disease epidemiology, and immunology.” He is also interested in high-performance statistical computing and open source software development for reproducible applied statistics.

item.title: Now Announcing the OpenDP Library 0.7
item.description:
The OpenDP Project is excited to announce the release of OpenDP Library 0.7, featuring important architectural additions that expand the framework’s flexibility and power for building differentially private systems. These architectural enhancements provide developers with more sophisticated tools for composing privacy-preserving analyses while maintaining the rigorous mathematical guarantees that are central to OpenDP’s mission.

Version 0.7 introduces new architectural components that enable more complex privacy accounting scenarios and support advanced composition patterns. These additions make it easier to build sophisticated data analysis pipelines that combine multiple differentially private operations while precisely tracking cumulative privacy loss. The enhanced architecture also improves support for interactive analyses and adaptive queries, expanding the range of use cases where differential privacy can be practically deployed without excessive privacy budget consumption.

item.title: Oliver Bertuch
item.description:
Oliver Bertuch

Developer, Dataverse Core Development Team

Oliver is a Research Software Engineer working on solutions for management, publication and archiving of research data and research software. His mission is bringing together these two worlds, fostering Open Science and Reproducibility. Located at the Central Library of Forschungszentrum Jülich, Germany, he works closely together with the IQSS as part of the Dataverse Core Team. His focus there is addressing topics like containerization and research software readiness of Dataverse repositories. As Co-PI of HERMES he develops a new key infrastructure element for automated, metadata rich research software publications.

item.title: On data centers, local vibes matter more than electricity prices
item.description:
A survey led by faculty affiliate Stephen Ansolabehere, the Elting R. Morison Professor of Political Science and Professor of Government at Harvard, explores what Americans prioritize regarding large data centers opening in their communities. The research found that local community concerns matter more to residents than electricity pricing when it comes to data center siting decisions, challenging conventional assumptions about public priorities in infrastructure development.

As demand for data centers surges driven by cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and digital services, companies and policymakers have often focused on electricity costs and power grid capacity as primary factors in location decisions. However, Ansolabehere’s research reveals that community members place greater emphasis on factors such as environmental impacts, effects on local character and quality of life, job creation, property values, and how well the facility integrates with existing community fabric. These “local vibes”—the intangible qualities that define a community’s identity and lived experience—emerge as more salient to residents than the economic considerations that dominate industry planning.

item.title: OpenDP Library 0.6 is Now Available
item.description:
The OpenDP Project is pleased to announce the release of OpenDP Library 0.6, a significant milestone that lays crucial groundwork for incorporating formal mathematical proofs directly into the OpenDP codebase. This release represents an important step toward the project’s long-term vision of providing not just privacy-preserving algorithms, but mathematically verified guarantees that the implementations faithfully represent their theoretical specifications.

Version 0.6 introduces infrastructure that will eventually enable automatic verification of privacy proofs, bridging the gap between theoretical differential privacy and practical implementations. This work addresses a fundamental challenge in privacy-preserving systems: ensuring that code actually provides the privacy guarantees it claims. By building toward machine-checkable proofs, OpenDP aims to provide unprecedented confidence in the privacy properties of deployed systems, reducing the risk of implementation errors that could compromise sensitive data.

item.title: OpenDP Seeks Interviewees for Software Study
item.description:
The OpenDP Project is seeking data analysts, researchers, and data professionals to participate in a software usability study focused on DP Creator, an innovative application designed to make differential privacy more accessible to practitioners without deep technical expertise in privacy mathematics. This research study aims to gather valuable feedback that will shape the development of tools that enable broader adoption of privacy-preserving data analysis methods.

DP Creator represents an important step toward democratizing differential privacy by providing intuitive interfaces for creating differentially private analyses without requiring users to understand the underlying mathematical complexities. The software study will involve testing the application with realistic data analysis tasks, providing feedback on the user interface and workflow, and sharing insights about how differential privacy tools can better serve the needs of working data analysts. Participants’ experiences and suggestions will directly inform ongoing development to make the tool more effective and user-friendly.

item.title: Our Impact
item.description:
These are examples of how IQSS drives tangible change in the world.

Investigating Flight Attendants’ Safety

The longest-running longitudinal study of its kind, led by Dr. Eileen McNeely, executive director of SHINE at IQSS. The study collected data on uniforms from major US airlines. Laboratory tests found harmful substances on a manufacturer’s uniforms. Analysis showed a connection between uniform introduction and reports of debilitating medical issues including respiratory problems and thyroid disease.

item.title: PaCSS 2022: Call for Proposals
item.description: The annual Politics and Computational Social Science (PaCSS) conference has issued its call for proposals for the 2022 meeting, inviting researchers to submit work that advances the intersection of political science and computational methods. This conference brings together scholars using innovative computational approaches to study political phenomena, from social media analysis and text mining to machine learning and network science applied to questions of governance, political behavior, and democratic processes.

item.title: Partisanship and pandemic preparedness in Indonesia
item.description:
Seth Soderborg explores how partisan politics in Indonesia can affect pandemic preparedness decisions, drawing parallels with U.S. experiences during COVID-19. His research examines whether the politicization of public health measures observed in American politics also manifests in other democratic contexts.

The study finds that in Indonesia, the relationship between partisanship and pandemic preparedness depends significantly on local context—particularly the political alignment between local and national leaders. This geographic variation provides leverage for understanding how political incentives can either promote or undermine public health responses.

item.title: Peer Pre-Review is now rapidPeer
item.description:
IQSS has rebranded its Peer Pre Review service as rapidPeer.

The service addresses frustrations with “the speed and quality of your journal peer reviews” by offering free, double-blind peer reviews for research papers, grants, or preregistration plans within 30 days. Reviewers are field-specific experts from leading institutions who provide feedback on both quantitative and qualitative research.

For Harvard researchers, rapidPeer delivers “quick, actionable insights that help refine your work and expedite the publication process,” potentially saving months in the submission cycle. To date, the service has supported 140 scholars in maximizing their publishing success.

item.title: Peter Bol
item.description:
Peter Bol

Charles H. Carswell Professor of East Asian Languages and Civilizations, Harvard University

Peter Bol is a scholar of Chinese intellectual and cultural history. His research focuses on the history of China’s cultural elites, both nationally and locally, spanning the 7th to 17th centuries. He also works extensively in geospatial analysis and digital humanities projects related to Chinese history.

He authored “This Culture of Ours”: Intellectual Transitions in T’ang and Sung China, Neo-Confucianism in History, and Localizing Learning: The Literati Enterprise in Wuzhou, 1100-1600.

item.title: Peter V. Marsden
item.description:
Peter V. Marsden

Edith and Benjamin Geisinger Professor of Sociology

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Philip Brookins
item.description:
Philip Brookins

Visiting Fellow, LISH

Philip Brookins is a senior research fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods in Bonn, Germany. His research uses game-theoretic techniques to model behavior in competitive settings like contests and tournaments, and experimental methods to test such models.

He examines how individuals and groups behave in contests when information-constrained, such as not being fully informed about competitors’ number or characteristics, and how they behave when competing as part of a team composed of heterogeneously talented members. He joined the Max Planck Institute in 2016 after earning doctoral, master’s, and bachelor’s degrees in economics and a bachelor’s in mathematics from Florida State University.

item.title: Pia Raffler
item.description:
Pia Raffler

Assistant Professor of Government

Pia Raffler is an Assistant Professor in Political Science at Harvard University. She studies the politics of development, focusing on “governance, bureaucracy, and electoral politics in Sub-Saharan Africa.” Her research examines political oversight of bureaucrats and its implications for public service provision, as well as electoral behavior. She “works closely with government agencies to understand impediments to accountable representation, often through large-scale field experiments.” She holds a PhD from Yale University and a Master from Columbia University and is an EGAP member.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV names epidemiology professor to Vatican advisory group
item.description:
Tyler VanderWeele, the John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and director of the Human Flourishing Program at IQSS, has been appointed by Pope Leo XIV to the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences. This prestigious appointment recognizes VanderWeele’s groundbreaking work on human flourishing, well-being, and the role of faith and virtue in health and society.

The Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences serves as an advisory body to the Vatican on matters related to social, economic, and political issues affecting humanity. VanderWeele joins an international group of distinguished scholars who provide guidance to the Holy See on complex social questions. His expertise in epidemiological methods, causal inference, and the measurement of well-being brings a rigorous quantitative social science perspective to the academy’s deliberations on human development and flourishing.

item.title: Powerful computing in comfortable surroundings: the IQSS Computer Labs
item.description:
by Danielle Benaroche Gottesman

Nestled within Harvard’s Knafel Building—known primarily for government and international studies—is a high-end computing refuge. It’s always open and filled with cutting-edge technology and software.

“Most computer labs have gray walls and feel very plain,” says IQSS Computer Lab Manager Randy Kiessig. “We have a colorful atmosphere, beautiful wood desks, and the winter garden—which feels a lot like a coffee shop.”

Students have long benefited from on-campus computer labs, but pandemic-era lifestyle changes shifted user habits toward personal computer use in isolated spaces. The labs aim to meet the full spectrum of needs for Harvard students, staff, and faculty, offering both pleasing and practical environments for focused work.

item.title: Preparing the Next Steps and the Next Generation: Latanya Sweeney's Data Privacy Lab
item.description:
Latanya Sweeney’s Data Privacy Lab and Public Interest Tech Lab explore digital information risks in today’s technology-filled world. The labs serve dual purposes: conducting cutting-edge research on privacy vulnerabilities while training the next generation of scholars who will grapple with these challenges.

Sweeney’s approach combines technical investigation—actively probing systems for privacy weaknesses—with policy analysis and public engagement. Her labs have exposed re-identification risks in health data, discriminatory patterns in online advertising, and surveillance capabilities hidden in everyday technologies.

item.title: PSR Helps Scholars Navigate Survey Research in Social Distance
item.description:
The Program on Survey Research (PSR), led by Associate Director Chase Harrison, helps a lot of people at Harvard and beyond with survey methodology. When COVID-19 forced a shift from face-to-face to online research, PSR became an essential resource for scholars adapting their methods.

Harrison and his team provided guidance on transitioning in-person surveys to digital formats, addressing challenges around response rates, sample representativeness, and measurement equivalence across modes. Their expertise helped researchers maintain data quality during an unprecedented disruption to social science fieldwork.

item.title: Qualitative Research at IQSS: Numbers and Narratives Combined
item.description:
Qualitative research forms the backbone of our knowledge about human society. Social scientists at IQSS explore crime, corruption, race, culture, violence, and well-being using methods that go beyond numbers to capture the richness of human experience.

While IQSS is known for quantitative methods, the institute recognizes that the deepest understanding of social phenomena often requires combining statistical analysis with qualitative approaches—interviews, ethnography, archival research, and case studies. This integration produces insights that neither approach could achieve alone.

item.title: Ra'ad Siraj
item.description:
Ra’ad Siraj

Senior AI and Data Executive

Ra’ad Siraj is a senior data and AI executive with more than 30 years of experience building and scaling enterprise data, AI, and technology programs in regulated industries. He is known for deploying AI at scale while embedding governance and accountability as operational infrastructure — not compliance overhead.

His recent work spans enterprise AI governance at MassMutual, where he built the governance program from the ground up, and global workforce AI governance at Amazon. Earlier in his career, Ra’ad held CTO and CIO roles at The Boston Company Asset Management (BNY Mellon) and Eaton Vance, and senior technology roles at pre-IPO firms including Endeca (acquired by Oracle) and Sermo. He also served as Director of Strategic Project Management at MITIMCo, supporting technology and data initiatives for the MIT endowment, and established a data aggregation and analytics business at State Street Global Exchange serving asset managers and asset owners globally.

item.title: Rachel Franklin
item.description:
Rachel Franklin

Executive Director, Center for Geographic Analysis

Email: rachel_franklin@cga.harvard.edu

Dr. Rachel Franklin started as Executive Director of the CGA in March of 2025, bringing more than 20 years’ experience as an educator and researcher in GIS, spatial analysis, and quantitative methods. Her research interests are in the sources and impacts of demographic change as it occurs at multiple spatial scales, and in the use of novel forms of data and analysis to identify and address that change. Her most recent research explores how smart city technologies contribute to and reinforce socio-economic and spatial inequalities.

item.title: Rafael Albuquerque
item.description:
Rafael Albuquerque

Visiting Scholar, CGA

Rafael Albuquerque is a Visiting Scholar at the Center for Geographic Analysis (CGA) at Harvard University and a PhD Candidate in Marketing at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS). His research explores “the intersection of consumer mobility behavior and economic growth in urban environments,” using geospatial data science, machine learning, and social media analytics.

Before joining Harvard, Rafael worked extensively in marketing analytics and strategic consumer insights. His work at CGA focuses on analyzing large-scale geolocated Twitter data to measure e-WOM and examine how this variable moderates consumer mobility and economic growth. His expertise spans geospatial analysis, digital marketing, and computational social science.

item.title: Rafaella Sadun
item.description:
Rafaella Sadun

Professor, Harvard Business School

Raffaella Sadun is a Professor at the Harvard Business School. Her research centers on “the economics of productivity, management and organizational change,” documenting economic and cultural determinants of managerial choices and their implications for organizational performance across private and public sectors, including healthcare and education. She co-founded the World Management Survey and the Executive Time Use Study. Her work has been published in leading journals such as the American Economic Review, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Economic Journal, and covered by major outlets including The New York Times, The Economist, The Wall Street Journal, and the Financial Times. She holds affiliations as a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Faculty Associate at the Centre for Economic Performance at LSE, Research Affiliate at the Center for Economic Policy Research, and Research Associate in the Ariadne Labs Program at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. In 2012 she “was nominated as a Junior Faculty Fellow at the Kauffman Foundation.”

item.title: Rajarshi Mukherjee
item.description:
Rajarshi Mukherjee

Assistant Professor, Department of Biostatistics

Rajarshi Mukherjee’s research focuses on “causal inference from observational studies using non-parametric methods, sparse signal detection problems in genomics, and networks analysis” with applications in neural spike train analysis.

item.title: Ramana Nanda
item.description:
Ramana Nanda

Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration

Ramana Nanda is the Sarofim-Rock Professor of Business Administration and Co-Director of the Private Capital Project at Harvard Business School. His research focuses on “financing frictions facing new ventures,” aiming to help entrepreneurs with fundraising and to illuminate how “financial intermediaries, corporate R&D and policy makers can improve the odds of selecting and commercializing the most promising ideas and technologies in the economy.”

item.title: Ramona Pop
item.description:
Ramona Pop

LISH Director, D^3 HBS

Dr. Pop currently serves as Director in the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard (LISH) at the D^3 Institute within Harvard Business School. In this capacity, alongside Prof Karim Lakhani and a team of investigators, researchers and collaborators, Dr. Pop is overseeing and contributing to the ongoing scientific projects and research initiatives within the laboratory and D^3. Her efforts are dedicated to supporting scientific and research activities that specifically address the integration and impact of artificial intelligence in business and society. Prior to assuming the role at LISH/D^3, Dr. Pop conducted research at FAS within two stem cell laboratories. Notably, in Doug Melton lab at Harvard, she performed research aimed at developing stem cell therapies for Type 1 diabetes. Dr. Pop brings a wealth of experience to her current position, boasting two decades of research expertise in natural sciences.

item.title: Rebecca Nichols
item.description:
Rebecca Nichols

Program/Project Manager

Rebecca Nichols is a results-driven program/project manager at Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS), where she “helps advance interdisciplinary research and innovation” to address complex societal challenges. She brings extensive experience managing technical, research, and administrative projects across academic, nonprofit, and Fortune 500 settings, specializing in connecting diverse teams and turning ambitious ideas into operational successes.

At IQSS, she leads initiatives in program development, research facilitation, and process optimization. She is proficient in both agile and waterfall project management and excels at coordinating university resources, launching programs, and supporting tools and services that promote collaborative, data-driven social science. She is recognized for her collaborative style—bringing together faculty, administrators, developers, and researchers to build community, create efficiencies, and enhance IQSS impact.

item.title: Register Early for the Dataverse Community Meeting 2026
item.description:
Early bird registration is now open for the Dataverse Community Meeting 2026, taking place May 12-15 in Barcelona, Spain. This year’s meeting is co-organized with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, bringing together the global Dataverse community in one of Europe’s most vibrant and innovative cities. The event promises to be a landmark gathering for researchers, data managers, repository administrators, and developers working with the Dataverse platform.

The Dataverse Community Meeting serves as the premier annual event for the worldwide network of institutions using Dataverse for research data management and sharing. Attendees will have opportunities to learn about the latest developments in the Dataverse software, share experiences and best practices, participate in hands-on technical workshops, and connect with colleagues from around the globe. The meeting typically features presentations on innovative uses of Dataverse, discussions of data curation challenges, and planning sessions for future platform enhancements.

item.title: Register now for the 2023 OpenDP Community Meeting
item.description:
The OpenDP Project is excited to announce that registration is now open for the 2023 OpenDP Community Meeting, marking the first in-person gathering of the differential privacy community centered around this groundbreaking open-source initiative. This event brings together researchers, developers, data practitioners, and privacy advocates who are advancing the science and practice of differential privacy through the OpenDP ecosystem.

The community meeting will feature technical presentations, hands-on workshops, and collaborative discussions about the latest developments in differential privacy tools and methodologies. Attendees will have the opportunity to learn about new features in the OpenDP Library, share implementation experiences, and contribute to the project’s future direction. Whether you’re already using OpenDP in production systems or exploring how differential privacy can enhance your data protection practices, this gathering offers valuable networking and learning opportunities.

item.title: Registration is open for Harvard DataFest 2021
item.description:
Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science is excited to announce that registration is now open for Harvard DataFest 2021, an intensive bootcamp designed to help researchers develop, refine, and advance their research projects through hands-on learning and collaborative problem-solving. This immersive event brings together graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and faculty members working across the social sciences to tackle methodological challenges and accelerate their scholarly work.

DataFest provides participants with concentrated time to work on their research while accessing expert guidance on quantitative methods, computational tools, and data management strategies. The bootcamp format combines structured workshops on specific technical topics with dedicated project time where attendees can apply new skills to their own research questions. Experienced instructors and peer participants create a collaborative learning environment where researchers can troubleshoot challenges, discover new approaches, and make meaningful progress on projects that might otherwise stall due to technical obstacles.

item.title: Registration is Open for the Winter 2022 GIS Institute
item.description:
Harvard’s Center for Geographic Analysis is pleased to announce that registration is now open for the Winter 2022 GIS Institute, a comprehensive two-week intensive training course that provides participants with foundational and advanced skills in geographic information systems and spatial analysis. This immersive program is designed for graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, faculty members, and professionals who want to incorporate spatial analysis into their research or professional practice.

The GIS Institute offers structured, hands-on instruction covering essential GIS concepts, software tools, and analytical techniques. Participants learn to work with spatial data, create compelling maps, perform sophisticated geographic analyses, and integrate GIS methods into research workflows. The intensive format allows for deep engagement with the material, progressing from fundamental concepts to advanced applications over the two-week period. Expert instructors from the Center for Geographic Analysis provide personalized guidance, helping participants overcome learning challenges and connect GIS methods to their specific research questions.

item.title: Registration Open for the 8th Annual Dataverse Community Meeting
item.description:
The Dataverse Project is pleased to announce that registration is now open for the 8th Annual Dataverse Community Meeting, bringing together the global network of researchers, repository administrators, developers, and data professionals who make up the vibrant Dataverse ecosystem. This year’s meeting offers a valuable opportunity to connect with peers, learn about the latest platform developments, and contribute to shaping the future of research data management infrastructure.

The 2022 meeting will feature a rich program of presentations, workshops, and discussions covering diverse aspects of the Dataverse platform and research data management more broadly. Attendees can expect sessions on new software features, case studies from institutions implementing Dataverse in innovative ways, technical deep dives for developers, and strategic discussions about data curation, preservation, and open science policy. The meeting provides crucial face-to-face time for collaboration and networking that strengthens the community bonds essential to successful open-source development.

item.title: Remembering Sidney Verba
item.description:
A tribute to Sidney Verba of Harvard, who passed on March 4, 2019. Verba was a towering figure in political science whose work on political participation, civic engagement, and democratic theory influenced generations of scholars. He was also a founding influence on what would become IQSS.

Verba’s research, particularly his landmark study “Voice and Equality” (with Kay Lehman Schlozman and Henry Brady), established the modern framework for understanding why some citizens participate in politics while others do not. His emphasis on rigorous empirical measurement of democratic engagement exemplified the quantitative approach that IQSS champions.

Deadline Currently on hold

  • Crowdsourcing, human subjects and payments

  • Technical services
  • Printing and publication costs
  • International travel
