item.title: Reshmaan N Hussam
item.description:
Reshmaan N Hussam

Assistant Professor of Business Administration

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Restructuring the Dataverse UI
item.description:
The Dataverse Project has announced ambitious plans to fundamentally restructure the platform’s user interface, transforming it into an API-first architecture that will provide greater flexibility, improved performance, and better support for diverse use cases. This significant architectural evolution represents a major investment in the long-term sustainability and extensibility of the Dataverse platform, positioning it to meet the evolving needs of research data repositories for years to come.

The move to an API-first architecture involves separating the user interface from the backend data and business logic, creating clean interfaces that allow for multiple front-end implementations. This approach enables institutions to customize their Dataverse interfaces more extensively while still benefiting from core platform capabilities. It also facilitates the development of specialized interfaces for specific communities or workflows, mobile applications, and integration with other tools and systems. The architectural change will make Dataverse more adaptable to different institutional contexts and research domain requirements.

item.title: Revolutionizing Research through AI-Powered Data Sharing and Curation
item.description:
TurboCurator by ICPSR is an interactive tool designed to streamline research data deposit at Dataverse, developed through intensive collaboration between institutions. The tool uses artificial intelligence to automate many of the time-consuming steps in preparing research data for sharing.

Traditionally, depositing data in a repository requires researchers to manually enter metadata, organize files, and ensure compliance with standards—a process that can take hours and discourages many from sharing their data at all. TurboCurator uses AI to suggest metadata, identify data types, and guide researchers through the curation process.

item.title: Richard Wrangham
item.description:
Richard Wrangham

Ruth Moore Professor of Biological Anthropology, Emeritus

Richard Wrangham is the Ruth Moore Professor of Biological Anthropology, Emeritus. He “received a Ph.D. in Zoology from Cambridge University, where he studied under the renowned ethologist Robert Hinde.” He served on faculty in departments of Anthropology, Psychology and Biology at institutions including Bristol University, Stanford University, King’s College Cambridge, and the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.

item.title: Richard Zeckhauser
item.description:
Richard Zeckhauser

Frank Plumpton Ramsey Professor of Political Economy

Richard J. Zeckhauser is the Frank Plumpton Ramsey Professor of Political Economy at Harvard University John F. Kennedy School of Government. He pursues a blend of conceptual and applied research. He believes society’s primary challenge is allocating resources according to citizens’ preferences. Much of his conceptual work explores possibilities for democratic, decentralized allocation procedures. His ongoing policy work examines ways to promote human health, help labor and financial markets function more efficiently, and support informed choices by individuals and government agencies. His current major research focuses on “the performance of institutions confronted with inadequate commitment capabilities, incomplete information flow and human participants who fail to behave” according to rational models (such as engaging in herd behavior). Financial markets and health risks serve as the subjects of his major empirical investigations.

item.title: Robert Bates
item.description:
Robert Bates

Eaton Professor of the Science of Government, Emeritus

Email: robert.bates.harvard.edu@gmail.com

Robert H. Bates is Eaton Professor in the Department of Government and a member of the Department of African and African-American Studies. He has also served as Professeur associé in the Department of Economics at the University of Toulouse. After rising to Full Professor at the California Institute of Technology, he became the Henry R. Luce Professor of Political Science and Economics at Duke University, where he also directed its Center for Political Economy.

item.title: Robert Gahl
item.description:
Robert Gahl

Visiting Faculty Fellow, Human Flourishing Program

Robert Gahl is the Vice Director of the Markets, Culture, and Ethics (MCE) Research Centre and of the Program of Church Management at the Pontifical University of the Holy Cross (Santa Croce) in Rome. He completed his bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering at Washington University in St. Louis, worked in Silicon Valley, completed his doctorate in philosophy at Santa Croce, and did postdoctoral research at the University of Notre Dame. Much of his recent research has focused on “classical virtue theory, the narrative unity of life, and their complementarity with cognitive psychology.” His current research focuses on “moderation, self-mastery, and sexuality within human flourishing” and he is offering a course entitled “Self-Mastery, Sexuality, and Neuroscience: Perspectives from Philosophy and Cognitive Science for Human Flourishing.”

item.title: Robert Gaudin
item.description:
Robert Gaudin

Visiting Fellow; Oral-Maxillofacial Surgery, Charite Berlin

Robert Gaudin, MD graduated from Medical School in Hamburg, Germany, defending his doctoral thesis in 2014. From January 2015 to June 2016, he was a research fellow at Harvard Medical School’s Department of Facial Plastics, working on developing a “Bionic Face” in an animal model and conducting basic clinical studies.

In July 2016, he began his residency at University Clinic Hamburg-Eppendorf in Oral-Maxillofacial and Plastic Surgery. His research interest grew around evaluating how well doctors rate dental x-rays and whether a superhuman algorithm diagnosing pathologies could improve diagnostic accuracy—leading to his involvement with Karim Lakhani’s Lab at Harvard. In February 2017, he transferred his residency to Charite, Berlin.

item.title: Robert Sampson
item.description:
Robert Sampson

Henry Ford II Professor of the Social Sciences

Robert J. Sampson is Henry Ford II Professor of the Social Sciences at Harvard University, where he was appointed in 2003. Before that he taught for twelve years in the Department of Sociology at the University of Chicago and for seven years at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Sampson was a Senior Research Fellow at the American Bar Foundation from 1994-2002, and in the 1997-98 and 2002-03 academic years he was a Fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences in Stanford, California. In 2005, he received a three-year RWJ Investigator Award in Health Policy Research and was inducted as a Fellow into the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

item.title: Roland Pongou
item.description:
Roland Pongou

Visiting Scientist; Assoc Professor, University of Ottawa

Roland Pongou is a Visiting Scientist in the Department of Global Health and Population at Harvard and an Affiliate of the Harvard Institute for Quantitative Social Science. He is an Associate Professor of Economics at the University of Ottawa in Canada, and an affiliated faculty member of the African School of Economics in Benin. He received his PhD in Economics from Brown University. He also has graduate training in Mathematics and Demography. He was formerly a Fellow in the Takemi Program in International Health at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, a PDGA Scholar at Harvard, and a Visiting Scholar in the MIT Department of Economics. Professor Pongou’s primary research interests are in political economy, health, economic development, and economic theory. His work focuses on the microeconomic analysis of formal and informal institutions, and on the effects of institutions on various aspects of individual and societal wellbeing. His recent research uses matching theory to study the effect of ethnic integration on sexual network formation and the spread of HIV and other sexually transmitted diseases in multiethnic societies. He has also published research that addresses questions in voting and political design, fairness in organizations, and gender inequality. Professor Pongou’s analytical approach combines microeconomic theory, game theory, social network theory, and quantitative methods. He has also published research that contributes to these areas. He is a recipient of multiple awards and fellowships. He is a member of the Econometric Society, the American Economic Association, the Canadian Economic Association, the African Finance and Economic Association, and the Population Association of America.

item.title: Ryan Enos
item.description:
Ryan Enos

Professor, Department of Government

Ryan D. Enos is a Professor of Government and Faculty Associate in the Institute for Quantitative Social Science specializing in American Politics, Political Psychology, and Race and Ethnic Politics. He studies political behavior and intergroup attitudes through “laboratory and field experiments and other methods.” He directs the Working Group in Political Psychology, described as “an interdisciplinary forum for research on the microfoundations of citizen and elite behavior,” as well as the Harvard Digital Lab for the Social Sciences. His research has appeared in publications including the American Political Science Review, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and the American Journal of Political Science, and “has been covered in major media outlets such as the New York Times and the Washington Post.” He earned his AB in political science and history from U.C. Berkeley and his MA and PhD in political science from UCLA. Before entering academia, “he was a teacher at Paul Robeson High School in Chicago, IL.”

item.title: Ryan Enos explores partisan segregation
item.description:
Professor of Government Ryan Enos has spent much of his career exploring how local geographic context shapes political behavior and partisan segregation. His research reveals that where people live—and who their neighbors are—profoundly influences their political attitudes and behaviors.

Enos’s work demonstrates that partisan segregation is self-reinforcing: as communities become more politically homogeneous, residents develop more extreme views and lose the ability to understand opposing perspectives. This finding has important implications for democratic governance and social cohesion.

item.title: Ryan Olson
item.description:
Ryan Olson

Faculty Affiliate, Human Flourishing Program

Ryan S. Olson is a research professor at the University of Virginia and a senior fellow at the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture. A classicist by training, Olson’s current scholarship focuses on the literary, historical, religious, and cultural context of ancient education from Archaic Greece through Late Antiquity, offering comparative insights for periods of cultural transformation, including the late modern world.

item.title: Salil Vadhan
item.description:
Salil Vadhan

Vicky Joseph Professor of Computer Science

Salil Vadhan is the Vicky Joseph Professor of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics in the Harvard University School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, and the Director of the Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society. He earned his PhD in Applied Mathematics from MIT in 1999 and served as an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow at MIT and the Institute for Advanced Study before joining Harvard’s faculty in 2001. His awards include “a Simons Investigator Award, a Godel Prize, a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Phi Beta Kappa Award for Excellence in Teaching, and the ACM Doctoral Dissertation Award.”

item.title: Salman Khan
item.description:
Salman Khan

Visiting Fellow, HGSE; Research Lead, Harvard Project on Workforce

Salman is currently a Postdoctoral Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) in the Economics of Crime, a Visiting Fellow at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, and a Research Lead at the Harvard Project on Workforce.

He completed his PhD from Harvard University in May 2025. His research focuses on investigating inequalities in the economics of crime, higher education and the labor market, and AI and the future of work. In his research, he draws on labor economics, econometrics, and large administrative datasets to identify the causal impacts of different policies in schools, colleges, and society.

item.title: Samuel Arbesman
item.description:
Samuel Arbesman

Research Fellow, Harvard Medical School

IQSS Visitor/Affiliate.

item.title: Satellite Imagery Analysis with Google Earth Engine
item.description:
Satellite Imagery Analysis with Google Earth Engine

Date: April 3, 2026

Time: 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM EDT

Location: CGIS Knafel Building, Room SB-12

A two-hour workshop introducing satellite imagery analysis using Google Earth Engine (GEE) via KNIME extension. Topics include how remote sensing supports social science, health, and humanities research; clipping and extracting imagery; and performing land use/land cover classification with accuracy assessment. Free for Harvard affiliates; $100 for others.

item.title: Save the Date: 2023 Dataverse Community Meeting
item.description:
The Dataverse Project invites the global research data management community to save the date for the 9th Annual Dataverse Community Meeting, taking place in the historic and vibrant city of Braga, Portugal. This highly anticipated gathering brings together repository administrators, developers, data professionals, and researchers from institutions worldwide to share experiences, discuss best practices, and shape the future of the Dataverse platform.

The meeting in Braga will feature technical presentations, workshops, and collaborative sessions covering the latest developments in Dataverse software, emerging trends in research data management, and strategies for supporting open science initiatives. Attendees will have opportunities to learn from peers managing Dataverse installations across diverse institutional contexts, from small university repositories to large international collaborations. The European location makes this an especially valuable opportunity for institutions across Europe, Africa, and the Middle East to participate in the Dataverse community.

item.title: Science needs contrarians, and contrarians need support
item.description:
The Extraordinary Claims, Extraordinary Evidence (ECEE) program at IQSS supports Harvard faculty undertaking high-risk research that could provide novel insights by testing dominant views in social science. The program provides tailored support including data expertise, infrastructure, and funding.

ECEE recognizes that scientific progress often comes from researchers willing to challenge established consensus—but that such work faces unique obstacles in traditional funding and publication systems. By providing a confidential environment with dedicated resources, the program enables faculty to pursue ideas they might otherwise set aside.

item.title: Scientific Programs
item.description:
Social Science One

Implements a new partnership model between academics and the private sector to use company data for societal issues while maintaining privacy and data security standards.

The Center for Geographic Analysis

Administers Harvard-wide GIS infrastructure, collects and disseminates spatial datasets, and provides training and consultation in the use of geospatial technologies.

The Future of Media Project

A partnership with HBS to further research and identify solutions to rebalance truth, privacy and power in the media industry.

item.title: Scott Bell
item.description:
Scott Bell

Lead Instructor GIS Institute; Professor, Univ of Saskatchewan

Scott is the Lead Instructor for the CGA GIS Institute. Scott has expertise in advanced applications of GIS and GIS training for academic research. He holds an MA and PhD in Geography from the University of California, Santa Barbara and has collaborated on interdisciplinary health, environmental, social science, and cognitive science research during his career. Scott is an Associate Professor of Geography and Planning at the University of Saskatchewan, and most recently was the Associate Director of Spatial Structures for the Social Sciences at Brown University. While his collaborative research interests are broad his personal research program is focused on spatial cognition and applied GIS for health geography. His research is funded by the Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR), the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC), and GEOIDE, a National Centre of Excellence focused on GIS for decision making.

item.title: Sebastian Bauhoff
item.description:
Sebastian Bauhoff

Assistant Professor of Global Health and Economics, HSPH

Email: sbauhoff@hsph.harvard.edu

Sebastian Bauhoff is an Assistant Professor of Global Health and Economics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and an affiliate of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science. His research focuses on “innovations in health care financing and service delivery that can increase access, efficiency and quality of care in low and middle-income countries.”

item.title: Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez
item.description:
Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez

Bluhm Family Assistant Professor of Data Science and Education

Sebastian Munoz-Najar Galvez is the Bluhm Family Assistant Professor of Data Science and Education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. He earned his doctorate in Sociology of Education from Stanford University’s Graduate School of Education. As a sociologist of science, he employs computational linguistics and network analysis to examine how research agendas evolve over time. More recently, he has shifted his focus toward “the study of adolescent experience, college admissions, and technologies of belonging.” His research has appeared in the American Sociological Review, the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science, and American Educational Research Journal.

item.title: Selim Yaman
item.description:
Selim Yaman

PhD Candidate, American University

Selim Yaman is a PhD candidate in Political Science at American University’s School of Public Affairs, where he specializes in political methodology and comparative politics. His research focuses on natural language processing and Bayesian statistics. Yaman also serves as a Fellow at the Center for Data Science at American University and replication analyst at Political Analysis. Before starting doctoral study, he lived and worked in the UK, and Turkey.

item.title: Shao-Yu Jheng
item.description:
Shao-Yu Jheng

Predoctoral Research Fellow

Shao-Yu Jheng’s research topics include “(i) (rapid) industrialization and premature deindustrialization, (ii) state capacity and industrial policy, (iii) institutions,” (iv) USA’s aid policy, spanning political economy, economic history, development economics, and industrial organization.

Previously working at National Taiwan University, his works explored USA’s lend-lease aid to China during WWII, Qing Taiwan’s land institutions, and impacts of Japanese colonial legacies on Taiwan’s postwar industrialization.

item.title: Shaoqing Zhou
item.description:
Shaoqing Zhou

Fellow, CBDB; Joint PhD Student, Harvard

Shaoqing Zhou’s research interest is digital humanity.

item.title: Sharon-Lise Normand
item.description:
Sharon-Lise Normand

S. James Adelstein Professor of Health Care Policy

Sharon-Lise T. Normand, PhD, holds the S. James Adelstein Professorship of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School and is a Professor in Biostatistics at Harvard’s School of Public Health. Her research centers on developing statistical methods for health services research, with a primary emphasis on Bayesian approaches. Her work encompasses quality of care assessment, causal inference methods, provider profiling, meta-analysis, and latent variable modeling. She has built an extensive research program analyzing treatment patterns and care quality for cardiovascular disease and mental disorder patients.

item.title: Shiyin Chen
item.description:
Shiyin Chen

Visiting Scholar, China Biographical Database

He majors in Confucian Classics and Ming history. In recent years, he has published some books about Confucian Classics study and Ming history, namely, Annotations about The Book of Rites (Fudan University Press, 2018), Supplementary Remarks of Chen Hao’s Explanation about The Book of Rites (Anhui Education Press, 2020), From Duke Zhou to First Emperor of Qin: Autobiographies of 12 famous people (Lijiang Press, 2019), Unstable Identity: A Brief History of Ming Dynasty Based-on Ritual System (Zhejiang Guji Press, 2021).

item.title: Siqin Wang
item.description:
Siqin Wang

Associate Chair, Spatial Data Lab, CGA; Assoc Professor, USC

Dr. Wang’s research focuses on geospatial science and spatiotemporal big data analytics (e.g., AI) applied to digital health geography, environmental health, population-health-environment interactions, and computational social science more broadly.

item.title: Sponsored Research Services
item.description:
IQSS Research Administration

The Sponsored Research Administration Team at IQSS is dedicated to supporting social scientists’ research by delivering services across the full lifecycle of sponsored projects.

The team consists of experienced sponsored research administrators offering both pre-award and post-award support. They primarily serve social scientists in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and across the University, assisting with proposal development and submission, grants management, and reporting. Their goal is to provide outstanding service to IQSS-affiliated investigators with all of their sponsored research needs.

item.title: Startup Foundry Success Stories
item.description:
TeamBirth / Unravel Healthcare

TeamBirth emerged from Ariadne Labs, a joint center of Harvard and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. The program addressed communication failures in childbirth that cause preventable deaths. After a 2019 pilot at four sites that demonstrated significant improvements in maternal and neonatal outcomes, the program scaled to over 200 hospitals nationwide.

Dr. Amber Weiseth transitioned from research scientist to CEO, leading the effort to bring the evidence-based intervention to healthcare systems at scale. The IQSS Startup Foundry provided comprehensive support: mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs, product design workshops to refine the technology platform, data science support for outcomes measurement, an HBS MBA intern to develop the business model, network connections to healthcare executives, and ultimately matched the team with a COO.

item.title: Stephen Ansolabehere
item.description:
Stephen Ansolabehere

Frank G. Thompson Professor of Government

Email: sda@gov.harvard.edu

Stephen Ansolabehere is Frank G. Thompson Professor of Government at Harvard University. He specializes in public opinion and elections, with extensive publications on elections, mass media, representation, political economy, and public opinion (particularly regarding energy and the environment).

He authored five books: Cheap and Clean, The Media Game, Going Negative, American Government, and The End of Inequality.

item.title: Steven Currall
item.description:
Steven Currall

Executive Director, Academic-Corporate Initiatives, OVPR

IQSS Faculty Affiliate. For full profile details, see the IQSS People directory.

item.title: Steven Worthington
item.description:
Steven Worthington

Director of Data Science Services

Email: sworthington@iq.harvard.edu

Steve has worked at IQSS since 2011. He earned a PhD in Biological Anthropology from New York University and is working on a master’s in data science at Harvard. He hails from northern England, but has lived in New York and Helsinki, Finland. During his graduate studies, he developed an interest in computational biology and statistical programming using R and Python. His expertise spans Bayesian and frequentist inference, deep learning, phylogenetic methods, and geometric morphometrics. In his free time, he enjoys playing with his dog, Beckett, and indulging his interest in photography.

item.title: Streamlining the Publication Process with Magaro Peer Pre-Review
item.description:
Stephen Chaudoin laments that “you only get so many bites of the apple with journals”—the traditional publication process is lengthy, uncertain, and offers limited opportunities for constructive feedback before formal review. The Magaro Peer Pre-Review Program addresses this gap.

The program, funded by a generous gift from Alexander and Diviya Magaro, provides researchers with professional-quality peer reviews before they submit to journals. Reviewers read full papers and offer detailed, constructive suggestions, helping authors strengthen their work and avoid common pitfalls that lead to rejection.

item.title: Suzanne Preston Blier
item.description:
Suzanne Preston Blier

Allen Whitehill Clowes Professor of Fine Arts and of African and African American Studies

Email: blier@fas.harvard.edu

Suzanne Preston Blier earned her Ph.D. in 1981 from Columbia and holds the Allen Whitehill Clowes Professor of Fine Arts and of African and African American Studies position at Harvard University. She is a historian of African art and architecture working in both the History of Art and Architecture and African and African American Studies Departments, and is a member of the Institute for Quantitative Social Science.

item.title: SV Subramanian
item.description:
SV Subramanian

Professor of Population Health and Geography

S (“Subu”) V Subramanian is a Professor of Population Health and Geography at the Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard Chan School of Public Health, and a senior core faculty at the Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies. He is also the founding director for an interdisciplinary PhD program in Population Health Sciences that is currently being developed at Harvard. He received his under- and post-graduate training at the University of Delhi, and completed his PhD in geography from the University of Portsmouth, UK in 2000. Subu has published over 425 articles, book chapters, and books in the field of social and contextual determinants of health, health inequalities in India with a special emphasis on nutritional inequalities among children and adults, and applied multilevel statistical models. He has co-edited 2 books titled Global Perspectives on Social Capital and Health and Social Capital and Health. Subu was the first to develop a course on the concept and application of multilevel statistical methods at Harvard, which he has been successfully teaching at Harvard Chan since 2001, as well as around the world. He has advised over 100 masters, doctoral and postdoctoral students as mentor, academic advisor and dissertation committee member. Subu has served as a permanent member of the National Institutes of Health Community Influences on Health Behavior (CIHB) Study Section, and as reviewer for several national and international funding agencies. He is the Editor-in-Chief (along with Ichiro Kawachi) for the international journal Social Science & Medicine (SSM), in addition to being a Senior Editor for the social epidemiology office of SSM. He is an editorial consultant to The Lancet, an international advisory board member for the Lancet Global Health, and serves as an academic editor to PLoS Medicine, besides serving as an editorial board member of several journals.

item.title: The art of the online interface
item.description:
By Colleen Walsh

New desktop application streamlines connection between IQSS’s Dataverse and Sid

A new application called LOOP, developed at Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS), aims to simplify the workflow for researchers who want to analyze data from the Harvard Dataverse using Sid—Harvard’s version of the open-source Open OnDemand dashboard that connects scholars with supercomputers.

Len Wisniewski, senior director of research computing at IQSS, leads the Sid team that co-designed the LOOP application with the Dataverse team. The software targets researchers across disciplines—from political science to psychology to the physical sciences.

item.title: The Community that Makes the Center: the Whiteboards of IQSS
item.description:
by Gary King

IQSS director Gary King reflects on the origins of the writing surfaces that cover the hallways of the Institute, as featured in a recent article by the Harvard Gazette.

When King started IQSS, he interviewed many current and former Harvard deans and presidents to understand what made the best centers succeed. He looked at places like the legendary Cavendish in London, Bell Labs, ISR, and others. Everyone he spoke with had a different story but arrived at the same conclusion. One person would emphasize great space, but then acknowledge that some great centers lacked great space. Others would stress funding, then concede it wasn’t really about money. But ultimately, every single person he consulted landed on the same answer: community. As King writes, “It is the intellectual community that makes the center.” He had a specific notion of how to build that community at IQSS, described in an article he wrote about IQSS, and notes that “this method wound up working great!”

item.title: The Enigma of the Undecided Voter
item.description:
by Vinay Mehra

Originally posted on Vinay Mehra’s Substack.

The article explores the conventional image of the undecided voter—the suburban mom or blue-collar worker who can’t choose between candidates—and argues this framing is far too narrow. Researchers at Harvard’s Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS) suggest that the firm distinction between “decided” and “undecided” voters may not actually exist.

The Real Swing

The article contends that so-called undecided voters aren’t a separate breed standing on a fence. Rather, they sit near the middle of the political spectrum, close to a threshold where political shifts make their vote changes more visible. The entire electorate sways together; those in the middle simply show the movement most clearly. Even solidly partisan areas experience shifts—just less obviously.

item.title: The IQSS Startup Foundry
item.description:
Transforming Social Science Research Into World-Changing Companies

The IQSS Startup Foundry helps Harvard faculty transform social science insights into scalable technology companies that solve global challenges.

The Untapped Opportunity

The social sciences are a massive, underexplored innovation pipeline. Quantitative methods have improved and analytical capabilities have expanded, yet commercial applications remain largely untapped. Most researchers are unaware their insights could become transformative companies, creating opportunities for both academics and business.

item.title: Thierry Warin
item.description:
Thierry Warin

Visiting Scholar, D^3 Institute

A Visiting Scholar at the Digital Data Design (D^3) Institute, Thierry Warin is an academic whose professional pursuits are deeply rooted in the application of data science methodologies to explore global transformations, including phenomena such as the platform economy and the dynamics of innovation. His research is characterized by the examination of institutions, economic dynamics, and the utilization of unstructured data to uncover insights into these complex areas. Warin places a high value on democratizing access to the burgeoning field of data science, viewing it as a pivotal step toward collaboratively addressing global challenges. His approach to research is fundamentally inductive, prioritizing a bottom-up methodology that is deeply rooted in data. This perspective not only enriches empirical understanding across various domains but also serves as a robust framework for testing, refining, and potentially redefining theoretical constructs and traditional economic indicators.

item.title: Thiri Shwesin Aung
item.description:
Thiri Shwesin Aung

Research Associate, TH Chan School

Thiri is an accomplished environmental scientist specializing in Land Cover and Land-Use Change (LCLUC) and energy systems. Her expertise spans “remote sensing, ecology, biogeochemistry, and land change modeling.” Her current research focuses on “advancing methods, models, and emerging technologies in data science” for processing and analyzing heterogeneous remote sensing data, with applications to Earth System Science, especially in “data-scarce conflict regions.” She uses geospatial science to “capture, analyze, and predict the intricacies of LCLUC at various scales,” enabling understanding of environmental and societal impacts through land system analysis. She has extensive experience investigating “the impacts of armed conflict on land use, cropland abandonment, and socioeconomics” using remote sensing and modeling approaches. Her work appears in over 20 peer-reviewed journals. Thiri leads the CEFWG, an organization using geography and remote sensing to connect environmental condition, land use, and climate change with “processes of conflict, displacement, and resilience.” Her research has received funding from the European Union, the World Bank, and the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She currently focuses on developing methods to “harness satellite data and artificial intelligence” to investigate human rights violations and environmental crimes during conflict and resource exploration.

item.title: Tian Tian
item.description:
Tian Tian

Visiting Fellow, CGA

Tian Tian is a doctoral candidate in Urban and Rural Planning at Wuhan University, specializes in employing data analysis and modeling methodologies within urban studies. Her research is dedicated to unraveling the intricate mechanisms that underlie urban interactions. At the CGA, she participates in the Spatial Data Lab project, advancing replicable geospatial data analytics with workflow-based case studies.

item.title: Timothy Colton
item.description:
Timothy Colton

Morris and Anna Feldberg Professor of Government and Russian Studies

Timothy J. Colton is Morris and Anna Feldberg Professor of Government and Russian Studies and the Chair of the Department of Government. His main interest is Russian and post-Soviet government and politics.

He authored The Dilemma of Reform in the Soviet Union (1986); Moscow: Governing the Socialist Metropolis (1995), which was “named best scholarly book in government and political science by the Association of American Publishers”; Transitional Citizens: Voters and What Influences Them in the New Russia (2000); and Popular Choice and Managed Democracy: The Russian Elections of 1999 and 2000 (with Michael McFaul, 2003). At the time of this profile, he was writing a book on Boris Yeltsin’s statecraft and coordinating a joint project on the post-Communist state.

item.title: Tomiko Brown-Nagin
item.description:
Tomiko Brown-Nagin

Daniel P.S. Paul Professor of Constitutional Law; Professor of History, Faculty of Arts and Sciences

Email: tbrownnagin@law.harvard.edu

Tomiko Brown-Nagin is described as “an award-winning legal historian and expert in constitutional law and education law and policy.” She has published in numerous prestigious journals including the Yale Law Journal, Columbia Law Review, Duke Law Journal, and Journal of Law & Education, covering topics such as equal protection jurisprudence, civil rights law and history, the Affordable Care Act, and education reform.

item.title: Torben Iversen
item.description:
Torben Iversen

Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy

Torben Iversen is Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy in the Government Department at Harvard University. His research and teaching interests include comparative political economy, electoral politics, and applied formal theory. He is the author or co-author of Big Data and the Welfare State: How the Information Revolution Threatens Social Solidarity (Cambridge UP 2022) (with Philipp Rehm), Democracy and Prosperity: Reinventing Capitalism through a Turbulent Century (Princeton UP 2019) (with David Soskice), Women, Work, and Politics: The Political Economy of Gender Inequality (Yale UP 2010) (with Frances Rosenbluth), Capitalism, Democracy, and Welfare (Cambridge UP 2005), and Contested Economic Institutions (Cambridge UP 1999). He has also authored or co-authored “more than four dozen articles on comparative politics and political economy.” He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has held fellowships including Radcliffe Fellow, Guggenheim Fellow, Hoover National Fellow, and “a BP Centennial Professor at the London School of Economics.”

item.title: Tracking the American electorate: the Cooperative Election Study
item.description:
The Cooperative Election Study, supported by IQSS, offers key insights into the minds of American voters. Running since 2006, the study surveys tens of thousands of Americans before and after each election, providing unprecedented detail about electoral behavior at the local level.

The study’s massive sample size—typically 50,000 or more respondents—enables analysis at the congressional district level, something impossible with standard national polls. This granularity has made the CES an essential resource for researchers studying representation, accountability, and geographic variation in political attitudes.

item.title: Training & Workshops
item.description:
Workshops Hosted at IQSS in Collaboration with Other Departments

Applied Statistics Workshop

A weekly, cross-disciplinary tour of Harvard’s statistical innovations and applications.

Learn more about the Applied Statistics Workshop

Tech Science Seminars

Weekly series on Technology Science from expert researchers, public interest groups, and others on the social impact of technology.

Learn more about Tech Science Seminars

Alberto Alesina Seminar on Political Economy

A seminar series on formal and quantitative political research that integrates the study of economics and politics.

item.title: Travel Grants
item.description:
Travel grants support IQSS graduate student affiliates who are enrolled in a doctoral program, intended to fund travel for presenting at professional conferences related to their research.

Note: IQSS travel grants are currently closed to applications.

Key Details
Eligibility IQSS graduate student affiliate, currently enrolled in a doctoral program
Amount $1,000 maximum
Deadline Rolling (currently closed)
Frequency One application per fiscal year (July 1 – June 30)

About

  • Designed to supplement costs not covered by the applicant’s home department
  • May be combined with other travel grant funds
  • Funds are not available for job market events
  • IQSS prefers not to grant Travel Grants retroactively — please submit your application as far in advance of the conference as you can

How to Apply

Submit a travel proposal to funding@iq.harvard.edu that includes:

item.title: Travel Time Estimation for Geospatial Big Data
item.description:
Researchers at the Center for Geographic Analysis explore drive time estimation’s importance in urban planning, transportation, public health, and healthcare accessibility. Their case study examines travel times to healthcare facilities across the United States, revealing geographic disparities in access.

The research addresses a fundamental challenge in geospatial analysis: accurately estimating travel times for millions of origin-destination pairs requires enormous computational resources and sophisticated algorithms that account for road networks, traffic patterns, and geographic barriers.

item.title: Tucker Sigourney
item.description:
Tucker Sigourney

Postdoctoral Fellow, Human Flourishing Program

Tucker is a John and Daria Barry postdoctoral fellow at the Human Flourishing Program. His main areas of study are ethics and action theory, especially within the broadly Aristotelian tradition, and his work so far has focused primarily on questions of forgiveness and love. He holds a Ph.D. in philosophy from Florida State University and undergraduate degrees in philosophy and physics from Grove City College.

item.title: Turns out two-parent households are no fix for racial inequality
item.description: IQSS affiliate Christina Cross, Associate Professor of Sociology at Harvard University, has published a book that critically examines one of the most persistent claims in debates about racial inequality: that promoting two-parent nuclear families is a simple solution to closing racial gaps in economic and social outcomes. Through rigorous analysis of demographic and economic data, Cross challenges this conventional wisdom and reveals the limitations of family structure as an explanation for racial disparities.

item.title: Tutorials
item.description:
LaTeX and Writing Tools

  • LaTeX Applications: A Beginner’s Guide — Covers recommended LaTeX editing options including Overleaf, VSCode, and Emacs, plus tools like GitHub and Copilot.
  • Overleaf: A Beginner’s Guide — Steps for signing up, editing documents, and collaboration in Overleaf.
  • Visual Studio Code: A Beginner’s Guide — Steps for installation and importing recommended settings, keybindings, and shortcuts.
  • Emacs: A Beginner’s Guide — Steps for installation, importing configuration, and common functions for LaTeX editing.

Version Control

  • Git and GitHub: A Beginner’s Guide — Steps for creating and cloning repositories, and using the command line.
  • GitHub Pages: A Beginner’s Guide — Steps for creating a personal website, downloading and customizing templates.

Data Science Methods

  • Rbuild: Create Your Own Packages in R — Best practices for R package development and version control using RStudio.
  • Matching and Weighting for Causal Inference — Covers propensity score analysis methods for adjusting confounding in observational studies. Includes R examples.
  • Web-scraping with Selenium Python — Guide to scraping both static and dynamic websites with Selenium Python.

item.title: Twitter Sentiment Geographical Index
item.description:
The Center for Geographic Analysis at Harvard’s IQSS explores how Twitter evolved from a simple social networking platform into a powerful tool for sentiment analysis and geographic understanding of public opinion. The development of the Twitter Sentiment Geographical Index represents an innovative application of social media data to track emotional patterns and attitudes across geographic regions, providing researchers with unprecedented insight into spatial variations in public sentiment.

By combining natural language processing techniques to analyze the emotional content of tweets with geolocation data, researchers can map sentiment patterns across cities, regions, and countries. This approach enables studies of how attitudes vary geographically and change over time in response to events, policies, or social trends. The Twitter Sentiment Geographical Index has applications across diverse research domains, from understanding political attitudes and election dynamics to tracking public health concerns and responses to natural disasters.

item.title: Tyler VanderWeele
item.description:
Tyler VanderWeele

John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology

Tyler J. VanderWeele is the John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology in the Departments of Epidemiology and Biostatistics at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, and director of the Human Flourishing Program and co-director of the Initiative on Health, Religion and Spirituality at Harvard University. He holds degrees from the University of Oxford, University of Pennsylvania, and Harvard University in mathematics, philosophy, theology, finance, and biostatistics. His methodological research focuses on “theory and methods for distinguishing between association and causation in the biomedical and social sciences” and more recently on psychosocial measurement theory. His empirical research spans psychiatric and social epidemiology; the science of happiness and flourishing; and the study of religion and health. He received the 2017 Presidents’ Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies (COPSS). He has published over three hundred papers in peer-reviewed journals and is author of the books Explanation in Causal Inference (2015), Modern Epidemiology (2021), and Measuring Well-Being (2021). He also writes a monthly blog posting on topics related to human flourishing for Psychology Today.

item.title: Undergraduate Research Scholars
item.description:
Program Benefits

For Faculty

Get funding to hire Undergraduate Research Scholars as research assistants for your project.

For Students

Gain valuable experience as a paid research assistant on new and exciting research projects led by Harvard faculty.

How to Apply

For Faculty

Applying for URS funding is simple and will benefit both you and the undergraduates you hire.

For Students

Students wishing to participate in the URS program can either apply for jobs on the opportunities page, or contact a faculty member they wish to work with.

item.title: Update on IQSS and Microsoft OpenDP Collaboration
item.description:
IQSS and Microsoft provided an update on their collaboration to develop open-source tools for differential privacy, enabling researchers to discover insights while protecting data. The partnership combines Harvard’s theoretical expertise with Microsoft’s engineering resources.

The update details progress on the OpenDP platform, which provides verified privacy guarantees for data analysis. The collaboration has produced both a software library (the OpenDP Library) and research advancing the theoretical foundations of privacy-preserving computation.

item.title: Using Data to Map the Political Legacy of Slavery
item.description:
Matthew Blackwell and Maya Sen’s book “Deep Roots” won APSA’s 2019 William H. Riker Book Award for the best book on political economy published during the past three calendar years. The book traces how slavery’s institutional legacy continues to shape American politics today.

Using a combination of historical data, geographic analysis, and modern survey evidence, Blackwell and Sen demonstrate that Southern counties with higher historical concentrations of slavery exhibit distinctive political attitudes and behaviors that persist into the present—even after controlling for contemporary demographic and economic factors.

item.title: Valerie OKane
item.description:
Valerie OKane

Director of Business Operations

Email: valerie_okane@harvard.edu

Valerie O’Kane is the Director of Business Operations at the Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS) at Harvard University with responsibility for the IQSS budget & long term planning, IQSS contract and grant administration, IQSS compliance & space, as well as managing the general day-to-day operations of the IQSS Business Office.

Valerie is a seasoned financial professional who began her career at Harvard in 1992 as a staff assistant in the Central Payroll Office. In 1994 she moved to the FAS Extension School as the Payroll Administrator/Assistant Human Resource Officer. Valerie returned to Harvard Central Administration in 2002 as an accounting assistant and in 2004 became one of two payroll accountants for the University. Valerie was recognized as a Harvard Hero in 2005 as part of the University’s W2 Team. In 2007 she moved to the Harvard Kennedy School as the Financial Manager of the Malcolm Wiener Center for Social Policy.

item.title: Vesall Nourani
item.description:
Vesall Nourani

Assistant Professor, Harvard Graduate School of Education

Vesall Nourani is an assistant professor at HGSE. His research explores “the roles of knowledge and learning in economic activity across sub-Saharan Africa.” He conducts research on educational programs promoting community-based research, investigation, and dialogue aimed at advancing community development. His current projects use randomized controlled trials and other causal inference tools to study program impacts in Uganda and Colombia.

item.title: Vinay Mehra
item.description:
Vinay Mehra

Associate of IQSS

Vinay Mehra is passionate about “curating academic literature to make new knowledge accessible to a broader audience,” emphasizing social science and data’s role in shaping worldview. His research centers on identifying social science ideas developable into commercial ventures for public benefit. He has a strong background in media and information, having held leadership positions at Politico and The Boston Globe, and has launched multiple companies as an entrepreneur in the data and information space.

item.title: Vincent Pons
item.description:
Vincent Pons

Associate Professor, Harvard Business School

He is “an Associate Professor at Harvard Business School” and affiliated with NBER and J-PAL.

His research focuses on understanding why representative democracies sometimes fail to produce leaders and policies that match citizens’ preferences.

His work has been published in top journals including Econometrica, the American Economic Review, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the American Political Science Review, with media coverage in outlets like The New York Times and The Economist.

item.title: Visiting Seoul National University for Dataverse
item.description:
Philip Durbin recounts a visit by five colleagues to Seoul National University for Dataverse talks and training, hosted by Professor Wonsuk Lee. The trip reflects the Dataverse Project’s growing international presence and commitment to supporting installations worldwide.

The visit included technical training sessions on Dataverse administration, presentations on best practices for research data management, and discussions about how to adapt the platform for Korean research communities. Such visits help ensure that international Dataverse installations receive the support they need to serve their local research communities effectively.

item.description:

Wanchun’s research focuses on political institutions from Han to Tang Dynasty. In addition, in the CBDB project, she is concerned with how digital humanities tools can be used to analyze families and regional groups in fence towns (fanzhen).

item.title: Waves 1 and 2 of the Global Flourishing Study Are Now Open to the Public
item.description: The Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University has made a landmark contribution to social science research with the public release of both Wave 1 and Wave 2 data from the Global Flourishing Study. This massive dataset includes responses from roughly 200,000 participants across 22 countries, making it one of the most comprehensive longitudinal studies of human well-being ever conducted. The data covers six fundamental domains of flourishing: happiness and life satisfaction, physical and mental health, meaning and purpose, character and virtue, close social relationships, and financial and material stability.

item.title: Wei Luo
item.description:
Wei Luo

Associate, CGA; Research Fellow, Harvard Medical School

Dr. Wei Luo is a Research Associate at the Computational Health Informatics Program (CHIP) at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and an Associate at the Center for Geographic Analysis at Harvard University. He has broad training backgrounds in Geography (GIScience), Public Health (Epidemiology), Computer Science (Visual Analytics), and Network Science. He proposed a new research area: geo-social visual analytics, which aims to integrate spatial analysis, social network analysis, and machine learning into visual analytics environments. He has designed and developed a series of geovisual analytics tools and high performance computational models for infectious disease transmission and control (i.e., influenza, HIV), international trade, social media, crime analysis, climate change impacts, and water crisis.

item.title: What science says about Moms happiness advice
item.description:
IQSS affiliate Daniel Gilbert, the Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at Harvard University, delivered a compelling lecture exploring the intersection of scientific research and timeless maternal wisdom about happiness. Gilbert, known for his groundbreaking work on affective forecasting and happiness research, shared insights from decades of psychological studies that validate many of the common-sense principles our mothers have been telling us for years.

During the lecture, Gilbert explained how rigorous scientific investigation into human happiness has repeatedly confirmed conventional wisdom about what makes people truly happy. From the importance of gratitude and social connections to the value of helping others and maintaining perspective during difficult times, research data consistently supports the age-old advice that mothers have been dispensing for generations. Gilbert’s presentation highlighted how psychological science has progressed from questioning these intuitive beliefs to understanding the mechanisms that make them effective.

item.title: What's Next for This Year's Graduating IQSS Affiliates
item.description:
The IQSS community includes affiliated graduate students across Harvard University engaged in a wide range of social science research. Each year, some graduate students depart as they complete their programs. Below are updates from graduating affiliates moving on to continue their work beyond Harvard.

Stephanie Kestelman (PhD, Economics)

Stephanie is remaining at Harvard for a postdoctoral fellowship, working with Professor Rebecca Diamond to evaluate potential impacts of Cambridge’s new zoning ordinance.

item.title: Where to Next? Outgoing IQSS graduate affiliates share plans
item.description:
IQSS staff piece about departing graduate student affiliates from programs across Harvard and their future plans. Each year, the end of the academic year brings the departure of affiliated graduate students who have been active in social science research.

The departing affiliates head to positions across academia, policy organizations, and the private sector, carrying with them the quantitative training and collaborative research experience they gained at IQSS. Their diverse career paths—from assistant professorships to research positions at think tanks to roles in tech companies—reflect the breadth of opportunities available to quantitative social scientists.

item.title: Where to now? Outgoing IQSS graduate affiliates share their next steps
item.description:
Profiles of departing graduate students from the IQSS community cohort as they share plans after the academic year ends. The 2023 graduating class represents the diversity of disciplines and methodological approaches that characterize the IQSS affiliate community.

Graduating affiliates are heading to faculty positions, postdoctoral fellowships, and research roles at institutions across the country and around the world. Their research spans political science, economics, sociology, public policy, and data science—united by a commitment to rigorous quantitative methods.

item.title: Why self-appraisals may not be best way to judge job performance
item.description:
Faculty affiliate Iris Bohnet, Albert Pratt Professor of Business and Government at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Women and Public Policy Program, has published new research challenging the widespread practice of using self-appraisals in workplace performance evaluations. Her recent paper examines how worker performance ratings are affected by various biases and structural factors that can undermine the accuracy and fairness of self-assessment processes.

Bohnet’s research reveals that self-appraisals, while seemingly empowering to employees, often introduce systematic distortions into performance evaluation systems. The study found that self-ratings are influenced by factors including individual confidence levels, cultural backgrounds, and gender, with some groups systematically underrating their performance while others tend toward inflation. These patterns can inadvertently perpetuate workplace inequalities, as more modest self-assessors may be disadvantaged in compensation and promotion decisions even when their actual performance is strong.

item.title: Workshop Materials
item.description:
We offer a series of data analysis and programming workshop materials to members of the Harvard and MIT communities, as well as to the public. Each workshop is self-contained and can be studied at one’s own pace.

Python Workshop Materials

Python Introduction

This hands-on workshop introduces the basic elements of Python by working through an example of how to analyze text data. Appropriate for those with little or no prior experience.

item.title: Xiang Zhou
item.description:
Xiang Zhou

Associate Professor of Sociology

Xiang Zhou is an Associate Professor of Sociology at Harvard University. His research focuses on “quantitative methodology, causes and consequences of economic inequality, and political culture in contemporary China.” He has published in several journals including Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Social Forces, Sociological Methodology, Sociological Research and Methods, and China Economic Review. Prior to Harvard, he “worked as a postdoctoral research associate at Princeton University.” He earned his PhD in Sociology and Statistics from the University of Michigan in 2015.

item.title: Xiao-Li Meng
item.description:
Xiao-Li Meng

Whipple V. N. Jones Professor of Statistics

Xiao-Li Meng is the Whipple V. N. Jones Professor and former chair of Statistics at Harvard, an Honorary Professor of the University of Hong Kong, and a faculty affiliate at the Center of Health Statistics at the University of Chicago. He is well known for his depth and breadth in research, his innovation and passion in pedagogy, and his vision and effectiveness in administration, as well as for his engaging and entertaining style as a speaker and a writer.

item.title: Xihong Lin
item.description:
Xihong Lin

Professor of Biostatistics; Professor of Statistics

Dr. Lin’s research interests lie in statistical genetics and genomics. She is interested in development and application of statistical and computational methods for analysis of high-throughput genetic, genomic and ‘omics data in epidemiological, environmental and clinical sciences, especially genetic and epigenetic epidemiology, genes and environment, and medical genomics. Current research projects include genome-wide array association studies, whole genome sequencing association studies, gene-environment interactions, and genome-wide DNA methylation studies, pathway and network analysis, and integrative genetics and genomics. She currently serves as the coordinating director of the Program of Quantitative Genomics of Harvard School of Public Heath. Her methodological work is currently supported by the MERIT award from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Methods for Correlated and High-Dimensional Biomedical Data,” and the PO1 from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Informatics in Cancer Research.” She is the contacting PI for the training grant entitled “Joint training in biostatistics and computational biology.”

  1. Extracting geographical knowledge from maps and remote sensing imagery.
  2. Analyzing big geospatial data to advance sustainable development.

He previously held the position of “Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at Harvard.” Before that, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Google Research and earned his PhD from UC Berkeley. His awards include the 2012 Best Student Paper Award at the ACM conference on Web Search and Data Mining, the 2010 Facebook Fellowship, the 2009 Microsoft Research Fellowship, and “several entrepreneurial awards for work on social networks.”

Associate Professor of Government

He is an Associate Professor in the Department of Government at Harvard University whose research focuses on “state institutions and state-business relations in China.” He authored Tying the Autocrat’s Hands: The Rise of the Rule of Law in China (Cambridge University Press, 2015).

He earned his B.A. and M.A. from Peking University in 2003 and 2006, and his Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Michigan in 2011. From 2011 to 2015, he served as assistant professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania.

Yuqi works on the China Biographical Database (CBDB) Project at IQSS. Her research interests span Quantitative History and Digital Humanities, focusing particularly on Social Network Analysis of archaeological data.

Yusuf Celik

Postdoctoral Fellow, Islamic Law, HLS

Dr. Yusuf Celik’s research focuses on “philosophical hermeneutics, posthumanism, and the Digital Humanities.” He has also been active in software engineering, working as an independent contractor for high-profile clients as a “lead developer, consultant, code coach, and Scrum master.” He is currently building tools and platforms that enable researchers to “derive quantifiable insights from historical and legal texts.”

item.title: Yuting Chen
item.description:
Yuting Chen

Visiting Fellow, CGA

Yuting Chen is a PhD student from the Institute of Space and Earth Information Science, the Chinese University of Hong Kong. Her research focuses on “virtual geographic environment, geographic knowledge engineering and geospatial big data analysis.” She has a computer science and software engineering background. During her PhD, she worked on a project involving “Collaborative Simulation and Evaluation of Interaction between Global Change and Human Activities and Environment Based on Virtual Geographic Environment,” dealing with intelligent data and model sharing and multi-dimensional visualization for collaborative geographic research. As a visiting scholar at CGA, she studies under the supervision of Prof. Jason Ur and Dr. Wendy Guan.

item.title: Zifu Wang
item.description:
Zifu Wang

Postdoctoral Research Fellow, CGA

Zifu Wang, PhD is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Center for Geographic Analysis (CGA), whose research lies at the intersection of Geographic Information Science (GIS), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and computational science. His work focuses on transforming complex spatial and textual data into evidence-based intelligence for public-policy applications in humanitarian response, crime prevention, public health, and transportation safety.

Dr. Wang develops GeoAI models that integrate natural language processing (NLP), computer vision, and remote sensing to extract, analyze, and visualize spatiotemporal patterns from unstructured and real-time data. His research advances the field of policy intelligence, leveraging AI-driven systems to translate data into actionable insights that inform decision-making at local, national, and global levels.

item.title: Zoe Szajnfarber
item.description:
Zoe Szajnfarber

Visiting Scholar, LISH; Assoc Professor, George Washington University

Zoe Szajnfarber is an Associate Professor of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering and of International Affairs at the George Washington University. Her research focuses on design and innovation management in complex systems, with particular emphasis on how the organizational and technical systems architectures interact, and affect engineering work, during the design and development process. She has spent most of her career studying the aerospace and defense sector, from traditional acquisition programs to open innovation contests. Szajnfarber received her bachelor’s degree in Engineering Science from the University of Toronto and conducted her graduate work at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. There she earned dual masters’ degrees in Aeronautics & Astronautics and Technology Policy and a doctorate in Engineering Systems. Outside of academia, Dr. Szajnfarber has worked as a systems engineer at MDA Space Missions (Canadarm Program) and Dynacon Inc. (Microsatellites); and as a researcher at the European Space Agency (Advanced Concepts Team) and NASA (studying multiple centers).

item.title: Welcome to the IQSS Archive
item.description:

We’re excited to introduce this comprehensive archive of the Harvard Institute for Quantitative Social Science website. This Hugo-powered site contains a complete snapshot of IQSS content, including:

What’s Included

  • 1,075+ People Profiles - Complete directory of IQSS faculty, staff, affiliates, and students
  • Research Programs - Information about ongoing initiatives and projects
  • Data Science Services - Resources for statistical consulting and support
  • Technology Services - Computing facilities and technical resources
  • News & Events - Latest updates and announcements
  • Historical Content - Archived materials for research and reference

Interactive Features

This site includes several modern features not available in the original:

email zma@g.harvard.edu
Zheng Ma is a PhD student in Social Policy and Government at Harvard University. His research interests lie primarily in leveraging computational methods to understand social phenomena and solve social problems. He hope to explore more how data-driven approaches can reveal intricate social dynamics and inform policy decisions in various contexts. Prior to coming to Harvard, he obtained an M.A. in Social Sciences from the University of Chicago and a B.A. in Economics and Political Science from the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

item.description:
Yujing Huang

Department of Linguistics, GSAS
person
email yujinghuang@fas.harvard.edu
Yujing Huang is a doctoral student in the Department of Linguistics. She is interested in how different components of language interact. Her research interest includes how meaning is expressed via syntactic structure (that is, the syntax-semantics interface) and how sound structure interacts with this structure as well (i.e., the phoNology-syntax interface). Her approach to these questions is mainly experimental. She is currently working on an eye-tracking experiment with adults on the interpretation of verbal arguments. She is also working on a tonal dialect in China.

item.title: Yuhan Zhang
item.description:
Yuhan Zhang

PhD Student in Linguistics, GSAS
email yuz551@g.harvard.edu
laptop_windows Website

Yuhan Zhang holds a BA in English Language and Literature from Tsinghua University, China, and is currently a doctoral student in the Department of Linguistics at Harvard, working with Kathryn Davidson. She is interested in using experimental and quantitative methods to understand semantics and pragmatics during communication and information interpretation. She also works on adult language processing by using the self-paced reading method to unravel the cognitive mechanisms underlying language comprehension and production. Her current experimental semantic project involves identifying contextual factors in conversations that cause referential opacity in belief reports. She is also using corpus linguistic methodologies to investigate the phonological correlation between stress shift and vowel reduction in English verb nominalization.

item.title: Yoly Yue Liu
item.description:
Yoly Yue Liu

PhD Student in Education Policy, GSAS/HGSE
email yolyliu@g.harvard.edu

Yoly Yue Liu is a PhD student studying how education drives systemic change. Her research uses causal inference to identify effective education policies and practices in low- and middle-income countries. Through field experiments, she investigates how teaching practices can cultivate intrinsically motivated, interactive, and lasting learning; how communities can mobilize local resources to support learning and address local challenges; and how stakeholders can collaborate to foster a learning culture rooted in local realities. Before her PhD, Yoly worked as a policy researcher with United Nations agencies.

item.title: Yichen Guan
item.description:
Yichen Guan

Graduate School of Arts and Science, Harvard University, Department of Middle Eastern Studies
email yichenguan@fas.harvar.edu
Yichen Guan is a second year master student in Middle Eastern Studies. Her current research mainly focuses on the relationship between the diverse forms of authoritarianism and authoritarian persistence in the Middle East. She is interested in quantitative methodology in political science, and she is currently working as a research assistant for Professor Gary King and Molly Roberts. In her future research, she plans to combine the rigorous theory of comparative authoritarianism in the Middle East with sound empirical testing with programming skills such as R and STATA.

item.title: Xihong Lin
item.description:
Xihong Lin

Coordinating Director of the Program in Quantitative Genomics
Professor of Biostatistics, TH Chan School of Public Health
Professor of Statistics, Faculty of Arts and Sciences
smartphone 617-432-2914
email xlin@hsph.harvard.edu
laptop_windows HSPH profile
laptop_windows Research group website

Dr. Lin’s research interests lie in statistical genetics and genomics. She is interested in development and application of statistical and computational methods for analysis of high-throughput genetic, genomic and ‘omics data in epidemiological, environmental and clinical sciences,  especially genetic and epigenetic epidemiology, genes and environment, and medical genomics. Current research projects include genome-wide array association studies, whole genome sequencing association studies, gene-environment interactions, and genome-wide DNA methylation studies, pathway and network analysis, and integrative genetics and genomics. She currently serves as the coordinating director of the Program of Quantitative Genomics of Harvard School of Public Heath http://www.hsph.harvard.edu/pqg.  Her methodological work is currently supported by the MERIT award from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Methods for Correlated and High-Dimensional Biomedical Data,” and the PO1  from the National Cancer Institute on “Statistical Informatics in Cancer Research.” She is the contacting PI for the training grant  entitled Joint training in biostatistics and computational biology.

item.title: Wei Luo
item.description:
Wei Luo

Associate, Center for Geographic Analysis
Research Fellow in Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School
email wei.luo@childrens.harvard.edu

Dr. Wei Luo is a Research Associate at the Computational Health Informatics Program (CHIP) at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and an Associate at the Center for Geographic Analysis at Harvard University. He has broad training backgrounds in Geography (GIScience), Public Health (Epidemiology), Computer Science (Visual Analytics), and Network Science. He proposed a new research area: geo-social visual analytics, which aims to integrate spatial analysis, social network analysis, and machine learning into visual analytics environments. He has designed and developed a series of geovisual analytics tools and high performance computational models for infectious disease transmission and control (i.e., influenza, HIV), international trade, social media, crime analysis, climate change impacts, and water crisis.

item.title: Wei
item.description:
Wei-Fang Hsieh

PhD Student in Linguistics, GSAS
email weifanghsieh@g.harvard.edu

Wei-Fang is a third year PhD student in the Department of Linguistics at Harvard. Her main research areas are syntax, semantics, the syntax-semantics interface and laboratory phonology. Her research interests include the syntax and semantics of reduplication, ellipsis and resultatives, and the phonetics and phonology of tone sandhi. Wei-Fang uses experimental methodology to investigate the tone sandhi pattern in Mandarin-English code-switching context. She seeks to relate the empirical data collected using experimental methods to the phonological theory. In particular, her current phonology project investigates how the phonotactic differences between Mandarin and English may have a distance effect on the application of tone sandhi in speech production of Mandarin native speakers code-switching between the two languages. Before coming to Harvard, Wei-Fang received her M.A. in Linguistics and B.A. in Foreign Languages and Literatures from National Chiao Tung University, Taiwan.

He is working on the project "Harnessing machine learning to understand change in social attitudes" with PhD students Benedek Kurdi and Tessa Charlesworth in Professor Mahzarin R. Banaji's lab. Victor is interested in conducting research at the intersection of computer science and other fields. Outside of research, he is a co-president of Harvard's Engineers Without Borders chapter.

item.title: Valerie O'Kane
item.description:
Valerie O'Kane

Director of Business Operations
email valerie_okane@harvard.edu
  • Linkedin

Valerie O’Kane is the Director of Business Operations at the Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS) at Harvard University with responsibility for the IQSS budget & long term planning, IQSS contract and grant administration, IQSS compliance & space, as well as managing the general day-to-day operations of the IQSS Business Office.

Valerie is a seasoned financial professional who began her career at Harvard in 1992 as a staff assistant in the Central Payroll Office. In 1994 she moved to the FAS Extension School as the Payroll Administrator/Assistant Human Resource Officer. Valerie returned to Harvard Central Administration in 2002 as an accounting assistant and in 2004 became one of two payroll accountants for the University. Valerie was recognized as a Harvard Hero in 2005 as part of the University’s W2 Team. In 2007 she moved to the Harvard Kennedy School as the Financial Manager of the Malcolm Wiener Center for Social Policy. Valerie joined the Harvard College Observatory in 2018 as the Assistant Director of Finance and Administration. Valerie stepped in as the Interim Executive Director of the HCO for 1 year (2021-2022) and in 2023 was promoted to the Associate Director of Finance and Administration & Chief Financial Officer.

Valerie has received her Masters in Business Management from Harvard - Division of Continuing as well as two Harvard Graduate Certificates in Strategic Management & Business Communication. She received her Bachelors of Science and Business Administration from Suffolk University and her Associate Degree from Bay State College - Boston.

item.title: Tyler VanderWeele
item.description:
Tyler VanderWeele

John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology, Harvard School of Public Health
Director of the Human Flourishing Program
email tvanderw@hsph.harvard.edu
laptop_windows Profile (Human Flourishing Program)

Tyler J. VanderWeele is the John L. Loeb and Frances Lehman Loeb Professor of Epidemiology in the Departments of Epidemiology and Biostatistics at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, and director of the Human Flourishing Program and co-director of the Initiative on Health, Religion and Spirituality at Harvard University. He holds degrees from the University of Oxford, University of Pennsylvania, and Harvard University in mathematics, philosophy, theology, finance, and biostatistics. His methodological research is focused on theory and methods for distinguishing between association and causation in the biomedical and social sciences and, more recently, on psychosocial measurement theory. His empirical research spans psychiatric and social epidemiology; the science of happiness and flourishing; and the study of religion and health. He is the recipient of the 2017 Presidents’ Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies (COPSS). He has published over three hundred papers in peer-reviewed journals; is author of the books Explanation in Causal Inference (2015), Modern Epidemiology (2021), and Measuring Well-Being (2021); and he also writes a monthly blog posting on topics related to human flourishing for Psychology Today.

item.title: Torben Iversen
item.description:
Torben Iversen

Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy, Department of Government
location_on CGIS Knafel K308
email iversen@fas.harvard.edu
laptop_windows Website

Torben Iversen is Harold Hitchings Burbank Professor of Political Economy in the Government Department at Harvard University. His research and teaching interests include comparative political economy, electoral politics, and applied formal theory. He is the author or co-author of Big Data and the Welfare State: How the Information Revolution Threatens Social Solidarity (Cambridge UP 2022) (with Philipp Rehm), Democracy and Prosperity: Reinventing Capitalism through a Turbulent Century (Princeton UP 2019) (with David Soskice), Women, Work, and Politics: The Political Economy of Gender Inequality (Yale UP 2010) (with Frances Rosenbluth), Capitalism, Democracy, and Welfare (Cambridge UP 2005), and Contested Economic Institutions (Cambridge UP 1999). He is also the author or co-author of more than four dozen articles on comparative politics and political economy. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has been a Radcliffe Fellow, a Guggenheim Fellow, a Hoover National Fellow, and a BP Centennial Professor at the London School of Economics.

item.title: Thierry Warin
item.description:
Thierry Warin

Visiting Scholar, Digital Data Design (D^3) Institute
email thierry.warin@mail.analytics.hbs.edu
laptop_windows Website
laptop_windows LinkedIn

A Visiting Scholar at the Digital Data Design (D^3) Institute, Thierry Warin is an academic whose professional pursuits are deeply rooted in the application of data science methodologies to explore global transformations, including phenomena such as the platform economy and the dynamics of innovation. His research is characterized by the examination of institutions, economic dynamics, and the utilization of unstructured data to uncover insights into these complex areas. 
Warin places a high value on democratizing access to the burgeoning field of data science, viewing it as a pivotal step toward collaboratively addressing global challenges. His approach to research is fundamentally inductive, prioritizing a bottom-up methodology that is deeply rooted in data. This perspective not only enriches empirical understanding across various domains but also serves as a robust framework for testing, refining, and potentially redefining theoretical constructs and traditional economic indicators.
